#### The Organizing Society: 

##### GDMB Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology 

The GDMB is a non-profit organization. Its activities focus on combining science with practical experience in the fields of mining, engineering, tunnelling, mineral processing, extraction, recycling and refining of metals, as well as on the manufacturing of semi and finished products. There is an increasing emphasis on associated environmental issues. The GDMB is internationally active with a European basis and covers a wide variety of topics from applied geology via processing to recycling. These include many important areas of chemistry, especially the complex metallurgical chemistry and, last not least, also analytical chemistry. As a consequence of their increasing importance, aspects of industrial minerals are addressed in addition to the traditional fields of metals and alloys. In order to remain a vibrant and attractive professional society, the GDMB draws on the experience and interests of its worldwide members.

#### Preface 

###### Copper – Indicator of the progress of civilization 

This is the motto for the 7<sup>th</sup> international copper conference, the most important copper seminar in the world, which has been organized by the GDMB, the German based Society for Mining, Metallurgy, Resource and Environmental Technology, together with IIMCh from Chile, MetSoc from Canada, TMS, SME from USA and MMIJ from Japan. 

The copper conferences bring together the highest level of science and technology: universities, metal producers, manufacturing companies, suppliers and finally the people who work with copper: scientists, technicians, engineers, traders and many more. 

An extensive programme has been arranged for this conference and an abundance of contributions from all over the world dealing with the different aspects of copper making and its use are registered already, for which we gratefully thank the authors. Apart from plenary addresses, separate sessions will be held for economics, mineral processing, pyrometallurgy, hydrometallurgy, electrowinning and -refining, downstream fabrication and application, process control and automation, recycling and sustainable development, environmental control, health and safety. Copper, one of the oldest metals used by mankind, is still today one of the most important industrial metals and indispensable for modern life. It is the indicator of industrialization and progress in every country. It is used everywhere, where electricity flows and thus is still valued so highly today. The increased economic potential of newly industrialized countries, above all East Asia and China, has increased the significance of the red metal once again. More recent technologies in production, processing and application often provide new answers to old questions. From the middle of the last century there was another innovation surge resulting in totally new technologies, a trend still going on. This has made each copper conference into an exciting adventure. It is positive and reassuring that particularly the high industrialized countries have become the vanguard, not just in technical innovation, but also protection of environment and nature and preserving resources. They repeatedly prove that ecology and economy may go hand in hand. 

Many sponsors have contributed to the conference’s success, for which I would like to express my sincere thanks! 

Hamburg is expecting its guests! Hamburg, the old Hanseatic city with a 1200 year long tradition, one of the biggest and most beautiful cities in Germany, combines a wonderful mixture of industry, commerce, nature and culture. Not only the “Copper 2010” in the Congress Centre awaits you, but rich offeri

ngs of sightseeing and shopping in a cosmopolitan city, one of the largest harbours in Europe, the Alster lake in the city centre, green parks and plenty of cultural events, some of which we hope to show you in the companions programme. 

We are delighted that you will join us and look forward to a highly interesting conference! 

_Michael Kopke_ Chairman Copper 2010

#### Plenary Lectures (Abstracts) 

Some of the full papers will be published in Volume 7 of the Proceedings of Copper 2010 and in World of Metallurgy – ERZMETALL. 

###### Is the Copper Industry Fit for the Future? 

Dr.-Ing. Bernd Drouven, CEO, Aurubis AG, Hamburg, Germany 

The copper world has already changed a great deal during recent years. But what still lies ahead of us? What are the changes in conditions that we have to cope with and how will our solutions look? 

The rise in the demand for raw materials is unrelenting. At the same time, both the primary and secondary feed materials have a specific complexity, the customers’ needs are becoming increasingly differentiated and their orders are placed at increasingly short notice. Production times for metals have to be faster and inventories minimised. 

The volatility of the metal prices has increased significantly in recent years and we will probably have to live with that in the future as well. The LME functioned well in the crisis, but the copper price is being influenced more and more by funds. 

How can the value added chain change to adapt to this? Which consequences will that have for process technology, production planning and logistics? How will the consolidation of our industry continue? 

This keynote will go into the various effects and challenges – in particular from the perspective of a European custom smelter and fabricator – and present possible approaches for solutions. 

###### Sustainable Growth Strategy for Japanese Copper Business 

Toshinori Kato, Managing Director, Mitsubishi Materials Corporation, Tokyo, Japan 

Business environment, for any industry, has changed dramatically over the last decade. Copper industry is no exception and those involved are experiencing an unprecedented period of upheaval. The landscape of the market has completely altered, with large-scale M&As taking place among miners - creating an oligopoly situation - and a rapid expansion of smelting capacity within d

eveloping countries, driven by strong economic growth. Traditional copper smelters and fabricators have been facing challenges, but a long-term sustainability of Japanese copper business is achievable. 

Firstly, an immense amount of effort has been made over the years to develop the clean and one of the most environmentally-friendly processes in the industry. Mitsubishi Materials (MMC) particularly plays a great role in establishing Japanese smelters’ reputation as the most energy-efficient operations in the world. It is our strong commitment to be a leader in this expertise by sharing our technologies with the industry. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

IX 



Secondly, infrastructures for copper smelting have been utilized in developing the recycling business. Exemplified by the operations at Onahama smelter, which has the world’s largest furnace for treatment of shredder residue, the industry has worked closely with other sectors and municipalities. Building an effective structure to make the best use of our facilities is a key for success in this field. It is fair to say that Japanese copper smelters, including MMC, are now regarded as an indispensable part of national environmental policy. 

Finally, progression of integration in the copper fabrication sector has strengthened the industry’s capability of providing a variety of high-value-added products to end-users. Tight relationships with the consumers have been beneficial in developing new use of copper. Evidence of a promising future can be seen in increasing use of copper in the growing sectors such as hybrid automobiles and renewable energy. 

###### Copper Sulphide Smelting: Past Achievements and Current Challenges 

Dr. Carlos M. Dнaz, Adjunct Professor, University of Toronto, Private Consultant, Toronto, Canada 

In the last three decades, increased oxygen consumption in copper sulphide smelting and converting and the implementation of computerized process control, among other factors, have led to higher process intensity and smelter concentrate processing capacity, decreased smelting energy consumption and improved SO2 capture from process gas streams. An annual primary smelting furnace throughput of one million tonnes of concentrate is the new industry standard. Top submerged lance smelting has become an important processing route in recent years. Two new continuous converting routes were commercialized in the 1990s. However, due to substantially improved converting practice and larger converters, Peirce-Smith converting still maintains its position as the dominant technology. 

A major realignment of world copper smelting has taken place in the last 30 years. Spurred by rapid economic expansion and the resulting huge increase in demand for basic materials, a number of modern, large capacity copper smelters have been built in China, India and other Asian countries. Only moderate growth in smelting and electrorefining capacity has taken place elsewhere. Moreover, ER cathode output

in the USA has substantially decreased. 

In this paper, the author examines recent technological advances and industry changes and highlights issues, such as energy consumption and the corresponding greenhouse gas emissions that will become the focus of future discussion. 

###### Energy as a Key Factor of Sustainability 

Javier Targhetta, Vice President, Freeport McMoRan, Phoenix, Arizona, USA 

Energy must be seen as the prime mover for development and is therefore vital for economic equilibrium and social welfare. Energy will continue to play a key role in the coming decades being not only an environmental challenge but also a fundamental issue in terms of the progress of humanity. Nevertheless, harmonizing several aspects related to energy management will be of essence for the 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

X 



near future and will make energy one of the greatest challenges of the 21<sup>st</sup> century. It is becoming increasingly important to maintain the appropriate equilibrium between environmental issues (global warming, the future of nuclear waste, the integration of renewable energies…), coordinated governments policies to ensure that global energy costs are kept competitive and companies finding a balanced, rational and fair model of energy utilization based on the review of ethical business aspects and the establishment of social responsibility principles. 

This paper develops the idea that the rules and procedures for future energy use must be based on a reasonable equilibrium between technical aspects mainly associated to environmental issues, political decisions made by governments and public administrations and social responsibility programmes that companies themselves must assume and implement. 

###### <mark>The Supply and Copper Producer Response to a Growing Demand Scenario</mark> 

Ricardo Alvarez, General Manager, Codelco El Teniente Division, Santiago, Chile 

<mark>The prospects for medium and long-term consumption of copper are promising. A recovery projected for developed economies, starting 2010, joins the growing impact on demand generated from the process of development and urbanization of emerging countries. The intensity of copper use will also maintain the positive growth started a decade ago based on factors such as providing solutions to combat global warming.</mark> 

<mark>The objective of this presentation is to analyze how supply may react and adjust to envisaged demand scenarios, bearing in mind some distinctive elements of the copper industry like:</mark> 

- <mark>Historical supply reaction to demand and price levels</mark> 

- <mark>Availability of resources and copper ore reserves, incorporating a dynamic analysis and the effects of geological exploration and possible technological changes.</mark> 

- <mark>Pipeline of probable and possible projects, analysing the effects of projects in less developed and riskier geographical locations</mark> 

- Technological changes under development that may

positively impact the amount of reserves available and the competitiveness of projects. - The growing role of scrap as a supply source for copper. The analysis of these points will allow us to confirm the capability of supply response to growing demand, ruling out revisited hypothesis of insufficient reserves ###### Implementation of Recent Global Copper Projects Tim J. A. Smith, Vice President, Copper, SNC-Lavalin UK Limited, Croydon, Surrey, UK Despite the recent global recession, a relatively strong copper price combined with continuing supply shortfalls continues to drive the implementation of a number of important new worldwide copper projects. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ XI Along with base metals projects in general, the scale and complexity of such projects has increased such that multibillion dollar projects are increasingly common. Together with expansion projects in the older traditional copper producing regions, new geographic areas are still being opened up. These frequently require major infrastructural development, environmental and global procurement capabilities as major components of such projects. ### Sulphide Bath Smelting: 19<sup>th</sup> Century Concept and Hollway’s Legacy 

P. J. Mackey Xstrata Process Support 6 Edison Road Falconbridge, Canada ON P0M 1S0 

A. E. Wraith 

86 Queens Road Exeter, UK EX2 9EW 

**Keywords:** Bath smelting, pyritic ores, matte converting, pilot trials, historic R+D 

#### Abstract 

Carbon, first as charcoal in ancient times and more recently as coke or coal, was thought indispensable as a fuel and reductant in primary copper smelting. But in 1878, Hollway discovered that, with sufficient oxygen, pyritic copper ores could be smelted to matte in a molten sulphide pool sustained only by the heat of combustion of the iron pyrites in the ore. Although apparently orespecific and therefore of limited interest, this discovery is now recognised as the vital precursor of modern bath smelting technology because, for the first time, it showed two things: that copper sulphide smelting could be achieved in a molten sulphide pool oxidised by tuyere injection, and that no additional fuel was necessary if the oxidation rate were high enough and the feed material contained sufficient sulphur as fuel. Hollway’s novel solution to the problem of obtaining sufficient blowing rate for heat generation to make matte was to use a Bessemer converter, concurrent with but probably independent of the development of the Manhes converter. This paper examines the experimental, theoretical and technological background to Hollway’s pioneering discovery and discusses its halting historical development in the context of current bath smelting practice. 

#### 1 Introduction 

From the beginnings of metallurgical history, copper smelting flourished by the use of carbon as both fuel and reductant [1]. The earliest copper ores were rich oxides smelted directly with charcoal to metal, requiring little or no flux. Over time, techniques gradually evolved to treat less pure ores and, ultimately, sulphide ores containing iron. Thus matte processing and the formulation and recovery of ferruginous slags emerged as integral elements of copper extraction. 

By the 1870s, copper pyrometallurgy centred around two distinct primary technologies: (i) blast furnace smelting of mixed, often roasted, copper ores in a wide range of copper contents, which was predominantly used in Europe [2], and (ii) reverberatory smelting of relatively rich ores, of which 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

945 

_Mackey, Wraith_ 



the most familiar ex

ample was the Welsh process, which predominanted in Britain [2, 3]. Every step of both process routes required the extensive use of carbon based fuels, either coke or coal. 

Meanwhile, the demands of a burgeoning chemical industry required increasing supplies of sulphuric acid, the sulphur dioxide for which was made by burning sulphur or high grade iron pyrites. Most pyrites sources suitable for acid making contained copper, and ‘spent’ pyrites became a feed material for copper recovery [4]. But cupriferous pyritic ores were also recognised as useful copper ores _per se_ and, although containing only 1.5 to 4 % copper, were roasted in the open and either directly smelted to matte with coke in a blast furnace [2] or, as in southern Spain, leached with subsequent copper recovery by cementation [5]. The cost of coke for smelting and iron for cementation were significant factors in production but, in addition, the environmental impact of the incessant SO2 emission to atmosphere from open-air heap-roasting was increasingly objectionable and litigious. Based on information reported by Salkield [5], the Rio Tinto Company roasted about 300,000 tons (~300,000 metric tonnes) of pyrites annually in the early 1880s. Moreover, the potentially valuable sulphur was irrecoverable. The time appeared ripe to examine alternative smelting methods that would recover the copper _and_ capture the sulphur in saleable form. 

In another arena, the mid-19<sup>th</sup> century saw the revolution in steelmaking brought about by Bessemer’s invention of pneumatic refining for blast furnace iron in an air-blown converter [6]. Provided that the oxidation rate was high enough, heat generated by the preferential oxidation of the dissolved carbon and silicon in the iron was sufficient both to meet the increasing liquidus temperature as carbon was removed and to negate the external heat loss and the cooling effect of nitrogen in the injected air. The realization that a high oxidation rate was essential to sustain a favourable heat balance in melt refining was key. Could the Bessemer principle be applied to generate process heat by the rapid oxidation of iron and sulphur in a bath of molten pyrites – literally, to use the iron and sulphur content of the melt as fuel? 

In the late 1870s, John Hollway investigated this possibility in a remarkable series of experiments at laboratory and process scale which ultimately demonstrated that matte could be produced continuously from cupriferous pyrite without additional fuel [7]. From this beginning, interest in the Hollway process for pyritic bath smelting flourished briefly, only to be overtaken in the mid-late 1890s by the arrival of sulphide concentrates and the fuel-fired reverberatory smelting furnace. More than eighty years were to elapse after Hollway’s pioneering experiments before bath smelting by submerged gas injection was ‘rediscovered’. 

The present paper examines Hollway’s work in light of its role as the precursor of modern

bath smelting and considers the significance of contemporary Bessemer converter practices in its development. The more recent manifestations of bath smelting are likewise examined in relation to Hollway’s pioneering work. A companion paper in preparation by the present authors extends this analysis using modern thermodynamic modelling tools to further examine Hollway’s results [8].

#### 2 Concept of the Molten Sulphide Bath 

The results of a remarkable programme of laboratory and pilot plant scale experiments extending over a period of twelve months were first reported by John Hollway in 1879 [7]. Having understood the weak heating conditions of heap roasting, he began by calculating the theoretical temperature produced by the combustion of the relevant sulphides in air. The estimated flame temperatures ranged from 1863 °C for PbS to 2225 °C for FeS; these temperatures were found to be somewhat lower than that estimated for pig iron (2748 °C) or 2787 °C for coal. The results however suggested to him “that the oxidation of sulphides would produce sufficient heat to render their smelting a selfsupporting operation”. He made no comment on the fundamental role of the _rate_ of heat generation yet it was clear that he had grasped its importance because he hit upon the idea that if air were injected rapidly enough into a _molten_ sulphide, “the maximum temperature of the combustion is attained, because all the oxygen of the air driven in is then utilized for oxidation”. 

Hollway’s assertion that a sulphide bath could be sustained in the molten state by the heat of its own oxidation appeared theoretically sound, but the presumption that there would be heat enough to melt added solids and to produce a medium grade of copper matte was unprecedented. The experimental programme was intended to prove the feasibility of this proposition; today the programme and its unexpected process outcomes will be recognised as an ambitious R+D project that was ahead of its time. 

##### 2.1 Testing the Idea 

It was essential to confirm the initial calculations. Three sequences of formative experiments “to simulate the oxidation of liquid sulphides” were therefore carried out in April 1878. 

1. Using a muffle furnace for heating and porcelain or fireclay lances (“tuyeres”) for gas injection, oxygen from a gas cylinder was: 

- (i) jetted on to the surface of a molten pool formed by melting FeS2 in a small fireclay crucible, producing “an intense incandescence with a violet light”; 

(ii) injected directly into the melt. Visible heating occurred and the FeO formed in the bath attacked the fireclay. The bath “soon became viscous” due to lack of silica to form a fusible slag. 

2. Spurred on by these remarkable results, the crucible experiments were repeated on a larger scale in a steel melting furnace with molten charges of cupriferous pyrite con

taining ~3 % Cu, now oxidized only by air injected through a submerged lance. Sand was added to help form a ferrous silicate slag. At the first attempt, thirty minutes’ blowing produced a silicate slag containing 0.104 % Cu and a low grade matte or ‘regulus’ which separated very distinctly from the overlying slag. It was reported that about half the iron was oxidized to form the slag. Based on this, it can be estimated that the remaining matte would have been fairly low grade at about 20 % Cu.

3. In similar crucible experiments, additions of cold pyrites were successfully melted, “showing that pyrites could be melted by the heat evolved by its own oxidation”. 

Hollway’s initial though rather limited thermodynamic analysis was vindicated. Moreover, in one simple experimental sequence, he had introduced three key ideas: 

- The concept of adding silica to flux iron when blowing a sulphide bath, 

- Effective phase separation is vital in this highly agitated system, 

- Bath smelting to matte was possible. 

#### 3 Industrial Scale Trials 

Although Hollway is not forthcoming with too many details about the funding for his work, the Rio Tinto Company was evidently involved [7]. The objective may have been to recover copper more profitably than hitherto from the company’s extensive deposits of low grade cupriferous pyrite in southern Spain. However, the Hollway process as described [7] offered the further possibility of producing elemental sulphur and rich SO2 gas as by-products, leading to the desirable prospect of reduced sulphur loss to atmosphere. The company profitably supplied pyrite to the sulphuric acid industry: offering sulphur in an alternative form, as elemental sulphur or as sulphur dioxide, therefore had commercial potential. 

##### 3.1 Bessemer Converter Trials 

The crucible experiments had shown that more heat was needed to make matte effectively. This would require a higher blowing rate than was possible in the lance-crucible set-up. In order to get it, the momentous decision was made to scale up the experiments by transferring the work to a 6 ton Bessemer converter. A programme of Bessemer experiments was initiated at the steel works of Cammell and Co. in Penistone, 18 km north west of Sheffield in early July 1878, eight or nine weeks after the final crucible experiments. Four sets of experimental trials were attempted, Trials 1 and 2 in July 1878, Trial 3 in October-November 1878 and Trial 4 in February 1879. The test set-up and conditions were as follows:

##### 3.2 Cupola Trials of Continuous Smelting while Blowing 

Attention now turned to finding a means to capture the elemental sulphur. The major component of the ore feed, pyrites, was thought to dissociate on fusion to form elemental sulphur, FeS2 → FeS (bath) + S(g)↑ (1) 

which occurred in the cupola when melting the pyrite charge. In Trial 3, the labile sulphur of cold charge added directly to the bath reportedly burned at the converter mouth, whereas SO2 generated within the bath by the oxidation of FeS to FeO passed directly to atmosphere, diluted by the nitrogen in the blast. The atmospheric fume at the Penistone works must have been spectacular. 

A new, original design of smelting unit was commissioned at a steel works of John Brown and Co. in Sheffield (believed to have been located at Carbrook, Sheffield) based essentially upon an existing speigeleisen cupola, with two objectives: 

- (i) To divert, condense and recover elemental sulphur in the absence of oxygen, and 

- (ii) To operate the smelting bath continuously: this would entail continuous blowing, direct solids additions essentially in a continuous fashion when and as required, provision for phase separation, and the ability to tap matte and slag when necessary during blowing. 

The cupola was modified as follows: 

- The normal tuyeres were replaced by three Bessemer tuyere blocks, each with 13 holes 5/16 in (~8 mm) bore set horizontally, and presumably symmetrically, in the wall of the bosh in a plane some small distance above the hearth. 

- A closed forehearth was constructed with a connection through the bosh wall to receive slag and matte in order to create quiescent conditions for matte-slag separation, and from which they could be tapped intermittently without interrupting the smelting process. Two tapholes were provided, an upper in the bosh wall well above the tuyeres for slag, a lower in the forehearth for matte. 

- An off-take flue for sulphur vapour was connected to two, later three, neighbouring cupolas in order to divert and condense the labile sulphur and other volatiles. 

This novel configuration took the process into uncharted territory. The ‘converter’ was now the fixed cupola hearth, with horizontal tuyeres apparently positioned to allow injection into the middle pyrite layer of a three-layer bath, clear of the matte layer below and the slag above. In addition, two new, untested elements had entered the process: continuous sulphur condensation in an atmosphere

1<sup>st</sup> Cupola Trial (27 March 1879): The cupola, preheated with coke, was charged initially with an ore-coke mixture to produce a molten sulphide bath. After an hour or so the coke was stopped and charging continued with ore and sandstone in the ratio 5:1. The pyritic ore co

ntained 1.7 % Cu. The furnace temperature rose and slag began to flow, rapidly at first and then torrentially, out of the furnace. The furnace contents were finally completely ejected and the bath disappeared, bringing the process to a halt. 5-6 tons of ore had been treated. A small amount of lean matte, 7 % Cu, was tapped from the fore hearth. In hindsight, Hollway’s review comments [10] on the disappointing results of this first trial can be interpreted as: 

(i) uncertainties about controlling the rate and state of oxidation in the sulphide bath, 

(ii) lack of knowledge on the role of furnace and burden geometry, and 

(iii) a need to understand the relationships between feed rate, feed composition 

(particularly in terms of ore-flux ratio) and blowing rate. 

2<sup>nd</sup> Cupola Trial (8 April 1879): A larger, modified cupola with a self-closing hopper charging arrangement, an enlarged fore hearth and three spray cooled condenser cupolas was then brought into use, intended mainly to show that solid sulphur could be collected. The cupola was preheated but no coke was used with the initial charge. Charging at a rate of up to 3 tons per hour of the oresandstone mix continued for three hours, increasing in the last hour. But the trial concluded much as before. A rapid and complete ejection of the overheated furnace contents occurred. Blockage by condensed volatiles that caused pressure to build up in the smelting cupola was thought to have been responsible. Much sulphur was lost as burning vapour from the slag tap hole and through the brickwork. When cool, only about 1 ton of condensed sulphur was recovered, a fraction of the total evolved. 

Subsequently, three more trials were attempted with the enlarged cupola. By an unfortunate combination of mishaps, two were inconclusive and the third, which had proceeded satisfactorily, came to an abrupt end when matte broke out from the cupola hearth. This final experiment was concluded on the morning of 2 May 1879. These disappointing results were presented by Hollway at a meeting in London the same evening [10]. He admitted that undue haste had been a factor in their lack of success. So ended a remarkable smelting project. 

#### 4 Contemporary Outcomes 

Apparently undaunted by his ultimate lack of success, Hollway published a summarized account of his process in July 1879 [11] that envisioned new applications and, in particular, reiterated the potential of the process for copper extraction. He claimed that in batchwise Bessemer operation, matte which had been converted to white metal could be further converted in the same operation to

##### 4.1 Sulphur Recovery 

Hollway showed that his process could increase the profit on copper [7] while also mitigating the environmental sulphur hazard, and that the sulphur previously wasted by roasting could yield income. But the sulphur produced by condensation in the cupola trials was difficult to capture and of poor quality due to contamination by volatiles such as As (anathema to the acid makers) and by slag carry-over [14]. A significant element of the perceived process benefits was therefore found wanting, a factor which must have contributed to the withdrawal of funding. However, Hollway made a startling and original proposal that SO2 produced in the bath by the tuyere-oxidation of iron (and copper) sulphides might profitably be diverted directly to an acid plant – the chamber process in use at that time. Analyses of off-gases during the Penistone converter trials showed up to 11 % SO2 in nitrogen [7], a productive gas strength and a portent of things to come. Incidentally, he also suggested SO2 liquefaction as a viable means of sulphur capture. 

##### 4.2 Process Development 

The progression of Hollway’s project from concept through analysis to laboratory scale, to piloting and finally to an industrial scale trial is a classic example of process development familiar in R and D practice today. It is easy with hindsight to see what might have been done better, and it also easy to recognise present-day constraints – tight deadlines (the Doetsch hydrometallurgical process [5] was looming ), the need to quickly acquire and adapt operating experience, shortfalls in engineering know-how, and the pressure of working near the edge of knowledge. If anything, it also showed the need for a certain degree of ‘stamina’ and a ‘long view’ in process development, as highlighted by Tarassoff [15] for example in reviewing the early development of the Noranda Process, and in the early Outokumpu flash smelting work [16]. Nevertheless, it is important to realize that unique operating practices had to be devised and perfected for the Bessemer trials at Penistone, practices new to Bessemer steelmaking which became conventions for all subsequent copper converter operations. Examples include intermittent vessel turn down for slag skimming and charge addition, the recognition of end points and the value of flame observation as an indicator of bath condition. Nor should it be forgotten that Hollway highlighted the role of Bessemerizing in minor element elimination.

Careful consideration by the present authors of the fuel cost estimated for this design indicates that it would consume about 12 t coal/t of copper. The Hollway process thus showed potentially important coal savings, a point made by several contributors to the discussion of the paper [7]. 

From costing data given by Hollway, the net operating return on this plant was indicated as 11 s/ton (£0.55/ton), compared with only 1 s 9 pence (£0.0875) for copper production via the conventional route of open air roasting, leaching and cementation. problematic. Rio Tinto appears not to have been persuaded, and though evidently tested briefly at Rio Tinto [5, 17] a commercial plant was never built. A smelter based on Hollway’s ideas was however erected, according to Collins [17], to treat Maidenpec ore in the former Serbia in 1884, but was apparently later abandoned. It is not clear if that plant ran for a period before closing. In contrast, it is interesting to note that by the 1930s a number of processes utilizing a reductant for sulphur production from smelter off-gases had been developed; the Orkla process developed by Orkla Grube Aktiebolag of Norway operated perhaps the longest before eventually closing [18]. Interestingly, one such plant was also installed at Rio Tinto in 1930 and operated for a number of decades [18]. 

Hollway’s patent [19] states three objectives: 

- (i) “to obtain sulphur in the form of free crude sulphur and sulphurous acid (i.e. SO2) or sulphuretted hydrogen (H2S), copper and other metals at one and the same operation”; 

- (ii) “to reduce the cost of the treatment by availing my

self (sic) of certain properties of the sulphides and utilizing them in lieu of the usual carbonaceous fuel . . .”, and 

(iii) “. . . utilizing the gases and vapours”. 

Clearly (i) and (iii) are complementary to the contemporary trade in pyrites for acid making (incidentally reducing the sulphur loss and environmental nuisance of heap roasting), but the key commercial interest that emerged was to recover copper. This is evident from similar autogenoustype applications elsewhere e.g. Mt Lyell and Cobar, Australia, and Toston, Montana up to about 1896, as indicated by Collins [17], Douglas [20] and Gowland [21], and also at other locations [22]. However, the process as originally conceived and designed by Hollway was evidently not widely adopted for copper extraction despite the acclaim it received, and had fallen into disuse by the mid1890s. 

In reality, production conditions for copper were changing, primarily due to the rapid growth in flotation treatment for low grade ores and the associated expansion of smelting in fuel fired reverberatory furnaces. Thus the remarkable Hollway concept of smelting in a molten sulphide bath was overtaken by a new technological and economic vision and lay dormant for more than half a century. The large reverberatory furnace treating copper concentrates or calcine thus held sway until about the beginning of the 1960s when Holloway’s idea for near-autogenous smelting re-surfaced under new names and technologies, essentially to meet, curiously enough, very similar challenges to those faced during Hollway’s time – energy efficiency and the need to contain emitted sulphur dioxide. And change inevitably continued so that by the early 2000s almost all traditional reverberatory furnaces around the world had closed. 

Hollway taught that utilizing sulphur in the feed as a fuel, charging and blowing while being able to tap the products, and using horizontal tuyeres in converters, were both feasible and effective. They remain in practice to this day.

#### 5 Into the Future and Hollway’s Legacy 

Although Hollway was not the first to see the possibility of Bessemerising for copper (note, for example, a number of references cited by Douglas [20] and Hofman [22]), he was ahead of his time in making it work, and in coupling theoretical back-up with practical application. The side-blowing of a sulphide bath is considered an outstanding development, apparently later ‘re-invented’ by Manhes, who must have known about Hollway, but the latter was never acknowledged. 

Was the continuous Hollway process too revolutionary an idea? Was it ‘ahead of its time’, or was the timing just not right? His process ideas essentially outstripped contemporary engineering expertise. He endeavoured to combine several distinct process steps into one continuous operation, but probably attempted too much in doing so, blinkered to a degree by the contemporary sulphur question. The industry wo

uld need to wait 60 years to see the sulphide bath smelting concept reemerge. 

Capitalizing on earlier flash smelting research, Outokumpu in 1949 [16] with pre-heated air – incidentally as proposed by Hollway – and Inco independently in 1952 [23] with tonnage oxygen, launched modern flash smelting “. . . by which sulphides are utilized for fuel”. A little over a decade later, Noranda [15] pioneered continuous bath smelting and converting, followed by El Teniente [24] and then Sirosmelt [25], the first of the modern top lancing systems now typified by the Ausmelt and Isasmelt technologies. These changes were timely and the technologies were economically attractive. Yet each new system had fresh components that made it feasible – including tapping while feeding and blowing (as pioneered by Hollway), effective methods of feeding large tonnages (such as the slinger, concentrate injection, flash burners and the like), together with matte grade control, effective slag treatment methods, durable refractories and finally, effective off-gas handling and acid plant operation. John Hollway, that courageous innovator, would have been mightily impressed!

#### Abstract 

The paper describes the ongoing innovation by Hatch with our smelting partners around the world to meet the challenges of copper smelting and converting in increasingly intensive processes. Recent developments and ongoing improvements have improved safety, extended furnace campaign lives and improved furnace integrity. Recent innovations applied in other smelting industries, directly applicable to the copper smelting industry, are also discussed. 

Modern pyrometallurgical design for high intensity processes requires technical excellence in the thermal, structural, refractory and instrumentation and controls disciplines. Hatch has world-leading technologies in each of these areas presently at work in the copper smelting industry, and expertise in the integration of these technologies into both new and existing furnaces. 

Examples of modern technology in copper smelting and converting to extend furnace campaign life and improve furnace integrity are discussed. Hatch’s high intensity waffle cooling elements, along with an integrated hearth and wall structural binding system, significantly improved the integrity of a Kennecott - Outotec Flash Converting Furnace. This design is applicable to Outotec Flash Smelting Furnaces, Outotec Direct to Blister Flash Smelting Furnaces and Inco Flash Smelting Furnaces. Hatch cooling elements are also used in a Mitsubishi converting furnace. A third example is Hatch’s circular binding system together with Hatch cooling elements, in a top blown Ausmelt type converting furnace. This design is applicable to both Isasmelt and Ausmelt furnaces. 

The use of innovative technology to extend furnace campaign lives and improve furnace integrity also includes the use of modern taphole designs. These designs significantly increase safety and extend taphole service life, incorporating the latest monitoring technology. 

The paper demonstrates that these proven, but not yet widely adopted, technologies extend furnace campaign life and improve furnace integrity. These technologies can be gainfully employed on

#### 1 Introduction 

The increasing need for robust pyrometallurgical furnaces is driven by three objectives in the copper industry: 

- Reduced risk of slag and metal leaks and exposure of employees to hazardous situations. 

- Increased production within a single furnace line by increasing smelting intensities, resulting in economies of scale for minimum capital and operating expenses per pound of copper, but also resulting in higher heat fluxes to the furnace walls. 

- High percentage online times (high availability) and long campaign life between rebuilds, to maximize the amount of copper produced during the campaign. 

For many years Hatch has succeeded in developing and implementing technological improvements to furnace designs to achieve the above three goals. 

A key feature of furnaces capable of operating at high rates while containing intense processes is a strong, thermally robust wall cooling system [1]. Equally important design aspects include a closely integrated furnace structural binding system, refractory lining, cooling water supply system and instrumentation/controls for monitoring and rapid mitigation of process excursions [1, 2]. 

This paper discusses design improvements that have been implemented in copper furnaces by Hatch, and reviews other copper smelting and converting processes where similar design improvements could be implemented to enhance furnace campaign life, improve furnace integrity and reduce risk to operating employees. 

#### 2 Hatch technology used to improve furnace campaign life 

Hatch has developed numerous furnace cooling, structural and refractory technologies that are in use in many furnaces around the world. Hatch cooling technology began with “finger coolers” [3]. The purpose of these cooling elements is to increase the effective conductivity of the furnace wall and to thereby reliably freeze a layer of slag on the hot face of the furnace wall to protect the refractory from chemical attack and erosion by molten slag. These finger cooling elements are approximately 150 mm square or 150 mm diameter in cross-section, and penetrate about 400 mm into the furnace wall between the bricks. The cooling water passage is typically of drilled and plugged design and is located external to the furnace wall for maximum safety. With the relatively long distance between the hot face of the furnace wall in contact with the bath and the cooling water 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

972 

_Extending Copper Smelting and Converting Furnace Campaign Life_ 



external to the furnace, the cooling effect of these elements depends on the conductivity of the copper between the hot face and water passage. 

Plate coolers, horizontally installed copper plates approx 75 mm thick and 1.5 m long, are an evolution of finger cooling elements. The plates penetrate into the refractory wall similar to the fingers, but have a higher heat flux capacity due to the higher ratio of copper to brick in the furnace

wall. The plates are typically installed in layers, with two or three courses (layers) of brick between each layer of copper. Plates, by virtue of their larger size, also reduce and simplify the interconnecting piping between elements. The plates’ heat transfer capacity can be increased somewhat by casting in a pipe to form the water passage closer to the element hot-face, rather than relying on a drilled passage external to the furnace. Plate cooling elements are adequate for the moderate heat flux zones of furnaces, such as the upper freeboard walls and roofs, and for the slag bath zone of furnaces operating at moderate intensities. Slag cleaning furnaces are an application where plate cooling elements can provide satisfactory service at minimum cost. 

For modern, high intensity primary copper production furnaces, composite copper/refractory watercooled elements equipped with a high density of cooling water passages, typically formed by casting in pipe are used in the bath zone. These Hatch “waffle” type cooling elements have been successfully installed in many types of copper smelting and converting furnaces. As further described below, they have proven to greatly enhance furnace integrity and substantially increase furnace campaign life. This success is largely dependent on the integration of these high intensity cooling elements with a robust three-dimensional furnace structural binding system and refractory design. Associated technological improvements also include the use of innovative taphole designs, which significantly reduce risk by incorporating the latest monitoring technology. 

##### 2.1 Hatch “Waffle” cooling element design 

Hatch “waffle” type cooling elements are so named because of the refractory-filled, dovetailed grooves provided on the element hot face. The elements have closely spaced cooling water passages formed by cast-in piping, a judicious ratio of copper to refractory on the hot face, and optimum geometry for the specific copper furnace process. 

The refractory-filled grooves on the hot face, together with the copper fins between them provide a composite refractory/copper hot face. The grooves retain a residual refractory and/or a frozen slag layer reliably. Of equal importance, is the ability of the composite hot face formed by the groove refractory and surrounding copper to limit heat transfer into the elements, in case of direct contact between the element and liquid matte or metal. 

By using quantitative methods such as Finite Element Analysis (FEA) to select the optimum ratio of exposed copper to refractory-filled grooves on the waffle hot face, the element can reliably freeze and retain a layer of slag build-up, while also being able to withstand direct contact with reasonably superheated metal or matte. The groove refractory insulates the copper mass of the cooling element

from full exposure to the potentially hig

##### 3.1 BHP Billiton San Manuel Flash Smelting Furnace (FSF) 

The BHP Billiton Flash Smelting Furnace in San Manuel (previously Magma Copper Company) completed its first campaign in May 1999. The flash furnace campaign length of 10.75 years set a world record for the longest running furnace campaign without major repairs to sidewalls or hearth. However, the furnace experienced several matte break-outs at the matte/slag interface level from 1995 onwards; this was the primary reason for finally ending the campaign in 1999 [5]. 

By the middle of 1996, the increasing number of hot metal breakouts and the loss of settler side wall cooling elements convinced operations personnel that the furnace should be relined for safety considerations. In early 1997, a flash furnace risk assessment workshop was carried out and concluded that the Flash Smelting Furnace should be rebuilt as soon as possible.

Hatch was selected to redesign the Flash Smelting Furnace using upgraded technology with the following objectives: 

- The new furnace would be capable of smelting at least 20 % more concentrate than current feed rates, that is a feed rate of 200 tonnes/h or 4800 tonnes/day of new concentrate to the upgraded furnace. 

- The new cooling system must be extremely robust. 

- The new furnace would have an improved settler gas flow/velocity profile. 

To achieve these objectives, modifications made included the following: 

- The settler side wall cooling elements included the latest Hatch cooling element technology consisting of a hot face waffle design with cast-in Monel piping. 

- The new f

### High Intensity Cast Cooling Element Design and Fabrication Considerations 

K. McKenna, N. Voermann, R. Veenstra, C. Newman

#### Abstract 

Among the many developments in copper smelting one common theme has been a steady intensification of the smelting processes. With increasing process intensities (increasing production rate per unit of furnace volume or hearth area), the need for more intensive furnace wall cooling became apparent to extend campaign lives. Cast copper cooling elements are the most widely used technology for high intensity copper smelting furnaces [1]. To achieve the highest cooling capacities, water cooling passages have needed to move closer to the process interface, commonly referred to as the “hot face”. Cast-in pipe coils have become the dominant method of forming water passages in high intensity cooling elements. 

Many design features influence the effectiveness of cast cooling elements in achieving their purpose of containing the process reliably over a long furnace campaign life. These features include integration of refractory on the hot face, configuration of cooling water passages and spacing between them, leak tight connections between individual elements, and materials of construction for both the cooling element and the cast-in pipe forming the water passage(s). In selecting a cast-in pipe material, it is important to balance thermal design considerations, quality of fabrication practically and repeatedly achievable, and cost

. The wrought pipe materials typically used in furnace cooling elements are: stainless steel, copper-nickel alloys and copper pipes. The above design features and materials are further discussed in this paper.

#### 1 Introduction 

To handle the high thermal intensities of modern copper smelting processes such as flash smelting and flash converting, robust cooling element designs are required, especially in the slag bath zone of the furnace walls. For a furnace side wall to achieve a state of thermal equilibrium, the process heat flux (heat flow per unit area) must be removed by the cooling element. The objective at equilibrium is to freeze a stable layer of slag on the refractory hot face, to protect the refractory from further attack and erosion by liquid slag. The relationships outlined by Voermann et al. demonstrate that at a given process heat flux the stable equilibrium furnace side wall thickness is proportional to the effective conductivity of the wall and inversely proportional to the distance to the cooling fluid [2]. It is for this reason that copper with its relatively high conductivity is typically used as the material of construction for furnace cooling elements. 

Hatch furnace cooling technology began with “finger” cooling elements. Their purpose is to increase the effective conductivity of the furnace wall and thereby freeze a layer of slag on the hot face of the furnace wall to protect the refractory from chemical attack and erosion by molten slag. These finger cooling elements penetrate into the furnace wall between the bricks. The cooling water passage is typically drilled and plugged and is located external to the furnace wall for maximum safety. With the relatively long distance between the hot face of the furnace wall in contact with the bath and the cooling water external to the furnace, the cooling effect of these elements is limited, and depends on the conductivity of the copper between the hot face and water passage. 

Plate cooling elements – horizontally installed copper plates typically having the same thickness as that of the surrounding wall bricks – are an evolution of finger cooling elements. The plates penetrate into the refractory wall similar to the fingers, but have a higher heat flux capacity due to the higher ratio of copper to brick in the furnace wall. The plates are typically installed in layers, with two or three brick courses (layers of brick) between each layer of copper. The plates’ heat transfer capacity can be increased somewhat by casting in a pipe to form the water passage closer to the cooling element hot-face, rather than relying on a drilled passage external to the furnace. Plate cooling elements are adequate for moderate heat flux zones of furnaces, such as the upper freeboard walls and roofs, and for the slag bath zone of furnaces operating at relatively low intensities. Slag cleaning furnaces are an application

where plate cooling elements can often provide satisfactory service at minimum cost. 

For modern, high intensity copper primary production furnaces, composite copper/refractory watercooled elements with a high density of cooling water passages are typically used in the bath zone. These elements are oriented vertically and form a “wall” of copper around the furnace perimeter to reliably freeze slag on the hot face even under very high heat flux conditions. The water passages of these elements are usually formed by cast-in pipe. Hatch “waffle” type cooling elements of this design are successfully installed in many copper smelting and converting furnaces, including Outotec type flash smelting and converting furnaces, and Top Submerged Lance (TSL) furnaces.

#### 2 Design features of high intensity cooling elements 

In this section the essential design features of high intensity cooling elements will be discussed. 

##### 2.1 Composite copper/refractory hot face waffle cooling elements 

Refractory-filled, dovetailed grooves on the cooling element hot face are a key feature of Hatch’s high intensity furnace cooling elements. They are termed Hatch “waffle” type cooling elements because of the pattern formed by these grooves on the hot face of the cooling element. The refractory filled grooves together with the copper fins between them provide a composite refractory/copper hot face. 

These hot face grooves provide a carefully calculated ratio of copper to refractory on the hot face, and optimum geometry for the specific copper furnace process. The grooves retain even a thin residual refractory and/or a frozen slag layer reliably. In the composite copper/refractory cooling element hot face design there is sufficient exposed copper on the cooling element hot face to transfer even the very high heat fluxes from the slag bath of converting furnaces to the cooling water. Of equal importance is the ability of the composite hot face formed by the groove refractory and surrounding copper to limit heat transfer into the cooling elements, in case of direct contact between the cooling element and liquid matte or metal. Such matte or metal contact on the large exposed copper surface of a smooth-surfaced (un-grooved) cooling element hot face has often resulted in the failure of such elements due to the high, uninhibited heat flux into the element causing steam blanketing of the cooling element water passages. 

The composite copper/refractory hot face geometry is designed to have sufficient conductivity to reliably freeze a slag layer on the hot face, while simultaneously insulating the cooling element from the potentially overwhelming heat loa

ds generated by large scale matte or metal contact. 

##### 2.2 Overlapped vertical cooling element joints 

Where multiple courses (layers) of brick work would have been laid in bonded fashion in a low process intensity side wall, the cooling elements must be similarly joined together to prevent leaks. Hatch waffle cooling elements have overlapping joints that reliably seal the furnace from slag leaks. These joints provide a positive seal, yet are free to slide to enable relative movement between adjacent cooling elements to accommodate furnace thermal growth. Movement of the individual cooling elements is limited to ensure that there is always a seal present.

##### 2.3 Cooling element/refractory contact 

Due to the location of the cooling elements and their cooling passages in the furnace wall, it is necessary to integrate the cooling elements with the furnace binding system [3]. Not only must the cooling elements be designed to carry loads vertically in the side walls, they may also need to transfer binding loads inwardly onto the furnace refractory. 

Hatch patented wall hold-downs are spring-loaded devices that provide a downward vertical binding force to complement the horizontal binding forces provided by traditional furnace binding systems. This vertical binding force promotes good thermal contact between the cooling elements and bricks, and keeps horizontal brick joints tight and free of infiltration of liquid bath. 

##### 2.4 Cooling water passages formed by cast-in pipe versus drilled and plugged passages 

Even with the use of high conductivity copper, in today’s more intense copper cooling elements, the thickness of the copper between the cooling passage and the hot face must be minimized to keep cooling element tip temperatures cool enough for long term operation without oxidation of the copper. This has forced the designers of cooling elements to move the cooling fluid inside the shell of the furnace. The requirement to move the water cooling inside the shell of the furnace results in unacceptable risk with some of the low cost methods for fabricating copper cooling elements. Drilled or extruded passages require mechanical or welded plugs. These are prone to leaks, and with water passages close to the hot face such leaks occur inside the furnace where they are more difficult to detect. Such water leaks can result in brick hydration and/or a steam explosion. To counter this risk, Hatch has designed its high intensity waffle cooling elements with pipes cast into the copper. By casting the cooling pipes into the cooling blocks, there are no plugs or seals inside the furnace shell. Furthermore, there are two levels of safety against leaks; the cast-in pipe is welded and pressure tested prior to casting to ensure it is leak tight, and the copper casting itself is also carefully manufactured to be leak tight.

##### 2.7 Thermal performance 

The first and foremost factor to consider in the design of high intensity cooling elements is the required thermal performance. Given that the cooling element is cast from bulk copper with cast-in pipe cooling water passages, the cooling element’s thermal performance will be governed by the cast-in pipe material’s thermal conductivity and wall thickness, density (spacing) of cooling coils and the thickness and conductivity of the cast copper between the pipes and the hot face of the cooling element. 

It is widely recognized that the furnace process conditions will dictate the requirements for heat removal by the cooling elements in order to maintain a stable equilibrium condition in the furnace side walls [2-4]. The required thermal performance is therefore the process heat loads plus a margin for process upsets, start-up conditions and refractory/accretion spalling. These heat loads define thermal design criteria for the cooling elements. 

The two categories of potential failure that must be considered in cooling element design are: 

- Catastrophic failure, resulting in significant down time of the process equipment and potentially also harm to personnel. 

- Capacity limiting failure, where irreversible damage is done to the cooling element and the process must be throttled to reduce the heat load on the cooling element, or to repair the cooling element where reversible damage has occurred. 

###### 2.7.1 Catastrophic failure 

Catastrophic failure of the cooling element can be defined as a breach of the cooling coil resulting in introduction of water into the process. This often causes a steam explosion or structural failure of the cooling element, resulting in a run out of the furnace’s molten contents. 

Such failure typically occurs when the heat removal capacity of the cooling medium is overloaded. In water-cooled elements this condition is known as film blanketing. Film blanketing occurs when the steam generated at the surface of the cooling passage creates a physical thermal barrier separating the inside surface of the cooling pipe from the bulk cooling water flowing through the pipe. Under these conditions, the cooling pipe (and copper cooling element) temperatures will rise rapidly and the heat removal will plummet due to the dramatic reduction in the convection coefficient at the surface of the cooling passage. The heat forced into the cooling element by the process in this case is larger than the heat removed by the water, which results in rapid overheating and then melting of the cooling element.

Careful cooling element design and fabrication, as well as competent installation and operation, is essential to minimize the potential for such catastrophic cooling element failure, and consequent furnace failure. 

The heat transfer betwee

n the cooling water and the inside surface of the pipe is largely independent of the pipe material. The thermal conductivities of various pipe materials affect the distribution of heat into the water passages. More resistive pipe materials spread the heat load around the pipe circumference, and help to slightly delay the onset of steam blanketing as process heat flux increases. Steam blanketing is best avoided with adequate water velocity in the cooling passages. 

###### 2.7.2 Capacity limiting failure 

The design of the cooling element must ensure that a capacity limiting failure will not occur under the predicted thermal conditions. Sources of capacity limiting failures include scale build up in the cooling channels, oxidation of the copper hot face surface, and loss of one of the cooling circuits in dual circuit cooling elements. 

Scale build up in the cooling channels is a product of deposition of scaling from the water to the water channel surface during nucleate boiling. While this build up may be removable with an acid flush of the cooling element, such a procedure generally requires considerable furnace down time to complete. It is of course desirable to implement an adequate cooling water flow rate to avoid nucleate boiling in the cooling element water passages. 

Although less common, oxidation of the copper hot face can result in gradual loss of cast copper from the surface of the cooling element. The cooling of the element must be sufficient to maintain the surface temperature of the copper hot face below approximately 500 °C, the temperature above which experience has shown the oxidation rate to be unacceptable.

- Layout of pipe coils and cooling element

- Cooling pipe material 

Of these parameters, cooling capacity will be discussed in relation to pipe material selection since geometry can be optimized largely independently of pipe material (although copper pipes can impact geometry somewhat due to a requirement for thicker pipe walls and hence larger bend radii).

#### 3 Fabrication 

In this section, issues associated with fabrication of high intensity cooling elements will be discussed. 

##### 3.1 Casting considerations – Bulk copper 

In the fabrication of copper cooling elements it is desirable that a metallurgical bond will be formed between the two materials. For this to occur the pipe material must be metallurgically compatible with copper and thermally able to withstand the casting process. Ideally, when cast, a layer of the pipe’s surface will partially melt and an alloy of copper and the pipe material will form at the interface. 

Copper is a challenging material to cast since it is prone to surface cracking, porosity problems and to the formation of internal cavities. While the casting characteristics of copper can be improved by the addition of small amounts of alloying elements, their detrimental effect on copper conductivity prevents their use in high intensity cooling

elements. 

Pouring temperatures for copper are typically kept as low as possible to suit the size and form of the casting, and to minimize turbulence during pouring. Since higher temperatures of the liquid result in higher gas solubility, higher pouring temperatures produce higher gas contents and create a greater possibility of porous castings. 

In pure copper, hydrogen solubility is greater in the liquid than in the solid state (approximately 5.5 cubic centimetres versus two cubic centimetres per 100 grams), which is why gas porosity is a problem in copper castings. During the solidification process, the solid rejects gas to the remaining liquid, as the hydrogen is less soluble in the solid state. Once the gas exhibits a pressure greater than the pressure of the surrounding atmosphere and metal head, a gas pore will be formed [6]. 

Molten copper, which dissolves oxygen readily, should be melted under oxidizing conditions to suppress hydrogen solubility and should be deoxidized with just enough de-oxidant to prevent reoxidation during transfer and pouring. If indications of gas persist in spite of adequate residual deoxidizer, the gas is probably hydrogen, which can be removed only by purging with an inert gas. 

The design of the feed and riser system in the mould must be carefully designed to eliminate surface sinks or draws, and to reduce internal shrinkage porosity to acceptable levels (less than one percent). Gates and risers need to be positioned such that directional solidification is ensured. Steep temperature gradients in the casting toward the risers should be developed to avoid shrinkage cavities.

##### 3.2 Casting considerations – Pipe bond 

The preceding paragraphs outline the challenges for simply casting copper alone, without the inclusion of metal pipes inside of the mould and the additional challenge to partially melt and form a metallurgical bond with these pipes. To partially melt but not breach the internal pipes, and establish a good bond between the pipe material and surrounding copper, requires different techniques depending on the melting point and wall thickness of the cast-in pipe material. 

During casting, ensuring that the pipe remains in its correct location in the cooling element is important to enable the cooling element to perform as designed in the furnace. Foundries use retaining bars or “chaplets” in the mould to restrain the pipe; these chaplets must be carefully sized and located so as to perform their function while not interfering with the cooling element’s thermal performance in operation. 

Copper castings and copper pipes are obviously metallurgically compatible and the main challenge when casting copper around copper is preventing complete melting of the pipe. This is typically achieved through actively cooling the pipe during casting. Additionally, the wall thickness of the pure copper pipe must be greater than that o

f the other materials considered, since copper has the lowest melting point. Copper pipes are always cooled during the casting process with some combination of air, water saturated air, or nitrogen. While this cooling is required to preserve the structural integrity of the pipe, it can prevent complete metallurgical bonds from forming with the bulk copper. This is due to the cold interface between the molten bulk copper and force-cooled copper pipe. In some cases coatings on the pipes are used to aid in the bonding of the copper pipes; however, this can introduce an undesirable thermal barrier to heat transfer. The necessity of using thicker pipes can also limit the density of the cooling passages (due to the larger bend radii required), which limits the thermal benefits of the higher conductivity pipe. 

Copper and nickel are mutually soluble in their liquid and solid states. The phase diagram for the two metals shows that a continuous series of solutions can be formed. Copper-nickel alloys typically range in solidus (melting point) temperature from 1170 °C to 1320 °C. Pipe coils with higher nickel content, and hence melting point near the top end of this temperature range, do not have to be cooled during casting. It is ultimately a balance between the degree to which the pouring temperature is above the melting point of the pipe and the degree to which the pipe is cooled that determines the quality of the bond. Different cooling elements may require different cooling and casting techniques depending on the cooling coil layouts and available gate and riser locations. 

Iron and chromium are not soluble in copper; therefore it is more difficult to bond cast copper to stainless steel pipes. The small percentage of nickel in stainless steels could form an alloy with the cast copper, but the high melting point and chrome-oxide layer on the surface of stainless steel are significant impediments to the formation of metallurgical bonds between the copper casting and the stainless steel pipes. However, the contact between stainless steel pipes and cast copper is in practice sufficient for low heat flux applications.

Thermal imaging, ultrasonic testing and thermal sensor calibration are three important ways to ensure that the desired positions and bonding of the pipes in the finished casting are achieved. Some or all of these techniques are routinely used to check the locations and bonding of the cast-in pipe in the host cast

ings. 

Thermal (infrared) testing is capable of identifying flaws in the casting if the correct procedures are followed when completing the testing. It is important that a high contrast set of colours are chosen over a narrow temperature range to highlight subtle differences in temperature that can provide the tell tale signs of a poor quality casting. 

Ultrasonic measurement of copper, while technically challenging to successfully execute, can yield excellent results. Hatch has developed procedures for ultrasonic testing of copper castings and has demonstrated through experimentation that when poor bonding of the copper and the pipe material occurs, the outside surface of the pipe is detectable while with good bonding, only the inside of the pipe is detected. The difference in the densities of the two materials will only produce relatively small errors in the final position however it is necessary to measure from multiple sides of the casting to determine if the ultrasonic waves are being reflected by the open inside face of the pipe or a poorly bonded interface of the pipe and casting. 

Hatch has developed a method to calibrate and measure local contact resistances between the cooling pipe and the copper casting. After several years of monitoring, it was found that the bond integrity remained constant. #### 4 Cost considerations 

Cooling elements fabricated from electrolytic copper billets tend to be about 35 % less expensive than cast cooling elements of similar dimensions. However the cast cooling elements can be designed to remove more heat than the similar sized machined elements because the water passage(s) can be located more optimally and/or closer to the hot face of the cooling element. For the same performance, it is necessary to decrease the spacing between machined plate cooling elements in the furnace wall, or to increase the machined copper plate thickness. Either change requires more copper to be purchased, and the theoretical cost saving compared to cast elements is lost or in some c

ases reversed. Most importantly, for the reasons noted above, machined copper cooling elements are limited in their heat removal capacity and may not be suitable for high intensity copper processes. 

For intensive cooling elements, the material cost of the pipe, as a percentage of the total fabricated cooling element cost, ranges from approximately two per cent for stainless steel to six per cent for Monel-400, with copper and copper-nickel pipes falling in the middle at about two and four per cent of the cost, respectively. The impact of pipe material selection on the total cost variance for a furnace rebuild is typically less than one per cent. While the difference in value may not be insignificant in absolute capital terms, it is relatively small in the scope of the total project. The importance of ensuring the cooling element performance or the long term furnace operation dominates, making the pipe material cost the least significant selection factor. 

#### 5 Conclusions 

Robust cast copper cooling elements are essential to enable the high process intensities and resulting economies of scale of the modern copper smelting industry. 

Hatch typically uses Monel-400 pipe in its cast copper cooling elements based on the balance of high heat flux capability, fabrication reliability and small cost impact. Hatch has also provided cast cooling elements with pure copper pipes and stainless steel pipes for specialized applications. 

For reliable performance, cooling elements require overlapping joints, refractory and structural (binding system) integration, as well as high heat flux capacity. For the design of these cooling elements copper dominates as the preferred casting material, but there is no single cooling pipe material that is optimum for all applications. Both experienced engineers and foundry personnel are essential for the successful design and fabrication of cooling elements for copper processing.

**Keywords:** Off-gas, heat recovery, gas flow, off-gas line, CFD, modelling, optimization 

#### Abstract 

The availability of the off-gas line is vital for Copper Flash Smelting process productivity. In addition to heat recovery and dust separation the off-gas line needs to function as a chemical reactor. Sulfation reactions are inevitable in the heat recovery boiler atmosphere and they should take place in regions that enables easy dust handling and maximises heat recovery. The oxygen potential of the gas line should be monitored and used as a controlling parameter influencing the oxygen feed. Appropriate amount of oxygen should be available for dust sulfation reactions, whereas excess oxygen will lead to weak acid formation and corrosion phenomena. 

Accretion formation in the gas line can effectively be minimized by optimising the dust oxidation and sulfation behavior. Sulfation reactions should initiate as early as possible in the boiler, before the dust particles come into contact with the boiler tubes. Also, the dust should be in oxide form when it enters the boiler. Injecting oxygen into gas through the flash furnace settler roof results in dust oxidation in the up-take shaft and enables dust sulfation to begin as early in the boiler as the temperature decrease allows. Injecting sulfation air into the boiler radiation section supplies required oxygen amount and turbulence for dust sulfation reactions. CFD-modelling is an effective tool for optimizing the oxygen partial pressure and flow field in the off-gas line. The optimization of injection locations, jet penetration and velocity, and oxygen amount of the injection nozzles can be performed through modelling. Outotec is using an advanced CFD model being able to predict the dust sulfation behavior in the boiler as well as the possible deposition locations of the dust.

#### 2 Combustion reactions in the Flash Smelting Process 

The oxygen amount fed into the reaction shaft of the Flash Smelting furnace is determined by the concentrate feed rate, melt composition and possible supplementary oxygen used for oil combustion. The ratio between oxygen and the solid feed amount largely determines the chemical and thermal qualities of the furnace end products and the off-gas. 

The combustion reactions in the reaction shaft consume almost entirely the oxygen fed into the reaction shaft of the furnace. A part of the remaining dust particles dragged towards the off-gas line are still sulfidic and injecting oxygen into the settler ensures that the oxidation of the dust takes place in the furnace, not in the heat recovery boiler. The oxygen fed into the settler roof is mostly consumed by the dust oxidation reactions taking place in the uptake shaft and thus more oxygen is needed at the boiler inlet to enhance the sulfation reactions. As a result of sulfation reactions taking place earlier in the gas line the heat generated from them is captured already in the radiation section of the boiler or in the first convection tube banks and less thermal load of the reactions is carried to the end part of the boiler and to the electrostatic precipitator.

CFD modelling can be used for optimization of nozzle location and injection velocity optimization. The models are able to show the mixing of oxygen into the main gas stream and the flow pattern of the gas in the settler and in the up-take shaft as shown in Figure 2.

##### 3.1 Measuring and controlling the oxygen potential 

Controlling the oxygen feed rate into the settler to enhance dust oxidation reactions may be based on continuous measurement of the oxygen amount in the off-gas line after the electrostatic precipitator. The same measurement may be used for controlling the amount of sulfation air fed into the boiler. Additional sampling may be used to determine the oxygen amount in the up-take shaft, for increased accuracy of the sulfation air amount control. 

#### 4 Dust sulfation reactions 

Sulfation reactions are inevitable in the heat recovery boiler atmosphere as metallic oxides are no longer stable in the sulphur dioxide containing gas at lower temperatures. The reactions should be directed in a way that maximizes the heat recovery and enables easy dust handling. 

It is important to aim for completion of the sulfation reactions before the dust particles enter the convection section of the boiler. In the radiation section the dust particles have the possibility to react in the gas suspension if the temperature is low enough and sufficient amount of oxygen and turbulence is available for reactions. Therefore the temperature after the radiation section should be monitored and kept at a low enough level. The cooling efficiency of the boiler radiation section may be improved by installing radiation tube screens or guiding baffle plate into the radiation chamber. The dust carryover in the gas hinders the radiation effectivity of the gas. By bringing additional heat transfer surface near the main gas stream in the form of suspended tube panels the cooling capacity of metallurgical heat recovery boilers can be effectively increased. 

If the temperature after the radiation section is high, the sulfation reactions tend to occur in the convection section of the boiler. Non-sulfated particles tend to be stickier than sulfated particles, thus sulfation reactions taking place in the convection section may form accretion on the convection tube panels. 

Figure 3 compares the dust reaction phenomena in system A, where settler roof oxygen injection and sulfation air injection are not applied and as a consequence the sulfation reactions take place in the boiler convection section resulting in accretion problems and blocking of the convection tube banks. In system B, applying dust oxidation and sul

fation air injection enable the dust sulfation reactions to take place in the boiler radiation section, where they do not cause similar accretion problems and decrease the risk of high temperature corrosion. 1006 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Management of Copper Flash Smelting Off-Gas Line_ Figure 3: Delayed sulfation behaviour of the dust (A), causing dust accretion problems at the convection tube banks and advanced dust reaction behaviour (B), with settler oxygen injection and sulfation air injection, enabling easy dust handling. It is also very important to optimise the location of the injection nozzles and the injection velocity of the air for maximal turbulence and mixing to enhance the reactions.
