Oxygen remaining in the gas from the combustion reactions taking place in the furnace is not always evenly distributed. In the gas flow there are often parts containing higher amounts of oxygen and others with minimal oxygen content. When pure oxygen is fed to the furnace there may be even pronounced channelling effect resulting in areas with high oxygen content. If these flow lines travel through the gas line without mixing properly in the boiler, they are likely to form weak acid in the latter part of the off-gas line. If proper mixing at the entrance of the heat recovery boiler is ensured, this oxygen becomes available for the sulfation rections and is consumed in the most effective way, minimizing the likelihood of weak acid formation and sulfation-caused accretions in the boiler. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1008 _Management of Copper Flash Smelting Off-Gas Line_ ##### 4.1 High temperature corrosion in the heat recovery boiler If the dust particles enter the boiler in sulfide form, there is a high risk of high temperature corrosion of the boiler tubes as the sulfide compounds react with the tube surface protective oxide layer and forms sulphate. Sulfide compounds in the dust may form locally reducing atmosphere on the tube surface. A brittle surface layer of sulphate is easily shattered off the tube surface, exposing more unprotected tube material to sulfation. This type of high temperature corrosion may advance very fast and result into tube leakages in the boiler. The effect is even more pronounced if chlorides and alkaline are present in the dust. ##### 4.2 CFD modelling of sulfation reactions and dust deposition CFD modelling is an effective

way of optimising the Flash Smelting off-gas behaviour. In addition to flow pattern, temperature and velocity profile modelling, the possibilities of the Outotec<sup>®</sup> CFDmodel reach to the modelling of the dust particle reactions in the off-gas line. Outotec CFD-model takes into account the flow pattern formed already in the Flash Smelting furnace. Modelling the flow field of the boiler only results in false interpretation of the boiler flow pattern because the actual velocity and the temperature profiles at the model inlet are not known. The gas flow pattern at the boiler throat is originated in fact already at the concentrate burner and formed during its flow through the settler and the up-take shaft. The geometry of the furnace has a significant effect on the flow pattern of the entire gas line and the furnace off-gas-line should be treated as an entity, both in regard to the gas flow pattern and in regard to the composition of the gas and the dust particles. 

The Outotec CFD-model can be used to select the optimal location of the sulfation air nozzles. Also the nozzle characteristics, such as the velocity and the amount of the injected air may effectively be designed with the help of CFD modelling. 

Outotec CFD-model has inbuilt characteristics that allow the calculation of the dust sulfation reactions in the boiler. The sulfation reaction model has been developed in co-operation with Еbo Akademi University [1]. With the model it is possible to predict the location of the reactions in the boiler and the possibility of dust accretion formation in the boiler due to un-optimized dust sulfation reactions. The model takes into account the temperature profile of the boiler and the boiler gas composition.

##### 4.3 Deposition CFD model 

In addition to flow and temperature modelling and modelling of the sulfation reactions Outotec has developed in co-operation with Еbo-Akademi University [2] a model for predicting the areas of the boiler walls where the dust particles are likely to hit. The model can be used to estimate possible areas of dust accretion formation. Together with the dust sulfation model it can be determined whether the particles hitting the walls are likely to stick to the wall or whether they are reacted enough to be shed off easily down to the hoppers of the boiler. Deposition model can also help in planning the additional rapping for the boiler. The deposition model combined with the sulfation model shows the conversion degree of the sulfation of the particles hitting the walls. The higher the conversion rate is, the less possibility there is for particle deposition. Dust deposition model is thus able to predict whether there is a likelihood of accretion formation or high temperature corrosion due to sulfation reactions taking place on the

tube panel walls of the boiler.

#### 5 Weak acid formation 

The oxygen amount in the gas line should be kept at a moderate level to avoid weak acid formation within the boiler and the sulphuric acid plant. Ingress air amount should be minimized e.g. by proper sealing of boiler hatches and air tight construction of the boiler and the dust handling drag conveyors. 

Excess oxygen in the off-gas line creates a risk of weak acid formation. The conversion of SO2 into SO3 is controlled both by thermodynamics and kinetics. In high temperatures kinetics are faster but the stability of the SO3 is low. On the other hand at lower temperatures, where SO3 is stable the kinetics of the conversion are slow. There is an optimal temperature area for the formation of SO3 at around 600 °C. High moisture content of the gas enhances the formation of the weak acid. High SO3 content in the gas causes a risk of reaching the sulphuric acid dew point in the low temperature areas of the heat recovery boiler and electrostatic precipitator. 

To avoid wet corrosion due to sulphuric acid condensation in the off-gas line, the temperature should be kept above the sulphuric acid dew point. Sufficient boiler water pressure, minimized air ingression and proper isolation are key elements in minimizing the risk of wet corrosion in the offgas line 

#### 6 Conclusions 

Outotec comprehensive process experience combined with modern CFD modelling tools enable optimization of the oxygen and dust behaviour in the Flash Smelting process. The feed particles enter the furnace in sulfide form and are oxidized in the reaction shaft combustion zone to the desired extent, depending on the preferred properties of the furnace outlet products. The sulfide dust must be converted to first oxides, then to sulfate form for optimal dust behaviour. The earlier these reactions can be achieved in the process, the lower is the risk for dust accretions and high temperature corrosion in the off-gas line. Applying Outotec’s method of injecting oxygen into the furnace settler roof and sulfation air into heat recovery boiler is an effective method of optimising the gas line oxygen potential and dust behaviour. Outotec’s CFD-model can be used to determine the most effective locations and parameters for oxygen and air injection and to predict the dust sulfation and deposition behaviour.

The main conclusions are as follow: - The Teniente converter is able to process in average 3500 tpd of copper concentrates with peaks of 4000 tpd without unburned concentrates traces onto the slag. - The injection rate of concentrates at 3500 tpd increased the slag and white metal tapping frequencies in 16 % and 14 %, respectively, when it is compared to the injection rate of 3000 tpd. These increments were found to be not a problem for the smelter operation, mainly due to the efficient use of the crane, and the continuous feeding of the slag to the slag cleaning furnace. - The high smelting rate of the Teniente converter in the Codelco Norte smelter is limited on the availability of the PS converters, and the concentrates availability. - The available heat in the Teniente converter permits to treat additional solid copper-base secondary materials fed throughout the garr-gun, the 6-injection tuyeres, and the mouth of the reactor, incrementing the copper recovery of the smelter, and positioning the Teniente converter as a versatile, flexible and stable reactor with a high metallurgical performance. - Depending on the co

pper concentrates mineralogy, the Teniente converter is suitable to process + 700 tpd of revert combined with a wide variety of copper-base secondary materials as: solid white metal and/or matte, wet concentrates, copper calcine, Teniente converter and flash furnace dusts, solid converting slag, and leaching residues, among others.

roblems, such as the formation of heaps in the settler, a rise in the dusting rate, a rise in Fe3O4 content in slag, and so on. Therefore it is very important to prevent fluidization in order to maintain stable operations. 

The means used to prevent fluidization are as follows. 

- Reduce the free fluid layer 

- Facilitate the flow of the materials under mass flow conditions 

- A secure de-aeration time 

Two drag chain conveyors were used to charge the dried materials into the concentrate burner in the original equipment (Figure 8), and this type of feeder caused a large free fluid layer above the chain. So as the feeding rate of the flash furnace increased, the greater the fluidization. Also, the shape of the original bunker caused much accretion to develop because of the poor shape of the bunker. Parts of stocked materials were carried by conveyor, and what is called a rat hole developed in the stocked material. When the materials around the rat hole collapsed, a lot of dried material moved down at the same time. So the feeding system was modified.

Figure 9 shows the new bunker and screw feeders. The free fluid layer has been decreased by changing from drag chain conveyors to screw feeders. Also, the new screw feeder has a choke to prevent fluidization between the screw and the casing. In addition, the lifetime of the screw has been improved by placing reinforcement welds on the vanes. The new bunker has an improved shape which prevents the formation of rat holes, and the materials move under mass flow conditions in the bunker. It is known that 95 % de-aeration is necessary to prevent fluidization; therefore the bunker was designed through many observations, to determine the de-aeration time. Through these improvements, the frequency of the fluidization of the dried materials has decreased markedly. The original concentrate burner had two concentrate chutes, and the dried materials were charged using two drag chain conveyors. This was modified to improve the movement of uniform dried materials into the concentrate burner. Two concentrate chutes were added, and thus four sets of screw feeders were installed for four concentrate chutes.

#### 4 Improvements to the Waste Heat Boiler 

Flash smelting furnaces treat powdered raw materials, so dust coagulation and build-up is a serious problem for waste heat boilers. The best way to solve this problem is to reduce the amount of dust by improvements to the concentrate burner. But the amount of dust increases when the feeding rate increases, despite an equal dusting rate. It was also necessary to improve a system for shaking the dust from the boiler tubes. 

Figure 10 shows improvements to the waste heat boiler. Sulphatized air is blown into the inlet of the waste heat boiler radiation section to prevent dust sticking, and

spring hammers have been installed _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1032 _Development of Sumitomo Concentrate Burner_ on baffle plates in the radiation section and on the inlet part of the convection section tubes [5], where much dust accretion has previously occurred. #### Abstract 

High arsenic-containing enargite concentrates can be smelted directly but most copper smelters limit their total arsenic inputs for both environmental and economic reasons. The average arsenic level in custom copper concentrates has also been increasing, further limiting the potential market for high-arsenic enargite concentrates. Roasting and hydrometallurgical process options for treating enargite concentrates will be critically reviewed. Commercially proven methods of fixing arsenic in weak acid scrubbing solutions from roasters will also be reviewed and the resulting arsenic residue disposal compared with that from hydrometallurgical processes. Finally, roasting and hydrometallurgical options selected for treating an enargite concentrate from Kinross Gold’s La Coipa mine in Chile are compared on a relative technical, economic and risk basis. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Enargite is a complex copper-arsenic sulphide (Cu3AsS4) mineral that typically contains significant gold and silver values, and poses many process challenges. Large enargite deposits are found in Chile as well as other countries and the increasing demand for copper and gold have spurred research into developing more effective methods of extracting value metals from enargite concentrates. Kinross Gold Corp’s (KGC) La Coipa mine located in Northern Chile, Figure 1, has a 15,000 tpd gold cyanidation mill and it has identified additional potential ore in a sulphide ore deposit, containing gold and silver associated mainly with enargite and pyrite. This paper presents a literature and techno-economic review of the process options for treating the projected enargite concentrate highlighting the comparative advantages/disadvantages of the selected process options together with the options for arsenic residue disposal.

Figure 1: Location of La Coipa mine in Chile 

Enargite concentrates are smelted directly by a few Cu smelters but most smelters limit their arsenic input for environmental reasons and only process clean copper concentrates, containing less than about 0.3 % As. The methods for treating enargite concentrates are similar to those used commercially for pre-treating sulphidic refractory gold ores and concentrates. These processes are: 

- Pyrometallurgical oxidation with air and/or oxygen in roasters; 

- High Temperature Pressure Oxidation (HTPOX) using tonnage oxygen in autoclaves; 

- Biological oxidation in stirred tank reactors. 

The gold and silver values are recovered from the oxidized product by cyanidation. All of these pretreatment processes for refractory gold ores/concentrates are well-proven in commercial practice and are well-documented [1]. The selection of one process over another is dependent on ore mineralogy and location. McMullen

and Thomas compared the economics of roasting versus HTPOX for refractory gold ores and concluded that there is little difference in capital costs but roasting has lower operating costs while HTPOX generally gives higher gold recovery [2]. 

To date, roasting is the only process used commercially to treat enargite concentrates with the resulting low-arsenic calcine being sold to Cu smelters for the recovery of the Cu, Au and Ag values. There has been considerable development of hydrometallurgical copper processes for chalcopyrite concentrates over the last 10 to 15 years, most of which could be applicable to processing enargite but as yet none have been used commercially [3]. Filippou has recently done an extensive review on the recovery of copper values from copper-arsenic minerals [4]. In view of these developments, and the advantage that most hydrometallurgical processes have of precipitating most of the arsenic in the leach residue in an environmentally acceptable form for disposal, the expectation is that hydrometallurgical processes may eventually become the preferred process for treating enargite concentrates in the future. This paper reviews the current status of roasting and hydrometallurgical processes for treating enargite concentrates and compares their relative project economics for treating an enargite concentrate from Kinross’s Mantos del Oro deposit in Chile.

Most custom copper smelters do not treat high-arsenic copper concentrates because of environmental limitations and the high costs of fixing and disposing of arsenic-containing waste residues. Most large custom copper smelters limit their total arsenic inputs in concentrate to less than about 1000 tpa As and usually treat only clean copper concentrates. The typical smelter penalty for arsenic in copper concentrate is in the range US$ 2.50-3.00 per 0.1 % As over 0.1 % or 0.2 % As (US$ 2.5-3.0/kg As). Although this penalty cost may seem excessive to mining companies, for most smelters it just reflects the high cost of treating and disposing of arsenic. To the authors’ knowledge, the only custom copper smelter in the world that currently smelts significant quantities of high-As concentrates is Xstrata’s Horne smelter in Canada. Codelco’s Chuquicamata smelter has, however, the highest arsenic input of any copper smelter in the world, typically in excess of 10,000 tpa As. 

#### 2 Review of process options to treat enargite concentrates 

##### 2.1 Roasting process options 

The only process used commercially to date for treating large quantities of enargite concentrate is partial roasting at temperatures in the range 600-750<sup>o</sup> C to produce a low-As calcine and arsenic trioxide for sale or storage. The resulting low-As calcine was sold to Cu smelters. Sale of significant amounts of arsenic trioxide is, however, no longer possible but the scrubbing of arsenic trioxide fr

om copper smelter gases and its fixation in an environmentally acceptable manner is well-proven by various methods at several smelters. A key issue in selecting the preferred roasting process flowsheet is minimizing the cost of arsenic fixation and disposal to satisfy the environmental regulations. 

Multiple-hearth and fluidized bed roasters have both been used commercially for treating enargite concentrates. Barrick’s El Indio mine in Chile used multiple hearth roasters to treat its enargite concentrate, containing up to 9 % As [5]. Lepanto in the Phillipines and Boliden in Sweden used fluid bed reactors to treat high-As copper concentrates. Regardless of the type of roaster, the chemical reactions involved are the same. Padilla showed that enargite decomposition starts at about 525<sup>o</sup> C, but maximum arsenic removal only occurred between 700 and 750<sup>o</sup> C [6]. Enargite decomposes during roasting according to the following reaction: 

Cu3AsS4 → 1½ Cu2S + ½ As2S3 + ½ S2 (1) 

The arsenic is volatilized as arsenic sulphide gas and the labile sulphur is released in elemental form. Usually the roasting is carried out with enough air to oxidize most of the sulphur to SO2. 

Arsenic sulphide is usually oxidized to arsenic trioxide after the gases have left the roaster either in the hot cyclones or after the hot cyclones in an afterburner. Since there is no longer a significant market for arsenic trioxide, any new roasting operation would scrub the gases to recover the arsenic into a weak acid solution before precipitating it in a proven environmentally acceptable manner, using one of the weak acid effluent treatment processes used by copper smelters. These methods

will be discussed later in the paper. The remaining sulphur dioxide-containing gas is then usually treated in a sulphuric acid plant. 

Typically, the roasting process is able to reduce the arsenic level in the calcine to less than about 0.5 % As from enargite concentrates. For example, the Lepanto roaster treated about 180 tpd of enargite concentrate containing: 11 % As, 31 % Cu, 15 % Fe, 34 % S and produced a calcine containing: 0.3 % As, 43 % Cu, 23 % Fe, and 20 % S. The Boliden roaster, with a capacity of up to 800 tpd concentrate, treated concentrates containing 1-2 % As and typically produced a calcine containing about 0.1 % As. 

From 1986 to 1991, Outokumpu operated a commercial reducing roasting process for treating up to 10 tph of high-arsenic sulphide concentrates. The concentrate was dried and fed into a rotary kiln together with preheated sulphur vapour operating at a temperature of about 800<sup>o</sup> C. Heat was provided by controlled combustion of the sulphur vapour with air at several locations along the kiln. The low-As calcine was then smelted in the copper flash furnace. The off-gases from the kiln, containing the volatilized arsenic sulphide and elemental sulphur vapours, sulphur dioxide

and entrained particulate, were cleaned in a hot cyclone to recover the entrained concentrate/calcine solids. The hot gases were then quenched and scrubbed in a high-pressure drop venturi to remove most of the condensed As and S, as an As-S polymer. Over 95 % of the As-S polymer solids were recovered to the scrubber solution. Although Outokumpu’s testing indicated that the As-S polymer was stable, Outokumpu later built a hydrometallurgical refinery to produce a high-purity As2O3 for sale. 

In a reducing roast, minimizing SO2 generation could potentially offer a lower capital and operating cost roasting option by directly producing an As-S polymer filter cake for disposal and eliminating the need for an acid plant. Therefore a conceptual flowsheet was developed and costed to compare its economics with the proven fluidized bed oxidizing roasting option. Although a similar process has been operated commercially by Outokumpu, further testing would be required, especially on gas cleaning and environmental stability of the As-S. 

##### 2.2 Hydrometallurgical process options 

Several new hydrometallurgical processes have been developed to treat copper sulphide concentrates and most are suitable for the treatment of enargite concentrates. Hydrometallurgical processes have a major advantage over roasting options as the arsenic is usually precipitated directly within the leach reactor as ferric arsenate, which is generally regarded as environmentally acceptable for disposal. 

###### 2.2.1 Pressure oxidation process 

The High Temperature Pressure Oxidation process (HTPOX) for chalcopyrite concentrate treatment was developed by Placer Dome in 1993 [7]. In the HTPOX process, the leaching autoclave is operated at a temperature of about 220<sup>o</sup> C and an oxygen pressure of around 10 atmospheres. The HTPOX process is also capable of leaching enargite concentrates but has not been used commer-

cially for this as yet. Most of the sulphide sulphur in the concentrate is oxidized to sulfate, which gives high tonnage oxygen requirements as well as generating a large amount of sulphuric acid solution that has to be either used on a heap leach or neutralized. Typically, for enargite concentrate leaching, an autoclave residence time in the range 1-3 hours is required. The autoclave discharge slurry is cooled and thickened to separate the Cu-bearing Pregnant Leach Solution (PLS) from the leach residue. The thickener underflow leach residue is washed, neutralized with lime and then subjected to cyanidation to recover the precious metals. Gold recoveries are generally around 95 %, but silver recovery is usually very low due to the formation of argento-jarosite. For concentrates containing significant silver values, it has been proposed to do a lime boil of the leach residue before cyanidation to increase silver extractions to the range 75-95 %. However, a lime

boil has never been used commercially for this application. It is a difficult process to operate and it would also decompose most of the scorodite reducing the stability of arsenic in the leach residue. 

Two variants of the HTPOX process that have also been developed to improve precious metal recovery, especially silver. These are the Platsol process and the Newmont process. The Platsol process is essentially HTPOX with the addition of 5-10 g/L chloride ion (as NaCl) [8]. The process is also able to dissolve both gold and platinum group metals (PGMs) as well as copper, in HTPOX leach. The gold and PGMs form chloro-complexes which eliminates the need for cyanidation for their recovery. Silver is largely converted to silver chloride, that is insoluble, the AgCl in the leach residue can be recovered by cyanidation. 

Newmont has developed its own variation of the HTPOX process for treating the precious metal rich, complex copper concentrates produced at its Pheonix project [9]. The Newmont HTPOX variation uses addition of limestone to control the pH in the autoclave to minimize argento-jarosite formation. Gold and silver extractions from the resultant cyanidation of the leach residue were both about 90 %. 

###### 2.2.2 Atmospheric leaching options 

Atmospheric sulphate-based leaching processes have also been developed for chalcopyrite leaching including: BHP Billiton’s BIOCOP process, the GeoBiotics‘ GEOCOAT process and Xstrata’s Albion process. These processes may also be applicable to enargite concentrates. The most developed atmospheric leaching process was BHP Billiton’s BIOCOP process that was tested in a 25,000 tpa Cu demonstration plant in Chile near Codelco’s Chuquicamata mine. This plant treated local arsenic-containing concentrates but it was closed after several years operation. Although bioleaching of secondary copper sulphide minerals is well proven, enargite is much more refractory under biotic conditions [10]. 

In the early 1990‘s, MIM Holdings (now Xstrata Plc) developed the Albion process to treat refractory copper concentrates [11]. The process uses a hot acidified ferric sulphate leach of ultrafine ground concentrate at atmospheric pressure in agitated tanks. The key part of the Albion process is the use of an IsaMill which grinds the concentrate to a very fine particle size, in the range 5-10 microns. The patent claims that at a temperature of 90<sup>o</sup> C, over 92 % of the copper was leached from

Dixon at the University of British Columbia has developed the proprietary Galavanox process for treating copper concentrates under atmospheric conditions using ferric sulphate as the primary oxidant [12]. The key to this process is adding up to five times excess pyrite to provide a galvanicallyassisted leach which prevents mineral passivation and produces a po

Geobiotics has developed a proprietary heap leach process called GEOCOAT in which refractory gold or copper concentrates are coated on to crushed and sized support rock, either inert or with metal sulphide values, and oxidized by mesophile or thermophile bacteria in an engineered heap leach. The only commercial-scale high-temperature heap bioxidation operation that has been operated to-date was Newmont’s “Bio-mill” process at its Carlin mine in Nevada where refractory gold ore was pretreated before being processed through a conventional milling-cyanidation process. Biomill tests suggested that arsenic was probably precipitated as scorodite at temperatures above about 50<sup>o</sup> C [13]. 

#### 3 Arsenic precipitation from roaster weak acid solutions 

Smelting of enargite and other As-containing concentrates results in the volatilization of most of the arsenic. The arsenic in the gases after hot gas cleaning is removed in the wet gas cleaning section that typically comprises a gas quench, a high-pressure drop venturi scrubber followed by further cooling, and a wet electrostatic precipitator before the cleaned SO2 gases go to the sulphuric acid plant. Several treatment methods have been developed by copper smelters to remove arsenic from the resulting weak acid solution in an environmentally acceptable manner, according to local environmental standards. These methods would be suitable for a roasting operation subject to local costs and environmental regulations. 

The Horne smelter in Rouyn-Noranda, Quebec has developed its own process for the precipitation of arsenic in its effluent treatment plant. The process minimizes the operating cost for arsenic precipitation by using Acid Mine Drainage (AMD) as well as the effluent from the smelter precipitator dust treatment plant as sources of iron and other base metals [14]. The weak acid stream coming from the smelter and the wet gas cleaning section of the acid plant contains an average of about 2500 ppm arsenic that must be treated to reduce the final arsenic concentration in the effluent to no more than 0.5 ppm. The AMD stream, the converter dust leach slurry and the weak acid stream, containing arsenic mainly the trivalent form, are combined in a reaction vessel where the pH is increased to about 4-5 and oxygen is injected to oxidize ferrous to ferric ion. Arsenic is precipitated as arsenical ferrihydrite. In the second stage reaction tanks, the pH is increased to about 9 to precipitate base metal hydroxides and produce a final effluent stream that contains approximately 0.5 ppm As. The (Fe<sup>3+</sup> +Zn<sup>2+</sup> ):As molar ratio is controlled above 4. The final precipitate is mixed with slag

m the slag concentrator and co-deposited in the tailings pond. The process is now well proven, and regular monitoring of the pond indicates that the final residue is stable even though most of the arsenic is in its trivalent state. 

Inco’s Copper Cliff Smelter in Sudbury has recently installed a new weak acid treatment process that also precipitates arsenic as arsenical ferrihydrites [15]. The arsenic containing solution is sent to an oxidation tank where it is retained for 60 minutes to oxidize as much of the arsenic, iron with the dissolved SO2 to form As<sup>5+</sup> , Fe<sup>3+</sup> and H2SO4, respectively. The efficient conversion of arsenic to its pentavalent state is surprising but SO2/air is a strong oxidant. Subsequent neutralisation at higher pH in a conditioning tank precipitates Fe<sup>3+</sup> and As<sup>5+</sup> as FeAsO4 and Fe(OH)3 compounds. Inco’s process operates with very high Fe:As ratios, up to 15:1, forming stable precipitates. Final neutralization to pH 8.0 with lime forms gypsum and metal hydroxide precipitates. Some of the gypsumarsenic precipitate is recycled back to the conditioning tank as a seed and the neutralized slurry is sent to a tailings impoundment. Arsenical ferrihydrites from Inco’s CRED plant has seen no sign of ferrihydrite breakdown in 30 years of operation [16]. 

The Saganoseki copper smelter in Japan precipitates the arsenic in solution, from its converter dust leach and its acid plant weak acid bleed, as arsenic sulphide using sodium hydrosulphide. The arsenic sulphide precipitate (40 % As) has a low bulk density (0.4 t/m<sup>3</sup> ) and it is further batch processed in an autoclave at 200<sup>o</sup> C and high pressure to dry, polymerize and densify it. The final arsenic sulphide polymer has a bulk density of about 1.3 t/m<sup>3</sup> . This process also increases the stability of the material that is then stored in a concrete pit on site [17]. 

The production of crystalline scorodite from arsenic-containing weak acid solutions using pyrite as the iron source in an autoclave is possible over the temperature range of 150-225<sup>o</sup> C and with a high oxygen overpressure (150 psi) [18]. Codelco has conducted bench scale tests using pyrite and lowgrade copper concentrates and pilot plant runs were carried out at SGS Lakefield treating a weak acid containing 14.8 g/L As and 26 g/L H2SO4. The arsenic precipitated out of solution quickly down to about 1.5 g/L As. 

Demopoulos [19] has developed the atmospheric scorodite process. Scorodite precipitation at atmospheric conditions eliminates the need for more expensive autoclaves required for HTPOX scorodite production. Lower operating costs, and lower consumption of iron and neutralization reagents are benefits that are claimed for the atmospheric scorodite process. The first step in the process is the oxidation of all of the arsenic from trivalent to pentavalent using sulphur dioxide and oxygen. Low cost sources of iron are used and scorodite prec

ipitation is completed before pH 2 is reached. Some scorodite/gypsum precipitate is recycled back to the first precipitator reactor to be used as a seed. The atmospheric scorodite process potentially offers lowers capital and operating costs, but the process has only been operated at a pilot scale.

##### 4.1 Evaluation of enargite roasting options 

The two roasting options: oxidizing and reducing were evaluated to determine if there was any significant economic benefit for reducing roasting that could justify its further development over the more proven oxidizing roast. The basic flowsheets for the oxidizing and reducing roasting options are shown in Figure 2.

The oxidizing roaster has been operated in both Fluid Bed Roaster (FBR) and Multiple Hearth Roasters (MHR). The design capacity for this application is at the limit for a single MHR so a FBR was selected as the design basis based on the proven operation at Boliden and Lepanto. The reducing roast option has only been operated commercially by Outokumpu using a rotary kiln. A FBR

cannot be used for the reducing roast option because of the high level of calcine carry-over that would result in high losses of metal value to the arsenic sulphide precipitate. 

In the FBR oxidizing roast option, most of the calcine will be recovered in the hot cyclones with a smaller amount from the FBR bed. After the hot cyclones, the off-gases are afterburned with air to ensure complete oxidation of arsenic sulphide and sulphur to arsenic trioxide and SO2. The off-gas, now at about 850<sup>o</sup> C, is cooled in a water spray cooler to about 350<sup>o</sup> C and then further cleaned in a hot electrostatic precipitator (ESP). Most of the small amount of remaining calcine is recovered as a dust from the ESP. The ESP dust has a higher As content than the rest of the calcine due to the condensation of base metal arsenates and its As content can approach that of the FBR feed. Since the metal value of the ESP dust is considerable, it must still be blended with the rest of the calcine thus slightly increasing the As content of the calcine product. The off-gas from the ESP is quenched with water to about 70<sup>o</sup> C and then scrubbed in a high-pressure drop venturi scrubber. To prevent buildups the As content of the scrubber solution is maintained at less than about 18 gpL As by continually bleeding off the scrubber solution to the effluent treatment plant (As ETP in Figure 2) for As removal to meet the environmental regulations. The quenched gases are then further cooled to about 30<sup>o</sup> C and then cleaned in a wet ESP before going to a conventional sulphuric acid plant. 

Based on t

his review of arsenic precipitation methods available to treat the weak acid from the oxidation roaster option, it was decided to use the HTPOX process with pyrite additions because of the availability of pyrite and it produced a similar final residue for disposal as the hydrometallurgical options. Also the extensive operating experience with HTPOX process treating refractory gold concentrates, containing pyrite, suggested that this would be a low risk option from an operating and environmental approval viewpoint. 

In the reducing roasting option, the concentrate is treated in a rotary kiln using a fuel oil burner to volatilize the arsenic as arsenic sulphide and most of sulphur as elemental sulphur. It was assumed that 25 % of the labile sulphur volatilised would be oxidised to SO2 through air inleackage into the roaster and its hot gas cleaning system. Most of the calcine is recovered from the kiln product. The kiln off-gases are cleaned in hot cyclones and then quenched with water sprays to about 70<sup>o</sup> C and then scrubbed in a high-pressure drop venturi to condense and recover most of the arsenic sulphide and elemental sulphur as solids. These are then recovered from the scrubber solution by pressure filters. The gases will then be further cooled and cleaned in a wet ESP and then the SO2 converted to sulphuric acid. Alternatively, the gases could be scrubbed to remove SO2. The calcine from the kiln is expected to be slightly lower in As than that from the FBR but metal recovery to calcine will be lower due to the losses of fine particules to the arsenic sulphide-sulphur filter cake. 

The design basis for the evaluation of the two roaster options was based on treating 98,550 tpa of enargite concentrate (25.6 % Cu, 6.5 % As, 26.9 g/t Au and 336 g/t Ag). Each roaster was assumed to operate for 350 days/year and 22.8 hours/day. Based on heat and mass balances, the key parameters for each roaster option are summarized in Table 1.

#### Abstract 

The efficiency of industrial combustion processes can be raised in two ways, either by preheating the fuel and combustion air with a high risk of the efficiency loss of dust in recuperators or by adding oxygen. The most important issue of the usage of oxygen burners is the substantially increasing melting rate by lowering the specific production costs because of the higher combustion efficiency and lower investment costs. The diluted or flameless combustion (internal off-gas recirculation) and the external off-gas recirculation solve the problem with the high flame temperature and lead to cold combustion and lower dross formation. The Oxipyr<sup>®</sup> -Air combines the technology of diluted combustion during air and oxygen usage decreasing the emission of pollutants. Constitutive of the Oxipyr<sup>®</sup> -Air

development a fuel-oxygen-burner, Oxipyr<sup>®</sup> -Flex, was designed for a maximum of flexibility for the customer. The Oxipyr<sup>®</sup> -Air and Oxipyr<sup>®</sup> -Flex have been developed for the specific needs of melting and recycling companies for all non ferrous metals. The paper shows the theory, practical installations and economical outlook.

The efficiency of industrial combustion processes can be increased in two ways (which can be seen in Figure 1), either by preheating the fuel and combustion air or by adding oxygen. - Oxygen fuel burners 

- Direct oxygen injection into the fuel air flame 

- Underlaying of the fuel air flame 

- Enrichment of the combustion air

##### 2.1 Flameless leads to „cold combustion“ with oxygen 

Flameless combustion, the correct scientific term is volume combustion, is a proce

ss in which the flame is diluted with exhaust gas in order to cool and lengthen the flame. As a result of this procedure, the flame becomes nearly invisible. The original intention lies in a substantial reduction of NOx values and a more homogeneous distribution of heat (a diluted flame still holds the same heat quantity). Although no nitrogen is introduced during an oxyfuel combustion, the high flame temperature aids the formation of NOx, which originates from nitrogen in the fuel or the leak air. With a recirculation of the exhaust gas, a dilution of the flame is achieved, which leads to a reduction of the temperatures at the mouth of the burner as well as a reduction of the NOx values. Dryga BHP Billiton Olympic Dam Operations, Australia **Keywords:** Process control, direct to blister furnace, copper, modelling, heat and mass balance #### Abstract Significant improvements in process control have been made by the development of heat and mass balance based modelling for furnaces at BHP Billiton’s copper smelter at Olympic Dam. Furnace control models have been used for both the flash furnace (direct to blister furnace) and more recently the electric slag cleaning furnace. The Flash Furnace

Control Model (FFCM) has greatly improved process stability by adjusting furnace inputs such as oxygen coefficient, flux charge rate and heat input (fuel oil and oxygen enrichment) in order to control three critical process variables: copper in slag (40 % improvement in standard deviation), slag dip temperature (7 % improvement in standard deviation) and iron to silica ratio in slag (98 % improvement in standard deviation). 

In a similar manner an Electric Furnace Control Model (EFCM) has been developed that monitors assays and quantity of furnace input and outputs to control coke feeding rate and cycle time. Previous models considered the furnace on a continuous basis, the new EFCM more accurately uses a mass balance that considers the batch nature of the process and takes into account the actual input and output stream volumes and assays. Since the implementation of the EFCM the standard deviation in copper in tails has been reduced by 28 % and specific coke efficiency has improved by 5 %. 

#### 1 Introduction 

BHP Billiton’s Olympic Dam is located 560 kilometers north of Adelaide, South Australia. Olympic Dam is a multi-mineral ore body and Australia’s largest underground mine. It is the world’s fourth largest copper deposit, largest uranium deposit and fifth largest gold deposit. Operations include the mine, processing plant and smelter. The smelter comprises an Outokumpu direct to blister Flash Furnace (FF), an Electric Slag Cleaning Furnace (ESF) and two fire refining anode furnaces. The smelter process is designed to smelt a copper-rich concentrate derived from a chalcocite/bornite deposit and hence uses a direct to blister process without a secondary matte converting stage.

#### 2 Smelter process overview 

The smelting process is a semi-continuous, semi-batch process. Copper concentrate, recycled dust and flux are fed to the FF and combusted in an oxygen rich environment. The FF produces blister copper, a slag of high copper content (~25 %) and an off-gas stream containing sulphur dioxide and dust. The FF slag is processed in the ESF to recover copper. The ESF produces blister copper, a slag of ~4 % copper that is reprocessable via milling and an off-gas stream. The blister copper from both the FF and ESF is fire refined in an anode furnace prior to being cast as copper anode. The off-gas is also further processed: dust is recycled through the FF to recover copper, waste heat is recovered as steam, and sulphur dioxide is used to make sulphuric acid. A schematic representation of the Smelter 2 furnaces is shown in Figure 1. 



Figure 1: Schematic representation of Smelter 2 

Control models designed to assist the Control Room Technicians (CRT) in the operation of the FF and the ESF are the Flash Furnace Control Model (FFCM) and the Electric Furnace Control Model (EFCM). Currently these control models are advisory, the decision to use the values advis

ed by the models is at the CRT discretion. The compliance of the model is 95 percent. The purpose of these models is to enhance understanding of the furnaces and give the CRT timely information with which to operate the furnaces efficiently and safely based on a steady state heat and mass balance of the process. This paper briefly discusses the basis for control of these smelting processes and the structure of the models. It also outlines the application and benefits of these models as used at Olympic Dam.

#### 3 Flash furnace control model 

##### 3.1 Understanding the flash furnace process 

The key to advanced process control of any system is to first understand the process and the basic information available for modelling the process. Once the process is understood, a simple first principle heat and mass balance model can be constructed [3]. The basic information contributing to understanding the FF process is outlined in this section. 

The FF is a typical Outokumpu flash smelter comprising a reaction shaft, settler and uptake shaft. The concentrate is high in copper (~44 %) and over 85 % of the feed material is sulphidic. The FF feed (concentrate, dust and flux) is combusted within the reaction shaft in an excess oxygen environment [1, 2]. 

The FF copper in slag varies from 23-30 % and the copper reports to the slag as a copper oxide with some entrained copper. The FF typically operates at a slag temperature of 1290<sup>o</sup> C to 1315<sup>o</sup> C with the blister copper of 1220<sup>o</sup> C to 1260<sup>o</sup> C temperature. The oxidation reaction between the concentrate and enriched air alone is sufficient to raise the feed constituents to FF operating temperatures. The reaction shaft and the settler burners are used to ignite concentrate in the reaction shaft and provide supplemental heat to the slag and blister in the settler. 

Copper concentrate is added continuously to the FF. The dip levels and assays provide the quantity and quality of material in the furnace and are taken on an hourly and two-hourly basis respectively. Similarly, temperatures are monitored on an hourly basis. 

To maintain furnace integrity the FF is lined with water cooled elements which maintain a set temperature and measure the heat loss. There is also an unmeasured heat loss term which includes general conductive, convective and radiative heat losses. 

##### 3.2 Basis for control of the flash furnace 

The primary purpose of FF operation is efficient recovery of metal in the form of blister copper. Efficiency is defined not only as maximizing throughput, but as maintaining key process descriptors within a certain operating range. These process descriptors are typically a set slag chemistry and a temperature range for slag and sulphur in blister (this is indirectly achieved by controlling slag chemistry). 

The greatest impact on these process considerati

ons is highly variable concentrate mineralogy. Also, due to concentrate composition 3-5 wt. % silica, the FF produces a fayalitic slag and this must be considered when determining the basis for FF control [1]. Benefits of a fayalitic slag system include the ability to lay a protective accretion over the refractory if slag conditions (iron to silica ratio) are controlled correctly. The feed iron to silica ratio varies, hence siliceous flux is added to control slag viscosity at operating temperatures, this affects the slag iron to silica ratio. A disadvantage of the

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Ranasinghe, Russell, Muthuraman, Dryga_ 



fayalitic slag system is that if the sulphide feed material is not oxidized whilst falling into the bath, slag foaming may occur. Indicators of incipient foaming are slag temperature and copper in slag below range. The use of excess oxygen to prevent foaming results in a slag with a high copper content which, if not controlled correctly can affect copper production [2]. 

In light of these limitations, control is required to obtain the desired outputs from the FF process. To summarize, the key parameters to be controlled are, copper in slag, iron to silica ratio in slag and slag temperature. These outputs are critical as they dictate, the amount of blister copper and slag produced, the formation of refractory-protective accretion inside the DBF, slag properties (stability and viscosity) which are critical to downstream handling and processing, and to a lesser extent the process off-gas waste heat and SO2 content. 

##### 3.3 FFCM control philosophy 

Understanding the FF process and the basis for control suggests a control model comprising three control loops that provide advisory furnace input values for control of the three key output parameters of copper in slag, slag iron to silica ratio and slag temperature. Copper in slag is controlled by the oxygen coefficient (Nm<sup>3</sup> /h oxygen provided for oxidation of each tonne of concentrate). Slag iron to silica ratio is controlled by the flux charge rate. The slag temperature is controlled both by concentrate burner oxygen enrichment (the amount of excess nitrogen introduced to the system as a heat sink), dust recharge percentage and burner fuel oil rate. 

These controllers are two term (proportional + integral) discrete form of feedback controllers which use a time delay to account for process response time. Integral action is used for improved control under process disturbances thus preventing overshoot of targets. As the system is a multivariate process, static decoupling is implemented between the heat loss controller and the controllers for oxygen coefficient and flux charge rate. This ensures that temperature control is not adversely impacted by changes to the oxygen coefficient or flux charge. The feedback controllers in the FFCM attempt to counter process excursions instigated by furnace dynamics. Setpoint changes are handled as incremental

changes to the controller output. The size of the control action implemented is based directly on heat and mass balance calculations. 

As a continuous process with batch output reliant on timely feedback from various sources (assays, temperatures), the FFCM incorporates a timer and deadband to surmount the delays in operating with a feedback system and to account for the effect of noise. 

There are several well defined equivalency correlations which define the model. Slag composition and temperature changes are proportional to concentrate burner enrichment, oxygen coefficient and flux on charge ratio. Feed and fuel rate are proportional to oil burner enrichment and concentrate burner enrichment. This sensitivity analysis allows the operator to anticipate changes to model outputs when inputs are modified.

The slag dip temperature controller advises changes to fuel input and oxygen enrichment in order to to achieve target slag dip temperature. A number of these inputs can be fixed for ease of use. The FFCM seeks to conserve fuel in the heat balance by optimizing fuel burner oxygen enrichment within limits (minimizing the heat loss to the nitrogen component of enriched air) to reduce fuel oil usage whilst keeping the difference in the two calculated heat balances at zero. It also takes in to account the set point of the velocity of the concentrate burner. 

The control model has rules-based logic which checks for adverse conditions within the furnaces and alerts the CRT. This is particularly useful for monitoring the onset of unsafe furnace conditions. 

The current limitation on the FFCM is that it is a steady state calculation which does not account for dynamic heat loads which occur, for example, when the FF is being heated on start up, or when accretion deposition/melting is occurring. With current model the operating discipline on compliance by the CRT is 95 % excluding the start-ups

Figure 7: Typical slag cycle of the ESF, showing definition of periods within the cycle _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1071 _Ranasinghe, Russell, Muthuraman, Dryga_ The purpose of the ESF process is to recover copper from the FF slag. Two cycles can be defined around the batch process, slag and blister. The EFCM tracks and monitors the slag cycle. A typical slag cycle is given in Figure 5 and consists of four periods, hold, slag tap in, cook and slag tap out. FF slag consists of copper and iron oxides with silica. Coke is added to reduce the slag copper oxides which produce an off-gas of carbon monoxide and carbon dioxide. The ESF is also used to process reverts (slags of a high copper content). The outputs of the ESF are, a slag with a copper content ranging from 2 to 10 %, blister copper and off-gas. While studies confirm that the coke reaction with the slag is a zero order reaction [4], there are a number of factors that hinder the contact of the coke with the slag and prevent this reaction from occuring. For example if there is a crust on top of the slag this will limit the ability of the coke to react with the slag, similarly if there is a layer of coke or revert on the bath, addition of more coke will not increase the rate of the reaction. Neither will the addition of coke during the cook time increase the reaction rate. Conversely if the bath is stirred by incoming FF slag then this will increase the rate of reaction. This leads to the practice of coking the ESF during tap in. A key unknown is the quantity of coke that reacts directly with incoming air instead of with slag. This can be estimated once a cycle is finished given the amount of coke added to the system and the final slag assay value. The amount of coke doing useful work is encapsulated as a coke efficiency. The oxidation reaction of coke forming carbon dioxide and monoxide is exothermic, generating heat which increases the off-gas temperature. Thus coke rate is controlled to preserve duct integrity. The reduction of the copper oxides in the bath is endothermic. Heat is added t

o the bath through three Sodeberg electrodes. Electrode power and position within the bath can be varied to distributie energy to the slag or blister. 

ESF bath levels and slag temperatures are taken on an hourly basis. Slag assays are taken when the ESF taps out slag. Blister temperatures are taken every four hours and when the ESF taps blister. 

##### 4.2 Basis for control of the electric furnace 

Similar to the FF, the primary purpose of the ESF operation is the recovery of blister copper, but from FF slag. For the ESF the key process descriptors are a target copper in slag of 4 % with range 2-6 %. Safety is paramount at Olympic Dam, so hygiene must be considered when setting operational targets; when there is less than 3 % copper in slag, the radionuclides<sup>216</sup> Pb and<sup>210</sup> Po report to the blister phase [1]. The ESF slag must also be suitable for further reprocessing via the mills, and reduction in standard deviation in slag copper content improves downstream copper recovery. Secondary metrics of the ESF performance are the amount of coke and power consumed and the minimization of wear to the ESF via temperature control.

Historically, copper in ESF slag has been highly variable due to variable inputs (FF slag composition, slag and coke quantity) and processing times. Based on the success of the FFCM, an Electric Furnace Control Model (EFCM) was implemented to reduce the variability of copper in slag. 

##### 4.3 EFCM model control philosophy 

The goal of the EFCM is to increase ESF volumetric throughput and reduce cycle time while achieving a target Cu in ESF slag (EFS) and maintaining the slag and blister temperatures within range. Understanding the ESF process and basis for control yields a model that provides recommendations on the coke rate, time of tap out, the current and power factor (PF), which relates to the depth of the electrodes in the bath. The model shows the current estimate of the bath copper in slag, the amount of coke added since the start of the cycle and the remaining coke needed to achieve the target copper in slag. 

The model can only reduce cycle time by reducing the cook time as defined in Figure 7. The time to tap in and tap out is dictated by volume. The hold time is dependent on when the FF is ready to tap slag (in theory, with proper scheduling, the hold time can be eliminated completely). 

Target copper in ESF slag can be obtained providing that sufficient coke is added to the system and that this coke reacts with the slag. Once the quantity and composition of the incoming FF slag is known, then given a coke efficiency, the amount of coke required to reduce the FF slag to the target copper in slag can be determined. 

Coke addition during the hold period can be beneficial to the operation of the furnace as the temperature of the coke is raised to the point where it will readily react when th

e tap in process stirs the bath. The complication of adding coke during the hold and tap in periods is that the exact quantity of coke required is not known until tap in has finished. This has led to the introduction of a FF slag estimator which the operators can use to estimate the amount of incoming FF slag. 

The model predicts the incoming FF slag which is dependent on the levels of the slag and blister in the FF together with the make rate of the slag and blister in the FF and the target slag level to be achieved in the FF after the tap in to the ESF is completed. This is a dynamic model which not only determines the quantity of slag but also the time taken for the tap in process. 

With the FF slag estimate, the required coke can be determined prior to completion of the tap in period and therefore coke addition can be completed when tap in finishes. In theory this allows for zero cook time which represents an ideal cycle time. In practise there may be some cook time added onto the process to allow for tappers to close the FF and move on to opening the ESF. 

Once the required amount of coke for the cycle is known, the option is given to the CRT to set a tap out time, in which case the model will determine a coke rate to suit, or to minimize tap out time which optimizes coke rate subject to off-gas temperature limits.

Blister and slag temperatures are controlled using the electrode current and Power Factor (PF) or depth of electrodes. Depending on what the blister and slag temperatures are in relation to their ranges the model will recommend changes to both electrode current and PF. At this stage the model calculates the electrode current and PF based on CRT experience. While this is rudimentary it ensures consistency amongst the CRT in the way power is applied to the ESF. 

Future work on temperature control will look at determining a bath resistance which will allow for an estimate of power based on electrode current. Along with the heat balance this will allow for an estimate of enthalpy added to the bath. However, how the enthalpy is distributed to the slag and blister will remain empirical. Trials on the temperature control indicate this may have an effect on the response time. Typically the larger the quantity of blister or slag the more power will be needed to maintain or change the temperature within a set time. 

##### 4.4 Electric Furnace Control Model (EFCM) structure 

The EFCM treats the ESF as a reduction bath where the addition of coke drives the reduction of the slag. The four streams in and three out of the EFCM are given in Figure 8, together with the chemical elements used in the mass balance. Unlike the FF, the ESF is a batch process and analysis control is done on a slag cycle basis. Further inputs include the existing heel slag and blister assays. 

Three sets of calculations are performed; mineralogy calculations determine stream compo

sition, mass balances determine stream element deportment and the heat balance determines the enthalpy of reaction. Control is then implemented by providing the heat and mass balance with current values and set point values and interrogating the model based on available information. For example, given a final ESF slag assay value one can find how much coke must have been added to achieve this. 

###### 4.4.1 Mineralogy 

Mineralogy modelling allows the enthalpies of the streams and thus the heat balance to be calculated. The slags and revert streams mineralogies have been inferred from the observed mineralogy of cooled slags which comprise fayalite and cuprospinel (non-stoichiometric magnetite). This model was developed to span the operational copper in slag range, up to 30 %. Blister mineralogy is identical to that used by the FFCM. Coke composition is assumed constant. 

###### 4.4.2 Mass balance 

The mass balance for the EFCM is based on the eight elements shown in Figure 8, representing seven non linear equations which are solved by a quasi-Newton iterative solver. For maximum versatility the mass balance is formulated so that a forward mass balance determines the output off-gas, slag and blister quantity and composition and a backward mass balance determines the amount of coke required to reach a particular target slag and blister.

###### 4.4.3 Heat balance 

Similar to the FFCM the heat balance of material streams can be performed once the mass mineralogy and temperature of all streams are known. Heat is also added to the ESF through the sodeberg electrodes and removed by cooling water and as general heat loss. At any point at which the model is run, the electrode power input and the heat loss to cooling elements are always known.

#### 5 Discussion 

The models have proved invaluable not only in realizing a cost benefit to the process but also in presenting information that improves understanding of the process. With this improved understanding comes a greater awareness and compliance to operating procedures together with a basis from which further ideas for improvement are generated and developed. Furthermore, as the composition 

1076 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Olympic Dam Heat and Mass Balance Process Optimization_ 



of the concentrate changes, the model provides a method of evaluating the effects of these changes on the operation of the furnaces. 

The process of developing the model has also forced a consideration of what, how often and how accurately we measure information about the process. In some cases new measurements have been instigated and the capture and storage of the information has also changed. 

A major limitation of the model is the absence of the true dynamics of the furnaces. While some dynamics have been incorporated in the model, the sub models are steady state in nature and therefore their ability to predict future furnace outputs is limited. This is most readily observed during the transient operation of the furnaces, i.e. during start ups or when feed rates rapidly change. Currently, transient operations are managed by a combination of procedures and control model inputs. 

A further limitation of the models, particularly the EFCM, is the absence of the coupling of the two models. Coupling of the models would help in managing the semi-continuous semi-batch operation of the furnaces. This is partly rectified by the FF slag estimator which was implemented for the EFCM, however a more seamless coupling is envisaged for the two, together with a control model for the anode furnace. This naturally leads to a production scheduler which would dictate when batches are processed to improve smelter throughput. Such a scheduler would also be able to manage maintenance downtime and changes in concentrate grades. 

Challenges facing furnace process control are based on time delays, measurement error and variation. Furnace assay values are obtained with a time lag. The delay in obtaining information proves a challenge with regards to understanding process noise and preventing CRT over-activity [3]. 

Along with the question of whether spot samples are representative, there is an error involved in the measured values, be they temperature, assay or dip level. Furthermore, temperature taken when slag is tapped differs from slag temperature taken through the dip hole. Again this variation can provide challenges to any model used to control the furnaces. In the past Kalman filtering was applied to remove some error and provide more t

imely estimates of feed streams [3]. In these models no such filtering is applied. Single point measurements are used by the models when they are available. While the models will alert the CRT when a values is out of a prescribed range, no averaging or filtering is done on the measured values, except for that which is done manually by the CRT, hence the sophistication of the control applied becomes more important. 

#### 6 Conclusion 

This paper describes the development, application and results of two control models for the FF and ESF at the Olympic Dam smelter operations. The modelling is based on a steady state heat and mass balance of the processes. The main controlled parameters are the copper in slag and temperature of slag for both furnaces. For the FF a further controlled parameter is the iron to silica ratio and on the

Future improvements to the models will look at implementing dynamics of the process so that the model can be used to better predict future states of the furnaces. This is particularly relevant for transient operations around start up and shut down. In addition, a long term goal is for the coupling of the two models and the development of an anode furnace control model and production scheduler.

#### 1 Introduction 

Clyde-WorleyParsons has been developing an advanced flash furnace feed system since 2004. This paper outlines the significant developments that have been made over the last two years. These developments have been undertaken as the technology moves towards commercialization. 

Flash furnace performance relies heavily on burner flame and reaction shaft control and stability. Optimum reaction shaft control requires a feed rate that is stable and accurate within the concentr

ate flash reaction timescale. Reaction shaft residence time is typically 0.5 to 1 second. Breakthrough technology would exhibit mass feed rate stability within ±10 % of target flow at the 0.1 second timescale; availability in the market of such high stability flash furnace feed technology would enable the next level of flash furnace performance optimization and development to occur. 

Clyde-WorleyParsons has been able to demonstrate that the proprietary RotoFeed based system as currently developed is capable of delivering solid feed to the burner at ±10 % mass flow accuracy on a 0.1 second timescale. Until now no industrially available solid feed system can weigh material at this accuracy and none has the capability of delivering solid feed to meet this requirement. The Clyde-WorleyParsons feed system is capable of this level of weighing and pulseless delivery to the burner offering the opportunity of revolutionizing flash furnace operation, providing significant economic benefit through both Brownfield and Greenfield installations, due to its ease of implementation.

These have assisted the particular smelters to more fully understand the issues surrounding the control limitations in existing feed systems and the potential for enhanced performance of their facilities. The high speed pressure measurements that show the true range and rapidity of variation of furnace pressure highlight the importance of smooth consistent delivery of solid charge to the flash furnace burner. The impact of feed rate variation has been a source of ongoing investigation and development in flash furnaces for many years. 

The result of poor feed control using existing feed systems in the flash furnace is that: 

- The heat balance cannot be accurately controlled because the solid feed (fuel) is not delivered consistently leading to a unstable combustion process 

- Process chemistry is effected because of the variable solid feed delivery, with the settler region of the furnace being utilized to remedy the poor reaction shaft utilization 

- Poor use of the furnace off-gas capacity due to the large variation in settler pressure resulting from the poor delivery of solids to the reaction shaft and leading to the need to use more negative draft set-points 

With these concerns and short falls in conventional feed systems understood, Clyde-WorleyParsons was challenged by an industry leader to demonstrate the mass flow accuracy and stability of the Clyde-WorleyParsons flash furnace feed system. In response to this request Clyde-WorleyParsons has successfully completed testwork that illustrates the mass flow accuracy and stability of the feed system. 

#### 6 Results of the measurement program illustrating the accuracy of the Clyde-WorleyParsons system 

Residence time in a flash furnace reaction shaft is typically less than 0.5 seconds. In order to prove Clyde-WorleyParsons’ claim, that the feed system is accurate and stable in the context of the flame residence time, it is necessary to demonstrate accuracy of the system over a much shorter time frame. The stability criteria set by the technology group of a major flash furnace operator was an accuracy of ±10 % feed rate deviation at the 0.1 second timescale. If Clyde-WorleyParsons could achieve this accuracy, in the view of the technology group, the feed system would allow a “step change in flash furnace reaction control”. That is, flow measurements were to be made 10 times per second (10 Hz) and the flow variation had to be within ±10 % of the average flow measured. In an attempt to do this, and to show how smooth the RotoFeed flow is, a series of RotoFeed injection

#### 7 Implications of Clyde-WorleyParsons system test results 

Deploying the Clyde-WorleyParsons flash furnace feed system with its demonstrated quality of feed control on either existing or new smelting facilities can enable furnace operators to significantly improve concentrate throughput and furnace efficiency, reaping significant economic benefits in the process. 

Issues associated with the previous generation of flash furnace feed systems have been publicized by numerous sources over many years. These furnace instabilities, evidenced by fluctuating operating pressures, have been demonstrated to result from: 

- Feed flow rate pulsations and instances of flooding the screws and drag conveyors 

- Inaccurate and poor mixing of feed constituents 

- Feed mal distribution at the burner tip 

These factors generate significant variability in furnace performance, limiting optimization of furnace availability, efficiency, productivity and capacity. Despite considerable effort by operators directed towards overcoming these technology shortfalls there has been no comprehensive solution. The reason for this is the inherent unsuitability of the feed systems currently on offer for the purpose of controlling concentrate flow rate at burner and reaction timescales. 

Air slide systems have recently been deployed in some smelters to solve issues such as the furnace pressure fluctuations caused by drag chain conveyors and other upstream feed system components. However these “solutions” do not address the primary causes of feed flow instability. The current loss-in-weight screw feeder does not address the fundamental issues of: 

- Preventing feed system flooding, where aerated feed flows are uncontrolled into the burner and furnace 

- Providing positive metering of furnace feed 

- Providing effective flow rate control at the flash reaction timescale 

- Additionally these units do not address the maldistribution 

Demonstration of the Clyde-WorleyParsons system’s ability to deliver feed in a fully mixed, fully suspended, pulseless stream to a typical burner connection point with an accuracy of ±10 % measured at 0.1 second intervals represents a major addition to the proof of concept data collected so far. 

#### 8 Conclusions 

Alongside development of the feed system itself, Clyde-WorleyParsons has developed furnace measurement techniques that show operators the unfiltered behaviour of key furnace variables at the timescale of the reaction of concentrate in the flame and the reaction shaft. Data is collected at high

Add-ons to existing gravity flow feed systems can appear to be attractive, low cost “solutions”. However, none to date have addressed the root cause of feed system generated burner and furnace problems. Furnace operators have indicated that improvements expected from these systems have not materialized. Whilst cheap, these add-ons are far from low cost. In economic terms, the most expensive feed system a smelter owner can buy is one that limits performance of the furnace and, consequently, of the whole smelter investment. 

Clyde-WorleyParsons’ development of a comprehensive solution to flash furnace feed system problems takes a completely different technological approach to the previous generation of flash furnace feed systems. It positively prevents flooding from occurring, eliminates process feed pulses, inherently promotes good mixing and answers poor distribution and provides the level of feed rate stability and accuracy needed for flame and reaction control. Gravity driven loss-in-weight feed systems, and their variants, are mechanically incapable of providing the short timescale accuracy and stability of feed control needed to maximize the productive capacity of any particular flash furnace.

#### Abstract 

In the last decade, the Teniente Converter has increased notoriously and doubled its smelting copper concentrates capacity. This has been possible due to the systematic application of basic sciences and engineering disciplines, including fluid-dynamic and thermodynamic analysis to the reactor. 

In this paper a review of the physical and mathematical foundations of the T

eniente Converter which has been the basic scientific support for the sustainable increment of this smelting capacity is presented. For instance, the Teniente Converter in the Codelco Norte smelter had increased notoriously its smelting capacity up to 3000 tpd, from its standard 1500 tpd in the 23 m long and 5 m diameter reactor, validating the fundamentals of the fluid-dynamic studies. Hence, the physical, mathematical, and metallurgical rationale which have also contributed to new concepts are presented. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The Teniente Converter (TC) was conceived in the early 70s and the first unit was commissioned in 1977 [1]. This reactor (Figure 1) has been crucial for the expansion needs of Codelco-Chile. A long line of improvements and operation changes have showed that the Teniente converter is an alternative for smelting/converting operations. Currently seven units are in current operation in Chile and three are in foreigner smelters as Nkana (Zambia), Ilo (Perъ), La Caridad (Mйxico) [1].

The authors concluded that air injection with two tuyere lines reduces slopping. An injection system with two tuyere lines allows wave diminishment within the reactor, which stabilizes the metallurgical process, decreases refractory damage and permits a more extended period of operation. ### Usage of Colemanite in Copper Matte Smelting 

Aydın Rьşen, Ahmet Geveci, Yavuz Ali Topkaya 

Middle East Technical University Department of Metallurgical and Material Engineering 06531, Ankara, Turkey 

**Keywords:** Pyrometallurgy, copper matte smelting, copper losses to slag, colemanite 

#### Abstract 

In copper matte smelting, an important objective is to minimize copper losses to slag. In the present study, the aim was to reduce copper losses to slag in copper production by using a boron compound, namely; colemanite (2CaO.3B2O3.5H2O), as flux. In order to reach to this purpose, flash furnace matte and slag obtained from Eti-Bakır Co. (EBİ) were used. Chemical analyses of flash furnace matte and slag were 45.87 % Cu, 25.05 % Fe, 18.10 % S and 0.88 % Cu, 36.10 % SiO2, 36.73 % Fe, respectively. Matte and slag, with the addition of various amounts of colemanite and for different durations were equilibrated at 1250<sup>o</sup> C under nitrogen atmosphere in silica crucibles. Results showed that it was possible to decrease copper losses by accelerated separation of matte particles from slag by the addition of colemanite; this was attained by the observed increase in flash furnace slag fluidity. 

#### 1 Introduction 

In the world, copper losses to the slag in the pyrometallurgical copper production constitute a major problem [1]. Studies [2-4] on this problem indicated that mainly there are two types of copper losses to slag, namely mechanical and physic-chemical losses. The former originates from mechanically entrapped particles or floating unstable droplets of matte which do not find enough time to reach the matte layer. Mechanical losses are mainly related to the viscosity of the slag. When slag viscosity increases, mechanical copper losses also increase. The latter is related to the solubility of copper in sulphide and oxide forms in slag. In other words, copper losses are present in the slag melt as copper ions. 

In copper smelting, fluxing agents are SiO2 and limestone (CaCO3) [5]. During smelting, silica combines with FeO which comes from oxidation of iron sulfide and forms fayalite (Fe2SiO4) phase. Thus, it affects the slag structure and provides good matte and slag separation. However, this slag, along with the presence of magnetite, constitutes a more viscous (less fluid) layer. On the other

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Rьşen, Geveci, Topkaya_ 



hand, addition of calcium oxide (CaO) makes matte-slag separation easy by combining with silica and forming a neutral slag. Also, it somewhat decreases the melting point of the slag. 

Matte particles formed during melting are separated by settling from the slag due to the density difference between matte and slag. During melting, some matte particles do not find sufficient time

to reach the matte region. These particles are carried with the slag and lead to mechanical copper losses [6-9]. 

In this study, the addition of colemanite (2CaO.3B2O3.5H2O) as a flux material into the system was investigated to reduce mechanical copper losses to slag during copper matte smelting. Flash furnace matte and slag obtained from Eti-Bakır Co. (EBİ) were used in the experiments. In the steel industry, studies [10-13] on colemanite use as flux showed that its addition also decreased the viscosity of the slag and decreased the melting temperature of the system. 

#### 2 Experimental Part 

##### 2.1 Experimental Set-up 

The experimental set-up consisting of a high temperature vertical furnace and a gas cleaning system used in the present study is shown in Figure 1. Argon (Ar) and Nitrogen (N2) were used to supply inert atmosphere during the experiments to prevent oxidation of slag. They were passed through the columns of silica gel to remove any trace of moisture. The gas flow rates were controlled and monitored by using DK-800S-4 model flowmeters. Further, gases were passed through a gas control unit and also a gas washing column before entering the furnace. Argon was used only for furnace flushing. So, all experiments were performed under nitrogen atmosphere. Slag and matte were melted in silica crucibles of 30 mm ±1 mm internal diameter; 38 mm ±1 mm external diameter and 80 mm ±2 mm height manufactured by slip casting and firing method.

#### 3 Results and Discussion 

In order to determine the effect of colemanite addition and reaction duration on copper losses to slag in copper smelting, a series of experiments were carried out. In this study, matte and slag with the addition of various amounts of colemanite (0 %, 2 %, 4 % and 6 %) and in different durations (30 min, 1 h, 2 h and 4 h) were equilibrated at 1250<sup>o</sup> C under nitrogen atmosphere in silica crucibles. Results of the experiments are given in Table 3 and Figure 3. 

These results could be examined from two different aspects. One of them is the effect of reaction duration and the other is the effect of colemanite addition on copper losses to slag. 

According to the results of the melting experiments, it can be seen that the increases in the reaction duration up to 2 hours caused decreases in copper losses to slag. There were no significant decreases in copper losses to slag after 2 hours. Therefore, in the following set of experiments, duration of the melting could be limited to 2 hours. 

When considering the average melting duration which is about 4 hours in industrial flash furnace system, it is clear that colemanite addition to the system tends to shorten the equilibrium duration of the copper matte smelting.
