### Furnace Condition Assessment and Monitoring by Utilization of Innovative Non-Destructive Testing (NDT) Techniques 

Afshin Sadri, Ehsan Shameli, Pawel Gebski David George-Kennedy Hatch Ltd. Kennecott Utah Copper Smelter - Rio Tinto 2800 Speakman Drive 11600 West 2100 South, Magna, Utah 84044 Mississauga, Ontario, L5K 2R7, Canada P. O. Box 6001, Magna, Utah 84044-6001, USA 

**Keywords:** Non-Destructive Testing (NDT), refractory wear, condition monitoring, infrared, acoustic emission, acousto ultrasonic-echo (AU-E) 

#### Abstract 

For most cases, remaining thickness and quality of the refractory lining is key to continuous operation of pyrometallurgical vessels in the copper industry. Melt penetration within refractory lining can result in delamination or, in severe cases, refractory lifting within the hearth of a flash or converting furnace. Formation of cracks and delaminations in hearth, sidewalls and roof refractory lining can lead to melt infiltration and increased likelihood of run-outs. Important areas such as tapholes should be constantly monitored for refractory deterioration within the tapping channel. Better lancing or drilling practice can be developed based on the feedback from such monitoring systems leading to increased tonnage of material tapped between each rep

air. 

This paper describes application of new and innovative non-destructive testing (NDT) techniques that have been developed and applied by Hatch NDT Group on Flash Smelting, Flash Converting, Noranda / Teniente, Isasmelt and Mitsubishi process furnaces. These techniques include the acousto ultrasonic-echo (AU-E) technique, where the thickness and integrity of the refractory lining is evaluated from the cold face as the vessel is in operation. Additionally, the Taphole Acoustic Monitoring (TAM) technique, where the system is monitoring the refractory lining within the tapping channel round the clock for wear and for tapping practice improvement, is presented. 

We will introduce these AU-E and TAM techniques, their principles and data collection mechanisms and discuss selected case studies. Both techniques combine traditional means of data acquisition with state of the art signal processing, including pattern recognition based on Artificial Neural Networks. The increased computing power and access to fast communication channels via internet provide new capabilities for either periodic inspections or for continuous monitoring of operating

furnaces. In addition, we also demonstrate the use of traditional techniques such as thermography and acoustic emission (AE) leak detection that was applied nontraditionally for refractory thickness measurements and cavity detection. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The cost and production impact of unscheduled shutdowns or reduced campaign duration have led the metal smelting industry to source or develop innovative technologies to monitor furnace integrity. Among all the concerns, refractory wear and deterioration is typically the reason for termination of furnace operation. This makes the knowledge of refractory thickness and quality an essential factor for determining campaign life of a furnace. Traditionally, thermocouples and various thermal models have been used to estimate the remaining thickness of refractory in the furnace. However, due to the limited number of thermocouples typically employed and formation of local anomalies in the refractory, these methods are providing a more general assessment of the furnace rather than a localized evaluation. Alternatively, an acousto ultrasonic propagation technique was developed to determine the thickness of the remaining refractory lining in operating furnaces. The AU-E technique works based on the reflection of broadband stress wave signals from the hot face of the refractory, where the contrast in acoustic impedance causes partial or full reflection of the signals. One of the advantages of AU-E technique is its capability of detecting poor bonding, delamination and joints within the lining at the local measurement point. Wherever the thermal data are available, AU-E is used to complement the thickness calculations and wherever there are no thermocouples; AU-E can be used to map the

inner thickness of the vessel [1-3]. 

Infrared thermography has been used frequently to identify the location of “hot spots” on furnaces, converters and process vessels. To expand the use of infrared cameras, a methodology was developed to determine the remaining refractory thickness in single lined process vessels such as converters and reactors. In addition, a methodology was developed to combine the infrared thermography and acoustic emission (AE) technologies to locate voids and cavities on the inner walls of dry Electrostatic Precipitators. 

The AE technology was developed further to monitor taphole conditions. The passage of molten metal from the tapping channel was used as the steady acoustic generator and the cooling coils were used as the waveguides to be able to monitor the tapping block inner refractory lining and integrity of the copper cooling block. This innovative taphole acoustic monitoring (TAM) system was further developed to identify tapping and lancing asymmetries within the tapping channel. 

#### 2 Acousto Ultrasonic-Echo Survey 

Acousto Ultrasonic-Echo (AU-E) is a stress wave propagation technique using both time and frequency data analysis to determine thickness and quality of refractory lining in operating furnaces. A 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1124 

_Furnace Condition Assessment and Monitoring_ 



mechanical impact on the surface of the structure (via hammer or a mechanical impactor) generates a stress pulse propagating into the furnace layers. Using an impactor with a spherical or semispherical head, it generates spherical waveforms with a broad bandwidth in the ultrasonic and acoustic range. The diameter of the “impact head” dictates the range of frequencies: when the impact head is small the bandwidth is high frequency and when the impact head is large the bandwidth is low frequency. The receiver is a displacement transducer that is heat resistant and mainly detects the vertical vibrations caused by the wave reflections from hot face of the refractories.

##### 2.1 AU-E Case Studies 

For monitoring the refractory wear and integrity, AU-E of the hearth in both Flash Smelting (FSF) and Flash Converting (FCF) furnaces has been performed on a routine basis. The effort had the aim of evaluating hearth refractory integrity as well as quantifying the thickness of a working layer build-up [8]. The FSF was tested on a total of four occasions, over a period of two years. The FCF was evaluated on two occasions over the same period. 

###### 2.1.1 Flash Smelting Furnace AU-E Comparison 

With observations and physical measurements obtained from the tear-out, all the AU-E measurements were compared. Approximately 90 % of the NDT data for the FSF correlate with the physical measurements. Samples removed during the tear-out were used to recalibrate the wave speed for the working hearth brick. As a result of the impregnation, the cold wave speed increased by an average of 18 % compared to a new Mg-Cr brick used at the time of construction. This increase in the wave velocity was due to copper impregnation into the bricks. 

For the remaining 10 % inaccuracies several parameters were studied. The causes were divided in two categories: Methodology and Material. 

Methodology is where the measurements were affected by the inspection errors which is a combination of human, instrumentation, analysis and interpretation errors. The methodological errors could be resolved or improved by better inspection practice. A “baseline” inspection at the beginning of the campaign would be the best methodological inspection, where the hearth is mapped at its original state and following periodical inspections will demonstrate the degradation of the lining over the period of the campaign life. 

Material is where the refractory characteristics are affected by molten mat

erial impregnation. The chromite in Cr-Mg refractories reacts with the copper resulting in copper impregnation and replacement in the working layer. The degree of matte impregnation into the working layer refractory

Figure 3 demonstrates a typical ESP that is used for dust capture in Flash Smelting and Flash Converting furnaces. The main ESP tank is surrounded by a thick (600 mm) thermal insulator and steel shell. 

A thermographic camera in conjunction with an acoustic emission (AE) leak detector was used to detect corrosion holes behind the shell and insulator. Thermography is the use of an infrared imaging and measurement camera to "see" and "measure" thermal energy emitted from an object. Thermal, or infrared energy, is the part of the electromagnetic spectrum that we perceive as heat. Unlike visible light, in the infrared world, everything with a temperature above absolute zero emits heat. Infrared thermography cameras produce images of invisible infrared or "heat" radiation and provide precise non-contact temperature measurement capabilities. Since the holes behind the shell were transferring more heat from the ESP than the surrounding, thermal camera was used to detect the potential position of the holes behind the shell and the insulators. 

A hand held acoustic emission leak detector was used for the inspection of the ESP’s. Acoustic emission (AE) leak detector allows an operator to detect and locate holes and cavities based on emission of noise due to a failed membrane. An Acoustic Sensor mounted on the exterior surface of a structural component detects leak-associated sounds which are generated by the leak source and in turn transmitted through the structure. The leak detector (electronic instrument) amplifies the acoustical signal, filters it, and then displays the level on the front panel meter. The acoustic energy propagating from the lead source decreases in amplitude as a function of distance from the source. This is known as signal attenuation. In this case, the noise from the ESP was emitting stronger from the holes, or with less attenuation, in comparison to the other areas. By applying the AE system in a uniform grid on the shell we managed to identify the position of the holes. 

Through combination of the two techniques, rapid and accurate detection of the holes was made possible. Figure 4 demonstrates the initial thermal image that lead to further investigation by the AE system and final exposure of the hole.

#### 5 Taphole Acoustic Monitoring System 

Water-cooled copper tapblocks are amongst those furnace components that are exposed to the most extreme conditions. At the hot face inside the furnace the block is exposed to high temperature and only isolated by the layers of refractory. The temperature at the cold face varies from low, while the taphole is closed, to extremely high, during metal tapping. The inside of the block is lined with refractory inserts, forming a tapping channel through which the molten metal is tapped. These inserts wear out due to thermal and chemical deterioration and need to be replaced on a regular basis. Moreover, depending on the technology used, the taphole refractory inserts can get severely damaged during lancing or drilling on the tapping channel. 

In order to provide means for continuous monitoring of tapblocks a Taphole Acoustic Monitoring (TAM) system was developed by Hatch Ltd. This state-of-the-art tool combines the functionality of Acoustic Emission technique with Pattern Recognition (PR) based on Artificial Neural Networks (ANN). The TAM system provides real-time continuous monitoring of the tapblock integrity. The alarms and warnings inform the furnace operators of any impending hazards. Long-term data analysis and trending allows for better maintenance, while a Lancing Optimization Module feeds instructions directly to tappers to assist in achieving compliance with best practice between operators. 

The TAM system operates by evaluating the sounds generated during tapping operations. In order to monitor a single taphole, a set of Acoustic Emission sensors, typically four (4) sensors are mounted on water cooling pipes or preferably waveguides cast in the tapblock. The objective is to recognize tapping-related noise from selected areas of the tapblock, determine the location of the source of the sound within the tapblock in real-time, and to prevent excessive wear due to tapping operations in particular areas of the block by providing visual warning indications to the tapping operator. By guiding the operator to prevent off-centre tapping, the lifespan of the taphole can be extended [12-15]. 

Initially, the main purpose of the TAM system was to detect anomalous Acoustic Emission (AE) signals associated with water boiling in the cooling coils of a tapblock. This is considered as an indication of molten material penetrating between the taphole linings and approaching the cooling circuits which could lead to catastrophic failure. AE sensors were installed on both coils, two sensors per coil. Having a pair of sensors on a pipe not only allows for detecting the AE signals, but also the source of the signal can be located using a linear source location algorithm. In order to identify the acoustic signature of boiling water, a two-stage approach was used:

Acoustic Emission from the monitored taphole was recorded during normal operation of the furnace. This data collected over a period of several months was archived and analyzed in terms of the values of the critical AE parameters, including: amplitude, energy, rise time and duration of each signal. The results were correlated against temperature readings of the thermocouples embedded in the tapblock. That way, a signature indicating safe operation was established and programmed into the TAM software.

#### 6 Conclusion 

This paper presented four innovative non-destructive testing strategies for condition assessment and evaluation of smelting furnaces. The ultimate goal of the reviewed techniques is to improve the furnaces’ maintenance quality and increase campaign life. 

Traditionally, the thermal imaging method has been used in the condition assessment of the furnaces. This method is easy to implement and fairly accurate in detecting areas of significant wearing or separation in the refractory lining. The thermal imaging method is based on the principles of heat transfer and uses several assumptions in evaluating the condition of the furnace. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1138 

_Furnace Condition Assessment and Monitoring_ 



The AU-E technique is based on the wave propagation principles and uses fewer assumptions compared with the thermal imaging. This method can provide localized information about the wear, cracks, delamination, accretion, metal penetrations and impregnations of the refractory linings at the point where the measurement is conducted. Acoustic emission (AE) is a passive monitoring system that uses complex pattern recognition algorithms. AE uses the sound and its variation in emission from the source to locate and detect the deteriorated areas, very similar to thermography. Although both methods have shown a great deal of promise in the metal smelting industry, the two methods, AE and infrared thermography, can be combined and used to complement one another. One such combination has been successfully implemented in the detection of voids in an electrostatic precipitator. 

For taphole areas where the condition assessment of the tapping blocks is of critical importance, the taphole acoustic monitoring (TAM) system can offer continuous 24 hours a day / 7 days a week monitoring. Via monitoring the acoustic intensity of the tapping block, the TAM system can significantly improve tapping practice consistency. 

All the methods discussed in this article have a proven track record in condition assessment of smelting furnaces and have made significant contributions to safer and more efficient operations. Periodic inspections of these furnaces not only provide “snapshots” of current condition, but together also show the deterioration rate and critical locations vulnerable to wear. Such re

sults are frequently used for maintenance scheduling and process improvement.

#### Abstract 

PT. Smelting’s Gresik Smelter and Refinery is the first and only copper smelter and refinery in Indonesia, and has been operating since December 1998. The original plant design capacity was 200,000 t/a of LME grade-A cathode, and built at the direct construction cost of 500 million US$. Since then, the plant has undergone a series of expansions, the first one in April 2004, which increased cathode production capacity to 255,000 t/a. The second expansion was completed in August 2006, and increased cathode production capacity to 275,000 t/a. The third expansion was completed in 2009, and brings cathode production capacity to 300,000 t/a, which is 50 percent higher than the original design capacity. The total cost of all three expansions is approximately 25 million US$, and only a fraction of the original construction cost, making the expansions very cost effective. These expansions could be carried out efficiently, due to the high versatility of the Mitsubishi Process employed by the smelter, whereby process throughput was increased by conducting only some minor modifications to material handling facilities and increasing oxygen content in blowing air, while keeping the same size of furnaces and off-gas handling facilities. Therefore, the majority of expansion cost was expended on refinery plant modifications. 

This paper summarizes the various expansion projects and recent operational result of PT. Smelting.

#### 5 Expansion Project at Acid Plant 

In the smelter operation after the first expansion, feed rate was often forced to be decreased due to the high SO2 concentration in tail gas at the high stack, caused by the high SO2 load on the acid plant. This proved that the capacity of acid plant for absorbing SO2 was not enough for further expansion. To cope with this problem, a scrubber for treating the acid plant tail gas was newly installed in the second expansion project. It employed a simple and efficient desulfurizing process (CASOX Process) which was developed and designed by Chiyoda Corporation. 

In the third expansion project, the amount of catalyst in CASOX scrubber was increased so that the SO2 limitation at the outlet of acid plant could be raised while keeping SO2 emissions below the limit of 306 ppm at the high stack. Furthermore, in order to cope with the additional amount of heat generation, a SO3 cooler was installed upstream of the intermediate absorption tower. 

##### 5.1 Tail Gas Scrubber 

The flow sheet of new scrubber is shown in Figure 5. The acid plant tail gas goes through the cooling tower and the absorbing tower with catalyst, where SO2 is oxidized to SO3, absorbed into water and recovered as weak sulfuric acid. Only water is required for the operation and the weak sulfuric acid is delivered to the acid plant for making the strong sulfuric acid product. The treated gas is heated up by gas-gas heat exchanger in order to prevent the steam dew from discharging out of the high stack. The process employs complete closed-circuit system without discharging waste and is free from clogging at the catalyst layer. The operation is quite simple, easy to control and the investment is relatively small. 

The CASOX scrubber utilizes the honeycomb-shaped newly developed catalyst. Four layers of catalyst

### FSF Online Process Advisor

#### Abstract 

Outotec Process Advisor is a process control model for a Flash Smelting Furnace. The model consists of mass and heat balances for the reaction shaft, settler and uptake shaft of the furnace. The Process Advisor calculates new operating parameters from the current operating data for the furnace. Online Process Advisor automatically transfers information between the process control model, the process control system and the laboratory. 

The Online Process Advisor system is always active and alerts if changes to the operating parameters of the furnace are needed. However, the operator always has the final decision and can always overrule the system. The system provides a uniform and standardized way of operating the furnace. The system automatically takes into account the melt levels in the furnace. This can be used to predict the melt level and tapping schedule in order to optimize for example the feed rate. The system also provides a way of first simulating different parameter changes without having to directly accept them as new parameters. The Process Advisor makes it possible to stabilize process operation by ensuring correct operating parameters in order to obtain targeted melt oxidation degree. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The traditional Outotec Process Advisor program is already in use in several smelters for daily operation. The Advisor program has been delivered either as a separate package or included in the delivery if the smelter has been a brownfield/greenfield type. Most of the Process Advisors have also been updated according to customer specific requirements. The current Process Advisor reference list is shown in Table 1.

#### 2 General Description of Online Process Advisor 

The Online Process Advisor consists of a PC that contains a process control model for a flash smelting furnace, a communication software for information transfer and a user interface. These components are adjusted for customer’s furnace, process control system and laboratory. The Online Process Advisor is installed together with the Outotec HSC Chemistry program [2].

#### 4 Communication with the process control system 

The Online Process Advisor is configured for automati

c information transfer with the process control system and the laboratory. The preferred communication method between the Online Process Advisor and the process control system is OPC (OLE for Process Control). The communication is set up as a client – server type of communication. The Online Process Advisor includes a OPC Client and the process control system is expected to include a OPC Server. However, if OPC is not available, other communication options can be arranged. 

OPC is a standard specification for communication of real-time plant data between control devices from different manufacturers. The standard is maintained by the OPC Foundation. The most common OPC specification is OPC Data Access, which is used to read and write real-time data. The OPC Specification was originally based on the OLE, COM, and DCOM technologies developed by Microsoft. OPC was designed to connect Windows based software applications and process control hardware. Usually the process control devices such as PLCs (Programmable Logic Controllers) or DCSs (Distributed Control Systems) can be equipped with a OPC Server that provide a method to access process control device data from many different software packages equipped with a OPC Client [3]. 

#### 5 Conclusions 

The Online Advisor is ready for pilot installation. The actual heat and material balance model is already in use in several smelters and the additional online functionality significantly reduces the operator workload and minimizes the risk of typing errors. The melt estimate graphs gives a quick method of optimizing feed rate as well as predicting changing slag analysis according to the current process restrictions in the furnace or downstream. The automatical trending and data collection are useful tools for analysing both the calculation history and other relevant correlations between process parameters and analysis. In the future filtering algorithms for analysis data and automatic control of oxidation degree based on the dynamics of the melt will be added to the program.

### Gas-Gas Cooler as Off-Gas Duct for a Slag Cleaning Furnace: Example of HSE Progress and Engineering Excellence 

Michael Strцder Outotec GmbH Ludwig-Erhard-StraЯe 21 D-61440 Oberursel, Germany 

Miguel Palacios 

Atlantic Copper (Subsidiary of Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold) Av. Francisco Montenegro, s/n 21001 Huelva, Spain 

**Keywords:** Gas-gas cooler, off-gas, slag cleaning, off-gas duct, maintenance optimization 

#### Abstract 

When the old Slag Cleaning Electric Furnace (SCEF) at the Atlantic Copper Smelter in Huelva/Spain had to be replaced by a larger one in 1995 after 20 years in operation, the off-gas

duct was the subject of long discussions between the engineers responsible on the customer side and those on the side of the technology provider. The off-gas duct of the old furnace was a refractory lined piece of carbon steel duct leading to a wet scrubber. This off-gas duct suffered from deposition of sticky dust which mainly consisted of zinc oxide. The dust particles were extremely fine since they were generated by desublimation from the vapour phase. Consequently, the electric furnace operation had to be stopped twice or three times a week and the dust accretions had to be removed manually. This was an exhausting and dangerous maintenance work since the dust was still glowing red while being removed and workers had to wear heat protection clothing. According to the state of the art at that time, the initial engineering approach had been to replace this off-gas duct by one with a larger diameter, but with the same characteristics. The customer's expectation was therefore that the same maintenance pattern would just continue after the replacement of the entire system. However, this did not appear to be satisfactory regarding the HSE policy of Atlantic Copper. 

The technology provider was therefore faced with the challenge of developing a new type of off-gas duct which would be safer and would create less maintenance work. One possible solution was the so-called Gas-Gas Cooler which had been developed in the cement industry as an alkali bypass and successfully applied in a pyrolysis pilot plant for spent pot lining in the aluminium industry. The Gas-Gas Cooler consists of a carbon steel duct shell without refractory lining; however, it has a much larger diameter where a shield of cold gas is introduced between the duct shell and the hot and dusty off-gas strand from the furnace. By slowly mixing the cold gas and the hot off-gas a

mixing temperature is achieved which does not affect the carbon steel, and the dust is cooled down below stickiness temperature before it can reach the duct shell. However, this Gas-Gas Cooler had only been proven on a much smaller scale for a different type of dust and off-gas. 

Scale-up of the Gas-Gas Cooler was supported by Computational Flow Dynamics. Some compromises were required due to geometrical limitations of the existing smelter building. After diligent evaluation and a risk analysis the decision was taken between the customer and the technology provider to proceed with the innovative solution. 

The Gas-Gas Cooler was commissioned together with the larger slag cleaning furnace in June 1995, after a shutdown period of 6 weeks, and has been in operation since then. Since the commissioning, not a single cleaning activity to remove dust or accretions has been required in the electric furnace off-gas duct. 

#### 1 Background 

Atlantic Copper is a company dedicated to the treatment of copper concentrates and their transformation into cathodes. It

is located on the south-western coast of Spain next to the city of Huelva. The history of Atlantic Copper goes back to 1873, when a group of British bankers and businessmen bought the mines of Riotinto from the Spanish government. The Rio Tinto Company Ltd., eventually employing 14,000 workers, was established in that year of 1873. 

The starting up of the present Smelter and Copper Refinery, in Huelva, happened in 1970. In 1993 Freeport McMoRan Copper & Gold, Inc., one of the largest mining groups in the world acquired Atlantic Copper in its entirety, which represented the beginning of a new stage. In 1994 Atlantic Copper decided to concentrate on its metallurgical activity, abandoning the mining activity and investing more than 200 million USD to double the capacity of the Smelter and Refinery. This allowed for the increase in the smelting capacity of above 1 million tons per year of copper concentrates and 260,000 tons per year of cathodes. The main by-products are sulphuric acid (around 1 million t/a) and anode slimes with high concentration in gold and silver. 

#### 2 Smelting process 

The smelting process consists of an Outotec Flash Smelting Furnace in turn equipped with an electric furnace for slag cleaning, a Foster Wheeler Waste Heat Boiler and three concentrate dryers, one natural gas burning rotary kiln plus two Kvaerner steam dryers. From the Flash Smelting Furnace, two liquid phases are obtained – matte, with a copper content of 63 %, and slag with 1.2 % copper. 

The slag flows directly to the Electric Furnace through water-cooled launders. Converter slag is also treated in the Electric Furnace. The final slag, as discharged from the Electric Furnace, contains below 1 % copper; it is then granulated with water to obtain a product with various industrial

#### 3 The old SCEF uptake 

Before 1995 the off-gas generated in the Electric Furnace was gathered by an uptake for scrubbing before being evacuated into the atmosphere. The union between the stack and the furnace “flat roof” consisted of a cylindrical element, covered with castable refractory<sup>1</sup> , see Figure 1. 

The most favourable conditions of operation were those in which the furnace had a slight draft inside to avoid fugitive gas formation. The draft control of the furnace was carried out by regulating the separation of the movable part of the uptake with the Furnace roof, so that if the separation was too high, it produced a great false air intake into the stack and it was impossible to evacuate gases from the Furnace, increasing the pressure in the EF. By contrast, if the separation was too small (or even if both elements were taken), the Furnace worked with an excessive draft. Movable conduit c

The off-gas duct of the old furnace was a refractory lined piece of carbon steel duct leading to a wet scrubber. This off-gas duct suffered from deposition of sticky dust which mainly consisted of zinc oxide. The dust particles were extremely fine since they were generated by sublimation from the vapour phase. Consequently, the electric Furnace operation had to be stopped twice or three times a week and the dust accretions had to be removed manually. This was exhausting and dangerous maintenance work since the dust was still glowing red while being removed and workers had to wear heat protection clothing. 

#### 4 The “Gas-Gas Cooler” concept 

The Huelva Expansion Project of 1995 (HEP) gave Atlantic Copper not only the opportunity to increase the production capacity, but also to implant the newest existing technology. The old 11 m shell inner diameter Electric Furnace was replaced by a larger one (12.2 m), and the initial engineering approach for the off-gas duct was also to replace the old one with a larger one with the same characteristics. This approach for the new off-gas duct could lead to similar maintenance problems as in the old one. Taking this into account, Atlantic Copper made a request to the technology provider to develop a new type of off-gas duct which would create less and safer maintenance work. Many different calculations of fluid flows and various schemes and designs were carried out. One of the simplest ideas was to adapt the Gas-Gas Cooler concept which had

_Gas-Gas Cooler as Off-Gas Duct for a Slag Cleaning Furnace_ 



been developed in the cement industry as an alkali bypass to the metallurgical industry. One step had already been taken by Lurgi earlier: the Gas-Gas Cooler had been operated sucessfully for a few weeks in a pyrolysis pilot plant in Lьnen/Germany. In this pilot plant, spent potlining from the aluminium electrolysis cells were treated. However this system had only been proven on a small scale and for different dusts. 

The Gas-Gas Cooler consists of a carbon steel duct shell without refractory lining where a shield of air at ambient temperature is introduced between the duct shell and the hot and dusty off-gas stream from the Electric Furnace. 

By slowly mixing the air and the off-gas, temperature of the off-gas decreases to around 550 °C, therefore dust particles are below their stickiness temperature before they can reach the duct shell. 

#### 5 The “Gas-Gas Cooler” development and design 

In the Gas-Gas Cooler the

hot, dusty off-gas is mixed with the ambient air in a controlled way. The overall length of the Gas-Gas Cooler was chosen to 12.5 m, the main internal diameter to 2.15 m (see Figure 2). The main design criteria are 

- a) The massflow of ambient air is determined be the desired mixing temperature. The mixing temperature should be below the sintering temperature of the dust. In the case of the Atlantic Copper Electric Furnace this was estimated to be between 550 and 600 °C. By selecting 550 °C as the mixing temperature, it was also possible to design the ductwork from the Gas-Gas Cooler to the wet scrubber from a low alloy carbon steel (16Mo4) without refractory lining. 

- b) The inlet velocity of the ambient air into the Gas-Gas Cooler is selected in such a way that sufficient energy is provided to cause turbulence at the interface between the ambient air shield along the internal wall and the hot off-gas strand in the center of the Gas-Gas Cooler. The selected degree of turbulence will cause just enough mixing of the two gas flows so that the radial temperature profile at the end of the Gas-Gas Cooler does not show any differences exceeding 50 K. 

- c) The ambient air inlet geometry is determined in such a way that the ambient air layer along the internal wall is stable. This is achieved by a single tangential inlet (see Figure 3). The ambient air will move in a spiral way along the entire length of the Gas-Gas Cooler and form a protection layer between the hot off-gas strand and the wall. By means of CFD calculations it was shown that even under the assumption of an adiabatic wall there is not a single spot along the whole length of the Gas-Gas Cooler and along the entire circumference where the wall temperature exceeds the mixing temperature (see Figure 4). In reality the Gas-Gas Cooler wall is neither refractory lined inside nor heat insulated on the outside so that there is a heat flow across the wall which keeps the wall temperatures well below the calculated adiabatic wall temperatures (see Figure 5). The density of the ambient air is higher than the density of the hot off-gas. This higher density is assumed to help stabilize the rotational flow of the ambient air through the Gas-Gas Cooler.

Since the Gas-Gas Cooler had to

be integrated into the existing smelter building in Huelva, a number of compromises was necessary, e.g. 

- one elbow of 20° in the body of the Gas-Gas Cooler was necessary to avoid an interference with the existing steel structure inside the building, 

- a conical section at the bottom of the Gas-Gas Cooler was required to avoid the interference with the Electric Furnace roof and its electrode guiding equipment, 

- it was not possible to install the ambient air inlet into the Gas-Gas Cooler just at the off-gas outlet from the Electric Furnace because of the roof supporting structure. Instead, the ambient air inlet was located approx. 800 mm downstream and a water-cooled copper elbow with an inside diameter of 1500 mm was chosen as the first section of the off-gas duct. This copper elbow has achieved a lifetime of 14 years by now, not showing any signs of accretions or erosion. 

- a metallic multi-bellows expansion joint was chosen to allow for heat expansion of the Gas-Gas Cooler without exerting excessive forces into the roof of the Electric Furnace, 

- a conical section at the top of the Gas-Gas Cooler was chosen to facilitate the connection to the downstream ductwork leading to the wet scrubber. 

The ambient air is being provided by two existing air fans which had been used as Fugitive Gas Fans before the Expansion Project. The drives of those fans were connected to the emergency diesel because there was no experience about the massflow and temperature of the off-gas during a power

The draft or slightly negative pressure in the top of the Electric Furnace is now being automatically controlled by variation of the inlet guide vane position of the Induced Draft Fan downstream of the wet scrubber. The pressure drop across the wet scrubber is also automatically controlled by means of an adjustable throat in the venturi section of this scrubber. These two control loops allow for continuous good atmosphere in the smelting building and constant gas cleaning efficiency, respectively, even when the off-gas massflow varies with the batchwise operation of the Electric Furnace. 

#### 6 Operational experience 

The Gas-Gas Cooler has operated as it was predicted during the development and design phases. It actually exceeded even the most optimistic expectations: since its installation in 1995, this is after 14 years in operation, there has been no need to take any action for the cleaning and accretion removal of the Electric Furnace uptake. Even during the scheduled longer shutdowns, there has been no need to take any action to clean the insides of the Gas-Gas Cooler. From the operator’s persp

ective, the Gas-Gas Cooler has transformed what was a routine problem – the periodic cleaning of the Electric Furnace uptake several times a week – into an efficient operational performance running successfully to the extent that this issue is no longer part of the day to day concerns. 

In addition, a proper control of ingress air (introduced by a fan instead of allowing air coming into the furnace through an open slot) has led to a more consistent operation, higher efficiency of the scrubber, lower consumption of both electrode paste and electric power. 

#### 7 Conclusions 

The aim of engineers is, in general terms, to provide simple technical solutions based on a proper knowledge of sciences and their principles. The Gas-Gas Cooler represents a good example of how engineering excellence permits successful and simple solutions that require a minimum or negligible investment cost and basically zero maintenance cost.

#### 2 Improvements in P-S Converters 

##### 2.1 References 

Kumera has supplied more than 20 converters for copper and nickel smelters located in 5 countries in Europe and Asia. 

##### 2.2 Increase in Size and Capacity 

Even though the Peirce-Smith Converter was invented 100 years ago, the principle and basic structure of the converter has remained almost the same. However, the converter batch capacity, i.e., the amount of matte charged to the converter, has increased significantly and the converting process has been intensified. The production capacity of a new copper smelter is typically in the range of 200,000-400,000 t/y Cu. Installation of many small converters is not feasible for such projects, instead new large P-S converters are required while the number of furnaces and production cycle remain the same. With large converters, copper smelter operation is more feasible and the plant layout is more compact. 

In the 1960’s the converters supplied by Kumera were approximately of size in 3.7 m diameter and 7.9 m in length, while today the largest ones are of diameter 4.5 m and length 13.41 m with final blister copper amount of 310 ton each. [1, 2] 

##### 2.3 Mouth Area Design 

The converter shell is made of boiler steel plate reinforced around its mouth. The converter mouth, lined with fire-resistant cast steel, is surrounded by an apron shield which protects the shell and tuyere valves against molten copper splashes. The apron shield also reduces air leakage to the converter hood

thus preventing dilution of the sulphur dioxide gas.

##### 2.4 Furnace Supporting Structure

### The Initial Years of the O-SR Process 

F. Tanaka, O. Iida 

Mitsubishi Materials Corp. 1-3-2 Otemachi, Chiyoda-ku, 100-8117 Tokyo, Japan 

K. Kiyotani Onahama Smelting & Refining Co. Ltd. 1-1 Onahama-nagisa, 971-8101 Iwaki, Japan 

**Keywords:** Mitsubishi process, O-SR process 

#### Abstract 

Onahama-type direct-laundered process of the S-furnace and reverberatory furnaces (the O-SR process) was started up in December 2007 after carefully managed engineering projects. The projects targeted to design and construct the optimum couple of existing and newly installed furnaces such that a new S-furnace for enhancing the treatment of copper concentrates is followed by two existing reverberatory furnaces for separating matte from discard slag while incinerating combustible wastes of 15,000 tonnes per month. In contrast to the S-furnace for smelting copper matte, reverberatory furnaces are assigned the dual task, "incinerating settler." Thus, concerns have been focused mainly on the metallurgical aspects of reverberatory furnaces. Nevertheless, reverberatory furnaces were suffered from metallurgical issues because full production was launched at the startup. The atmosphere in reverberatory furnaces changed vastly depending on the cycle of receiving melts from the S-furnace and existing P-S converters, and the amount of combustible waste incinerated in reverberatory furnaces as well. Consequently, reverberatory furnaces experienced wide range of furnace conditions from zinc fuming due to over reduction to hearth build-up due to spinel precipitation in the first half of 2008. These extraordinary phenomena have been avoided and, further, the variation of the furnace atmosphere having been decreased by changing operational cycles and parameters. Improvements are, now, definite on both the operational results and the slag chemistry of reverberatory furnaces. The present paper will describe metallurgical concepts of the O-SR process, extraordinary conditions experienced in the early operations, and recent metallurgical improvements in the reverberatory furnaces. It will also demonstrate what have happened in terms of metallurgical fundamentals while the stationary reverberatory furnaces were getting active. 

#### 1 Introduction 

Onahama smelter started custom smelting of copper concentrates in 1965, emp

loying a couple of a green-charge reverberatory furnace and P-S converters. Smelting facilities were subsequently expanded to two reverberatory furnaces and five converters in 1973 in order to meet domestic demand

_Tanaka, Kiyotani, Iida_ 



of electlytic copper [1]. The oil crisis happened in the same year, however, has changed the fuelconsuming aspect of reverberatory furnaces to a serious drawback to be overcome. Such economics have long been the background of technological innovations leading to the establishment of the O- SR process. 

Innovative technologies [2-5], which developed and applied at Onahama smelter, are classified into two categories: technology to utilize alternative fuel to lower the unit cost of fuel and technology to reduce the energy required to operate reverberatory furnaces. In 1980's, a huge amount of bunker oil to heat the reverberatory furnaces was substituted with pulverized coal and scrap tires, while a part of copper concentrates was injected into the P-S converters through specially designed tuyeres in order to reduce the energy requirement in the reverberatory furnaces. Further developments were managed to utilize high calorific value of shredder residue derived from end-of-life vehicles, electric home appliances, and vending machines. Shredder residue has been incinerated in the reverberatory furnaces as an alternative fuel since 1993. As a result of the innovations above, the heat input of bunker oil in the reverberatory furnaces was reduced to 7 % of total fuel, while copper concentrates smelted in P-S converters increased to 35 % of total throughput at the end of 1990’s. 

In the last decade, social and political movement to preserve natural resources and global environment has encouraged recycling businesses to grow quickly. This movement has led to the heating up of urban mining especially in Japan under unforeseeable business circumstance. At Onahama smelter, capacity for treating shredder residue was expanded from 3000 to 12,000 metric tpm in the year 2000, while copper concentrates were smelted intensively in the P-S converters to reduce the consumption of pulverized coal. Although drastic change in the smelting process has caused hightemperature corrosion in waste heat boilers, the reverberatory furnaces have processed full capacity of shredder residue, and valuable metals included in shredder residue have been recovered effectively into molten matte [5]. Consequently, thermo-materials recycling of shredder residue has been established before the O-SR process was devised conceptually. 

Long practices at Onahama smelter have revealed that a large hearth of a reverberatory furnace is not productive for smelting copper concentrates but quite effective for incinerating combustible materials. Own technological knowledge has resulted in the design concept of the O-SR process, which consists of the optimum couple of the Mitsubishi S-furnace for smelting copper concentr

ates and existing reverberatory furnaces for incinerating combustible waste, and settling copper matte as well. The O-SR process was started up in December 2007, and then the design performance was validated in the next month. Technological development during the design work has been described previously [6], mainly from engineering aspects. 

The present paper will describe metallurgical concepts of the O-SR process, extraordinary conditions experienced in early operations, and recent metallurgical improvements in the reverberatory furnaces. It will also demonstrate what have happened in terms of metallurgical fundamentals while the stationary reverberatory furnaces were getting active.

#### 2 Process Description 

Figure 1 illustrates a schematic process-flow diagram of the O-SR process. The S-furnace is operated in the same manner as the Mitsubishi Continuous process [23]. Copper concentrates are injected into a molten bath through top blowing lances. Oxygen-enriched blow makes turbulent circulation of the bath, thereby ensuring productive smelting. Melts in the S-furnace overflow into a reverberatory furnace through a covered launder having a length of over 60 m. The flow direction is switched periodically to the other reverberatory furnace by the use of a tilting launder. In the reverberatory furnace, shredder residue is incinerated to form molten ash, which is mixed with the melts from the S-furnace. Thus, the reverberatory furnaces are expected to perform as “ _incinerating settlers_ ”. Air blast from the front wall is impinged to shredder residue to enhance incineration. A slight amount of copper concentrates is also smelted in the reverberatory furnaces because piled concentrates protect the furnace sidewall and resulting gaseous sulfur destabilizes dioxins. Matte containing 55-60 mass % of copper is tapped off into ladles and then transferred to the P-S converters to produce blister copper. Two converters are blown at one time among three hot converters. Converter slag is skimmed into ladles and recycled to the reverberatory furnaces to recover copper. 



Figure 1: Schematic process-flow diagram of the O-SR process 

#### 3 The Metallurgical Concept 

The O-SR process is the optimum combination of continuous smelting and batch-wise converting. The influence of continuous operation in the S-furnace and staged operation in the P-S converters

1201 

_Tanaka, Kiyotani, Iida_ 



are assimilated into the reverberatory furnace operation, where shredder residue is incinerated continuously. How to make homogeneous melts in the reverberatory furnaces was of prime concern in the design stage of the O-SR process. 

The most serious event expected to happen in the reverberatory operation is the precipitation of metallic iron, because practices at Onahama smelter has demonstrated strong reducing ability of shredder residue stemming f

rom its metallic components. The amount of metallic components which dissolves in matte or slag is estimated by the amount of sulphur which could be released from FeS2 (we call this "free sulphur"), and the amount oxygen which could be released from FeO1.5, (we call this "reactive oxygen"). These materials balance may follow reactions (1) and (2). 

FeS2 + 2Cu = Cu2S + FeS (1) 

2FeO1.5 + Fe = 3FeO (2) 

If iron disulfide is deficient, reaction (3) may proceed to the right-hand side instead of reaction (1). 

2Cu+ FeS = Cu2S + FeS (3) 

Therefore, solid iron will precipitate when ferric oxide is deficient in reaction (2), or when ferric oxide is not enough to compensate for the deficiency of iron disulfide. These materials balances are determined by the input of condensed materials since reverberatory furnace is a heating hearth intrinsically and oxidizing/reducing reactions are not controlled by the consumption of gaseous oxygen. 

The switching interval of melts from the S-furnace affects the sulfur-oxygen balance in the reverberatory furnaces decisively. If the switching interval is infinitely long, a reverberatory furnace receives all the melts from the S-furnace, which contains a huge amount of ferric oxide and iron disulfide. In this case, the other reverberatory furnace, which receives nothing from the S-furnace, becomes deficient of free sulfur. Figure 2 shows the oxygen balance of the reverberatory furnace receiving nothing from the S-furnace. In the lower figure, reactive oxygen supplied from converter slag is consumed from the dashed line to the solid line so that the deficiency of free sulfur is compensated. The net amount of reactive oxygen decreases with increasing matte grade in the S-furnace because the amount of converter slag decreases with increasing matte grade. As a result, reactive oxygen becomes insufficient to process 7500 metric tpm of shredder residue when matte grade is over 60 mass % Cu. The upper figure expresses the oxygen potential estimated from the Fe<sup>3+</sup> /Fe<sup>2+</sup> ratio of FeO-Fe2O3-SiO2 slag saturated with silica [7]. Solid iron separates definitely from the melts when matte grade is over 60 mass % Cu. Accordingly, the switching interval should be no too long.

##### 4.1 Zinc Fuming in the Reverberatory Furnaces 

Zinc vapor fumed constantly from the outflows of the reverberatory slag and matte during the spring of 2008. Zinc fume was visible when a reverberatory furnace did not receive melts from the S- furnace. It was also evident that zinc fume was getting thicker when a long time had passed after the inflow from the S-furnace was switched to the other reverberatory furnace. These observations implied that the melts in the reverberatory furnace were getting deficient in ferric oxide during the stopping the inflow from the S-furnace. 

Figure 4 demonstrates the oxygen potential of the outflows of a reverberatory furnace measured indirectly by oxygen concentration cells utilizing zirconia-based solid electrolyte. Upward triangles denote slag samples and downward triangles denote matte samples. Dashed lines are also drawn to illustrate the CO2/CO ratio over the melts. Since most heat radiates from combustion flames and the roof bricks in the reverberatory furnaces, the slag temperature becomes over 100 °C higher than the matte temperature. Despite such a wide range of temperature, the CO2/CO ratio gives a consistent measure to the melts containing ferrous/ferric oxides, as noted by Yazawa [9]. It is, accordingly, seen from Figure 4 that the CO2/CO ratio ranged mainly between one and five in the early operations.

[19] reported recently that chlorine-induced corrosion is accelerated greatly when dilute H2S is introduced in the atmosphere. Therefore, coherent attacking by chlorine and sulfur was the presumptive cause of the accelerated corrosion. From the discussions above, it is seen that the coherent corrosion in the early operations stemmed from reducing atmosphere in the reverberatory furnaces. From simple thermodynamic calculations by the authors and vaporization experiments by Zhang et al. [20], it is supposed that zinc vapor combined with chlorine to form ZnCl2 in the radiation section and SO2 in the furnace gas is slightly reduced to H2S. The reverberatory operations, therefore, influenced greatly on the corrosive environment in the waste heat boilers and induced the coherent corrosion on the superheter tubes. This case study implies that furnace operations and boiler conditions should be evaluated simultaneously in recycling smelters. Thus, materials technology as well as applied chemical-metallurgy is necessary to establish an innovative recycling process successfully. #### 5 Following Improvements The extraordinary conditions in the reverberatory furnaces and the waste heat boilers have been moderated greatly by modifications applied both metallurgically and mechanically. As a result, treating shredder residue of over 15,000 metric tpm has achieved in August 2008 while the design capacity of copper concentrates was fed in the S-furnace. The course of the modifications was obvious because the origin of metallurgical issues was the deficiency of reactive oxygen in the reverberatory melts. The switching interval has been shorten

ed from eight hours to four hours to decrease the variation of furnace atmosphere. Drafting capacity has also been reinforced to ventilate around the tap holes. These modifications have improved tapping practices, leading to a stabilization of furnace conditions. The operational results will be discussed from metallurgical aspects in a subsection below. 

Strategic measures have been conducted to avoid boiler failures. At first, an additional blasting port was equipped to each reverberatory furnace in order to separate the air blast into two streams so that corrosive gas is evenly distributed to two boilers. This modification has attributed to moderate the corrosive environment over boiler tubing and resulted in a considerable reduction of unscheduled repair due to boiler failures. Furthermore, a research and engineering project for updating the corrosion protection program having been executed, where materials technology has been supported fully by experts in high-temperature corrosion and protections of engineering alloys.

#### Abstract 

This paper highlights a new invention for improving slag cleaning as applied in the metal-producing industry, showing great potential above all for the non-ferrous industry. In addition, the unit is suitable for the recovery of ferro-alloys, the recycling of steel mill waste and the reconditioning of waste deposits. 

The rectangular-shaped DC furnace is equipped with large magnets for producing an intensive slag stirring due to the magneto hydrodynamic effect (MHD). Numerous parallel process phenomena cause the major part of the metal/matte to separate and sink to the bottom of the reactor. 

The fundamental principles are presented on the basis of the example of copper recovery together with the latest results of FEM and CFD simulation and pilot-scale test work, carried out for a Chilean copper producer. 

In 2010 the process principle will be demonstrated in an improved larger and more flexible pilot plant, which is installed at a European copper producer. Further areas of application will be also introduced in this paper.

Figure 3: Basic illustration of the intensive slag cleaning reactor [3] The slag is charged into the reactor continuously via a launder situated at the short side and is tapped on the opposite side via an overflow. This overflow maintains a constant bath level, eliminating the necessity for electrode control. Matte is tapped periodically. A floating coke bed on the slag surface, in contact with a graphite electrode, serves as the anode. The copper matte layer, in contact with a graphite block, is present as a liquid cathode on the furnace hearth. This provides an electric field in between the slag and the metal/matte layer. Magnetic poles are placed outside the furnace shell on the long side in the vicinity of the underside of the electrode tip (see Figure 4) and provide a strong magnetic field in this area. The resulting main Lorenz forces, occurring primarily under the electrode tip, create a strong movement of the slag and cause a stirring pattern inside the slag layer. 1216 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Latest Results of the Intensive Slag Cleaning Reactor on the Basis of Copper_ Figure 4: Velocity distribution in the liquid phase (I = 20 kA, B = 0.01) [3] The utilization of a DC electric furnace with a superimposed permanent magnetic field for treatment of slag generates a set of complex phenomena occurring in parallel. Basically, the left part of the reactor represents the reactive stirring zone whereas in the right part excellent setting conditions are present. Due to the ability to further reduce the valuable metal content and to the stirring pattern in the first zone of the furnace, the unit has the internal nickname “washing machine”. In principle, the intensive cleaning effect is caused by several overlapping effects: - Joule’s heat liberation for additional temperature increase - Additional chemical reduction => accelerated rate of reduction - Cathodic and anodic reactions => accelerated rate of reduction - Injection of alternative reduction agents such as CaC2 to accelerate the rate of reduction (option) - Enhancing of mass transfer to the reductant surface due to stirring by the magnet - Forced migration of metal/matte droplets under the electric field (electro-capillary motion phenomenon) - Coalescence of metal/matte inclusions due to the stirring - Settling caused by coalescence, resulting in larger metal/matte inclusions by gravity - Destabilizing of the emulsion of matte or metal inclusions in the slag _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1217 _Warczok, Riveros, Degel, Kunze, Kalisch, Oterdoom_ Alternatively, the principle can also be operated in batch mode following the main process steps: 1. Charging period: Filling of the furnace with the liquid discard slag 2. Stirring period: Intensive stirring with a multiple magnet system situated on the long side

of the reactor 

3. Settling period: Switching off the magnets while maintaining the power input, resulting in forced settling by gravity combined with electrocapillary motion phenomena 

4. Tapping period: Tapping of the slag and metal/matte 

#### 3 Overview of past activities regarding the intensive slag stirring reactor 

During the past years, numerous development milestones have been achieved: 

- 2000: Theoretical evaluation of the process principles 

- 2002: Extensive fundamental R+D at UDC in Chile 

- 2003: Continuous 10 kg/h tests at two test units at the UDC 

- 2005: Detailed CFD modelling to support an upscale of 1-2 t/h pilot plant and a 100 t/h industrial plant 

- 2007: Test on 1-2 t/h pilot plant at Anglo American Charges in Chile 

- 2007: Conceptual engineering completed for industrial plant 

- 2008: FEM and CFD modelling, basic and detailed engineering and manufacture of 4 t/h pilot plant 

- 2009: Supply of 4 t/h pilot plant to European Metal Producer 

In the initial project phase, a mathematical model of gravitational coalescence combined with forced slag motion showed the effective removal of copper matte inclusions from the slag. 

The results of subsequent laboratory pilot-scale tests on continuous slag cleaning showed fast slag reduction and confirmed the improved metal removal from the slag. Simulation and laboratory test results also showed great potential for use in various other non-ferrous industries. 

Subsequent complex CFD modeling demonstrated the possibilities of intensive slag motion at lower magnetic field intensity. Semi-pilot-scale tests on continuous slag cleaning showed promising results of very fast slag reduction and effective metal recovery. 

Additionally, pilot tests (1-2 t/h of slag charge) were carried out at the Anglo American plant in Chagres, Chile and demonstrated the functioning of the process principles. The tests encouraged SMS Siemag as well as one of the leading European copper producers to proceed with test work

### 3D-Refractory Engineering Using the Example of a MAERZ Tilting Furnace 

Dr. Christine Wenzl, Stefan Ruhs, Dr. Andreas Filzwieser METTOP GmbH Peter-Tunner-StraЯe 4 8700 Leoben, Austria 

Dipl.-Ing. Ladislav Koncik University of Leoben, Nonferrous Metallurgy Franz-Josef-StraЯe 18 8700 Leoben, Austria 

**Keywords:** Refractory engineering, off-gas duct, 3D model, 3D-drawing, development 

#### Abstract 

METTOP uses 3D refractory engineering to optimize refractory linings and furnace concepts. 3D refractory engineering requires a full design of all lining details during the construction and drawing stage. This is a big advantage compared to 2D refractory engineering, as cutting bricks on site can be avoided with the detailed 3D design. Consequently, time and also costs during installation can be saved. Furthermore, the 3D refractory engineering allows a step-by-step visualization of the installation procedure. This again facilitates the refractory installation. Using the example of a MAERZ tilting furnace the advantages of using 3D refractory engineering are described. 

#### 1 General 

METTOP uses 3D refractory engineering for optimization of refractory linings of different furnace types in nonferrous metallurgy, for example drum type furnaces, tilting furnaces, and shaft furnaces. Although

different smelters use the same furnace type, there are differences in steel structure and refractory, making every furnace a unique aggregate. 3D engineering allows a good visualization of the steel structure and actual lining situation, even of complex geometries, and facilitates the actual lining installation. 

In the following, the advantages of 3D refractory engineering compared to conventional 2D drawings are lined out, and visualized using the example of an Andritz MAERZ tilting furnace. 

#### 2 Description of the Andritz MAERZ Tilting Furnace 

The Andritz MAERZ tilting furnace is a well-proven aggregate in copper secondary metallurgy: it can process big tonnages and different scrap qualities. The modern refining system using several 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1233 

_Wenzl, Koncik, Ruhs, Filzwieser_ 



tuyeres, which are used to introduce oxidation air and reductant, allows rapid and efficient removal of accompanying elements from the copper by optimized introduction of reaction media below the bath level. Due to the special design the furnace can be tilted to both sides, thus providing good furnace handling and efficient operations. The furnace operations include the following process steps [1]: 

###### 1. Charging and smelting 

The furnace is charged periodically through 2 charging doors till the desired filling level is reached. Burners, which are installed on the front side of the furnace, provide the required energy for smelting by burning natural gas. After smelting the oxidation step begins. 

###### 2. Oxidation 

For oxidation the furnace is tilted by about 15° to the side of the tuyeres to position the tuyeres of the refining system below the copper bath. To prevent blocking of the tuyeres a certain air flow is applied through the tuyeres during the tilting process. Usually, oxygen-enriched air is used for refining, namely for removing the impurity elements from the copper by oxidation. The impurity oxides as well as a certain amount of copper oxide are collected in the slag phase. The oxidation time for reaching the required final copper purity is dependent on the scrap quality used and the corresponding impurity levels. The duration and extent of oxidation, namely the bath oxygen level, in turn affects the refractory lifetime. 

###### 3. Deslagging 

After oxidation, the slag contains the oxides of the removed impurities and also a certain amount of copper oxide. The slag has to be removed before the start of reduction in order to prevent a rereduction of impurities to the copper. For deslagging the furnace is tilted by about 10° to the side of the deslagging door and the slag is removed through the deslagging door. 

###### 4. Reduction 

After deslagging the reduction step starts. For reduction the furnace is again tilted into refining position with the tuyeres below the copper bath. The purpose of the reduction is to lower the oxygen content in the copper bath, which is high after oxidation, to levels suitable

for casting. A reductant, for example natural gas or oil, is introduced into the bath through the refining tuyeres to remove the oxygen. The reduction is stopped after reaching the required oxygen level. 

###### 5. Casting 

For casting operations the furnace is tilted on the casting side and the refined copper is cast into anodes, which are further processed in electrorefining, or directly into wire if the copper purity is sufficiently high. The casting velocity is controlled by the tilting angle, which can be adjusted according to the bath level in the furnace.

The main furnace components are the steel structure (Figure 1) and the refractory lining (Figure 2). The furnace can be divided into different sections, namely side walls (tuyere side, charging side), end walls (burner end wall, off-gas end wall), bottom/floor, and roof/ceiling. These sections are subjected to different conditions regarding for example molten phases, mechanical loads, and offgas, and therefore, require different refractory solutions for optimum furnace operations. The charging side is mainly lined with bricks that have a hanging or a sophisticated geometry (wedge-shaped) to keep the bricks in position during tilting of the furnace. The roof/ceiling consists of hanging bricks, which follow the curvature of the roof construction.

### Ionic Liquids – The New Way in Cooling Technology 

Dr. Christine Wenzl, Dr. Andreas Filzwieser, Dr. Iris Filzwieser, Eva Raaber 

METTOP GmbH Peter-Tunner-StraЯe 4 8700 Leoben, Austria 

**Keywords:** Cooling technology, ionic liquids, water-cooling, cooling media, refractory engineering, development 

#### Abstract 

More intense furnace operations require effective cooling in order to achieve low refractory wear and good furnace lifetimes. Hence, water-cooling is used in the most critical furnace regions. Different methods of water-cooling have been developed, the most effective being cooling elements inside of the furnace walls with water flow outside or inside the furnace wall. However, these systems have certain disadvantages. The biggest advantage of cooling elements with water flow inside the furnace wall is the cooling media water itself, as it can cause hydration problems and explosions. Hence, new developments in cooling technology have to focus on finding an alternative cooling medium. 

#### 1 Introduction 

The continuous trend towards higher process intensities in metallurgy (e.g., higher temperatures, more intense bath movement) as well as more and more complex and corrosive metallurgical phases requires new furnace solutions. The aim is to increase production and at the same time avoid excessive refractory wear. 

Because of the different requirements and interactions between refractories, cooling systems, and the furnace steelwork, all these components have to be considered for process intensification or optimization. METTOP, together with its cooperation partner Andritz-MAERZ, of

fers furnace integrity solutions, namely perfectly compatible furnace components and optimized heat up curves. 

The latest development is METTOP’s patented cooling technology with ionic liquids. 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1247 

_Wenzl, Filzwieser A., Filzwieser I., Raaber_ 



#### 2 Cooling of Furnaces in the Nonferrous Metals Industry 

Different cooling technologies for metallurgical furnaces are described in literature [1-6], for example: 

- Air cooling 

   - Natural convection 

   - Forced convection 

- Water-cooling 

   - Ripple cooling 

   - Spray cooling 

   - Water-cooling elements 

      - On the wall 

      - Inside the wall 

      - In tap holes 

The systems mentioned above can achieve different levels of heat transfer, the systems using watercooling inside the furnace wall being the most effective (about 100,000 W/m²). Water-cooling in the furnace walls can be designed with water flow inside or outside the furnace shell. In flash smelters and electric furnaces, cooling systems with water flow inside the furnace wall are well known. 

The requirements for a cooling system are heat removal to protect refractories (and therefore prolong refractory lifetime and furnace campaigns) and steel construction, as well as providing process safety. However, the latter is a critical issue when using systems with water-cooling inside the furnace wall. 

Whatever type of cooling system is used, it is essential to consider the whole furnace construction: a harmonic design of refractory and cooling system is required to achieve optimum results, namely effective cooling, good refractory protection, and long furnace campaigns. 

#### 3 Water-cooling – Today’s Standard 

There are different types of cooling systems with water flow inside the furnace wall [2, 3, 5, 7] that use different technologies for the cooling water channels: 

- Drilled channels 

- Cast-in pipes 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1248 

_Ionic Liquids – The New Way in Cooling Technology_ 



For the cast-in pipes again different materials are used, for example, Monel, pure Cu, or Cu coated with Ag or Ni. The advantage of cast-in pipes compared to drilled channels is the possibility of curvatures. It is important to avoid a gap formation between the pipe and the surrounding Cu element during the casting (and cooling) of the cooling element. However, at least as important as a good contact between pipe and Cu element is a good contact - and consequently heat transfer - between refractory and Cu element. Air gaps between the refractory and Cu element can form during operation and the corresponding thermal cycles, hence decreasing the cooling efficiency. Therefore, the cooling element has to be designed in a way to avoid this air gap formation: one possibility is the Composite Furnace Module (CFM) (Figure 1 and Figure 2). The fingers of the CFM ensure a good contact with the refractory and create a homogeneous hot face temperature, so that the refractory lifetime and f

urnace campaigns are extended. 



Figure 1: CFM cooling element – components (University of Melbourne) 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

1249 

_Wenzl, Filzwieser A., Filzwieser I., Raaber_ 





Figure 2: CFM cooling element (METTOP) 

The main problems with water as cooling medium is the medium water itself and the resulting strong cooling. Problems with water can arise both during heat up of the furnace and during operation. 

During furnace heat up, the residual water from the refractories is evaporated. Hence, the temperature during heat up of the furnace should be increased rapidly up to 200 °C, as in the temperature range between 40 and 180 °C hydration occurs, if MgO-containing refractory material is used: 

MgO+H2O → Mg(OH)2 



This reaction from periclase, MgO to brucite, Mg(OH)2 is associated with a volume increase of up to 115 %. The effects are refractory damages, ranging from cracks to the total destruction of the bricks, which can also lead to damages in the furnace structure. 

Even if the temperature is increased in a rapid way, hydration problems are likely to occur in the regions near the cooling elements. Due to the temperature of the cooling water (< 100 °C) and the resulting strong cooling, the temperature of the cooling elements is low compared to the temperature in the other parts of the furnace. Hence, the water evaporating from the refractories condenses in the region near the cooling elements, leading to hydration and associated damages. 

During operation, water leakage is a big problem: On the one hand, it can lead to the above described hydration problems when contacting the refractories, and on the other hand, it can lead to 

1250 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Ionic Liquids – The New Way in Cooling Technology_ 



explosions and severe damages when contacting the liquid copper. These explosions are a problem regarding work safety and are also an economic issue. If the damage of the furnace requires a standstill, each standstill day causes a tremendous financial loss. 

To avoid leakages and associated damages, many furnace campaigns are stopped early, to be on the safe side and to have a sufficient amount of refractory material remaining. Also this operation mode results in certain unnecessary costs, as a certain amount of refractories is wasted if the furnace is relined before it is really necessary. 

The water-cooling also has disadvantages at the tap hole cooling, e.g. in flash smelting furnaces: The strong cooling effect leads to a substantial SO2 evolution in the tapped matte due to the intense cooling and, hence, to splashing. 

Further disadvantages of water-cooling are dew point corrosion and abolition of heat. 

The H2O and SO2 (and SO3, respectively) content of the flue gasses in combination with the strong cooling effect of water can cause corrosion failures, as the temperatures drop below the dew point (i.e., the temperature at which the first liquid starts to condense from the gas phase – this te

mperature increases with higher SO2 and SO3 content, respectively) and flue gasses condense on the cooling element [7]. As a consequence, damages of the cooling elements and leakages occur. 

When using water as cooling medium the generated heat is used for steam production. However, this is not possible when the cooling is only applied in small (i.e., critical) areas or in case of subsequent installation, as the installation of a steam generator is not feasible then. Therefore, the heat is lost and wasted. 

Generally, the temperatures would not need to be that low as when using water, as for example, also a temperature of some hundred degrees would be still sufficient for forming a protective slag layer, and also dew point corrosion could be avoided with higher cooling element temperatures. 

#### 4 Alternative Cooling Media – New Ways in Cooling Technology 

As described above, the main problem of current cooling technologies is the cooling medium water itself. Hence, a new cooling medium has to be found to overcome the described disadvantages of water. 

Ionic liquids (ILs) are a promising alternative to water: They are salts with a wide liquidus range. One characteristic of these salts is their low melting points of below 100 °C or even room temperature (room temperature ionic liquids, RTIL), caused by their badly coordinated ions. ILs consist only of ions. Therefore, dislocated charging and one ion based on an organic molecule are necessary to avoid the formation of a stable crystal lattice. Important properties of ILs are [12]: 

- Non flammable 

- High ionic conductivity 

- Wide temperature range for liquid phase 

- Large electrochemical window 

- Practically no vapour pressure below decomposition temperature 

- Relatively low viscosity 

Properties like melting point, viscosity, and solubility are defined by the substituents of the organic compounds and their counterion. The dependence of the properties of the ILs on the anion/cation/substitution patterns, and which – if any – properties change in systematic ways, are still a topic of research. Cations are typically big, bulky, and asymmetric, accounting for the low melting points, whereas the anions determine the air and water stability. The melting point can easily be changed by structural variation of one of the ions or combining different ions. The structure of an ionic liquid directly affects its properties; in particular, the melting point and the liquidus range. Alkali metal chlorides result in high melting points, whereas chlor
