The combination of halide salts with Lewis acids leads to ILs with reduced melting points through the formation of eutectic compositions, complex anions being formed [9]. 

Further important properties of ILs are the size and shape of their cations. These features are very important in controlling the melting point. Symmetric cations like 1,3-dialkyl have a higher melting point in comparison to asymmetrical ones, which continue to decrease with increasing alkyl substitution, up to the critical point around eight to ten carbons, then increase with increasing additional substitution. The formation of low melting ILs results from the reduction in the magnitude of the Coulombic attraction term and distribution of packing efficiency [9]. 

The main requirements for using ILs as cooling medium are: 

- Suitable viscosity for pumping 

- No corrosion on contact with used materials (piping, heat exchanger, copper element/pipes) 

- Unproblematic behaviour on contact with liquid copper: no explosions 

- Minimum environmental damage: minimum ecologic hazard/nontoxic/environmental friendly in case of leakage in cooling system 

Generally, ILs are viscous

compared to molecular solvents and have a broad range of viscosity from 0.035 to 0.500 Nsm<sup>-2</sup> . However, the viscosity is determined by the strength of their Van-der-Waals interactions and by their tendency to form hydrogen bondings. ILs are generally divided into two classes of fluids: Newtonian fluids and Non-Newtonian fluid. Newtonian fluids have a constant viscosity regardless of strain rate, like low molecular weight pure liquids, whereas Non-Newtonian fluids do not have a constant viscosity and will either thicken or thin when strain is applied [10, 11]. 

Basically, ILs have a higher density than water. It seems that it is the physical property least sensitive to temperature variation. A great advantage of ILs is the fact that they have no measureable vapour pressure (i.e., negligible values). Their thermal stability is limited by the strength of their heteroatom-carbon and their heteroatom-hydrogen bonds, respectively. The heat capacity of several ILs was determined over a temperature range between -50 and 300 °C, and it was found that it has a relatively weak temperature dependence. Moreover, the thermal conductivity is an important quality for heat transfer applications. The effect of water contamination is significant for thermal conductivity [9, 11]. 

The general idea to use ILs as a substitute for water is to overcome the problems with water and achieve the following advantages: 

1254 

_Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 

_Ionic Liquids – The New Way in Cooling Technology_ 



- No hydration due to strong cooling 

- No hydration due to leakage 

- No explosions due to leakage 

- No dew point corrosion problems 

- No excessive cooling of tap hole (SO2 evolution and splashing) 

- Adjustable cooling 

- Steam generation from temperature difference in heat exchanger 

- New possibilities for application of cooling 

When using ionic liquids as cooling medium, the inlet temperature can be higher than when using water, for example up to 500 °C. The cooling intensity can be adjusted, also during heating up. Due to the high cooling element temperature (> 100 °C) no condensation of water vapour can occur. Consequently, the risk of refractory hydration during heating up is minimized. Hydration due to leakages can be avoided, too. 

Due to the low vapour pressure of ionic liquids there are no explosions in case of leakage and, therefore, the work safety is improved. 

The adjustable cooling is also beneficial regarding the tap hole cooling: excessive cooling and corresponding SO2 evolution and splashing can be avoided, which again improves work safety. 

Additionally the higher cooling medium temperatures that are possible with ILs help to avoid dew point corrosion and consequent damages resulting from condensing H2O and SO2 (and SO3, respectively) containing flue gasses and allow steam generation from the heat exchanger. 

The application of ILs as cooling medium extends the application of cooling systems: new possibilities for the

application of cooling are created, namely cooling of areas and devices that cannot be cooled with water as this would be too dangerous in case of failure, for example, lances in TSL reactors and applications below the bath, becomes possible. By using IL cooling for these areas and devices, their lifetime could be increased, leading to an overall process cost reduction. 

The construction, design, and calculation of cooling elements using ILs as cooling medium can be done in a similar way to the current procedure for water as cooling medium, using the material data (e.g., heat capacity) of the selected ionic liquid. 

The IL for cooling purposes has to be chosen according to the required properties, as described above. There are already some ILs available that are suitable for this application.

Cooling technology is an important aspect of furnace operations. Ionic liquids (ILs) are a promising alternative to water as cooling medium in cooling elements in metallurgical furnaces. ### Gold Extraction from Copper Ferrite Residue Produced by Oxidizing Roasting Copper Matte 

I. Wilkomirsky, E. Balladares N. Rojas University of Concepciуn

Pedagogic and Technological University Dept. of Metallurgical Engineering Boyacб Chile Colombia 

**Keywords:** Gold, silver, white metal, copper, extraction, residue, recovery, roasting 

#### Abstract 

Gold and silver can be recovered by cyanidation from the ferritic leach residue produced by a new alternative of processing copper matte or white metal. The leach residue contains mainly, cupric ferrite, hematite insolubles and the precious metals. By cyanide leaching this residue, over 95 % of gold can be extracted with solutions containing 0.06 g/l of KCN at 45 °C in 24 h. Silver extraction was less than 2.5 % for the same conditions, with significant amounts (45 %) extracted only under strong KCN concentration of 1.2 g/l. 

The low silver dissolution is the result of the roasting step of the copper white metal. Although no direct evidence of a silver-iron ferrite or silver-copper double oxide were found in the residue, results indicate that silver dissolves in the ferrite matrix, which decreases its extraction by cyanidation. 

#### 1 Introduction 

As an alternative to copper matte or white metal converting, a new process involves an initial dead roasting of the matte or white metal with air at 800 °C followed by an acid leach of the calcine with spent electrolyte from the electrowinning cells to selectively dissolve the copper oxide from the calcine. The resulting pulp is then thickened and filtered and the high purity electrolyte can be directly electrowinned to recover the copper as cathodes. 

The insoluble residue generated from the leaching step contains hematite, cupric ferrite, the precious metals, remmant sulphide and the insolubles. This residue is then cyanide leached to extract the gold and silver contained. 

The final residue, after the precious metals has been cyanide leached, still contains from 5 to 15 wt. % of copper, most of it as cupric ferrite, and can be returned to the smelting-converting cir-

For the same conditions, silver extraction is very low, with less than 0.5 % extracted. Cyanide solutions concentration has a negative effect on the gold dissolution being the highest at low concentration and the lowest (68 %) for 1.2 g/l KCN at 45 °C. The opposite effect was found for silver, with an extraction increase from 2.5 % for 0.06 g/l KCN concentration to 30 % for 1.2 g/l KCN. Temperature has a large effect on the extraction of both gold and silver, although in the opposite direction: for gold in 10 h reaction time, 25 °C and 0.06 g/l KCN extraction was 31 %. At 65 °C and the same cyanidation conditions, extractions reach 90 %. For silver, under the same condition, at 25 °C extraction was 12 %, with only 7 % at 65 °C. Copper dissolution was low in all cases with less than 8 % even under high strength KCN solutions and high temperature. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1271 _Wilkomirsky, Rojas, Balladares_ Silver appears dissolved in the cupric ferrite matrix, although no direct evidence was found of the formation of silver ferrite or silver-cupric double oxide. To achieve simultaneously high smelting temperature, long reaction time and to have a close oxygen potential control, a molten-layer reactor is been developed by the University of Concepciуn and CODELCO Divisiуn Norte. In this a new concept of smelting reactor, instead of forming a reacting flame like in flash or cyclone processes or a reacting bath like in Ausmelt or El Teniente reactors, all reaction takes place in a molten layer of material flowing by gravity along the inners walls of the reactor, which allows to have a reaction time of several minutes of the liquid phase with the gaseous atmosphere, reaching the equilibrium conditions before the metal is separated from the slag. Chilean patent application Nº3350-2008. 1285 _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1286 ### Distribution of Precious Metals between Matte and Slag and Precious Metal Solubility in Slag Katsunori Yamaguchi Iwate University Department of Materials Science and Engineering Ueda 4-3-5 Morioka, Japan **Keywords:** Iron-silicate slag, copper matte, precious metal #### Abstract There is an increasing trend in the copper smelters to recycle electronic materials, which contain relatively high concentration of precious metals. The precious metal lost in the slag is increasing with increasing of treated scrap amount. To determine the portion of the precious metals chemically dissolved and that associated with the mechanically trapped matte in the slag will be a key factor to improve the recovery of those metals. An experimental study was carried out to determine the distribution of precious metals (gold, platinum, pall

adium, rhodium, and ruthenium) between copper matte and FeOx-SiO2 slag phases and the solubility of platinum in FeOx-SiO2 slag. The distribution ratios of precious metals were measured at 1573 K and a fixed partial pressure of SO2 of 0.1 atm for the matte grades between 40 and 70 mass % of copper. It was found that the distribution ratios are around 10<sup>-2</sup> for ruthenium, 10<sup>-3</sup> for gold and platinum and palladium and 10<sup>-4</sup> for rhodium. The distribution ratios show a tendency to increase when the grade of matte is increased. 

In addition, the solubility of platinum in FeOx-SiO2 slag equilibrated with a pure platinum and the Pt-Cu alloy was determined at 1573 K and the range of oxygen partial pressure from 10<sup>-9</sup> to 10<sup>-7</sup> . The solubility of platinum in the slag tends to increase with increasing oxygen partial pressure and content of copper in the slag. 

#### 1 Introduction 

There is an increasing trend in the copper smelters to recycle electronic material scraps, which contain relatively high concentration of precious metals such as gold, platinum, palladium, rhodium, and ruthenium. As a consequence of increasing of the treated scrap amount, the precious metals lost

in the slag phase is increasing. The portion of the precious metals chemically dissolved and that associated with the mechanically trapped matte in the slag will be a key factor to improve the recovery of those metals. The distribution ratio of silver metals between iron silicate slag and Cu2S-FeS matte at 1573 K is only reported by Roghani et al. [1]. 

The present study was carried out at the oxygen-smelting conditions with _p_ SO2=0.1 atm and controlled partial pressures of O2 and S2. The distribution ratios of precious metals of gold, platinum, palladium, rhodium, and ruthenium between iron silicate slag and Cu2S-FeS matte were investigated at 1573 K. The results will indicate the lowest content of precious metals that would be expected in the industry and also give indication of the range of matte where recovery of precious metals can be optimized. 

The distribution of precious metals has been found to increase with increasing content of copper in the slag and oxygen partial pressure. The solubility of platinum in the iron silicate slag equilibrated with a pure platinum and the Pt-Cu alloy has been is investigated at 1573 K and the range of oxygen partial pressure from 10<sup>-9</sup> to 10<sup>-7</sup> controlled with CO-CO2 gas mixture. 

#### 2 Experimental Procedure 

The experimental apparatus is illustrated in Figure 1. The furnace consists of a silicon carbide heating element and an alumina reaction tube. CO-CO2-SO2 gas mixtures with a flow rate regulated at 2.5Ч10<sup>-6</sup> m<sup>3</sup> /s were used to control the partial pressures of SO2, O2 and S2. A CO gas train was equipped with soda lime and P2O5 columns to trap CO2 gas and moisture, respectively, while CO2 g

as passed through a P2O5 column. The gas mixture was introduced into the reaction chamber through an alumina tube with an inner diameter of 6Ч10-4 m and a height of 0.6 m. The partial pressures of O2, S2 and SO2 were calculated by using FactSage software [2]. The input of CO2, CO and SO2 gases and the calculated partial pressures of O2, S2 and SO2 are indicated in Table1. The experiments were made under the partial pressure of SO2 at 0.1 atm under conditions typical of oxidation of the matte by air. A total 6 g of pre-melted slag of approximate composition of 35 mass % SiO2 - 65 mass % FeOX was equilibrated with a nearly equal amount of Cu2S-FeS in a magnesia crucible with an inner diameter of 1.1Ч10-2 m and a height of 5Ч10-2 m. The master slag was synthesized in an iron crucible and the Cu2S and FeS were prepared by vacuum sealing the required metals and sulfur in a quartz tube. Temperature was controlled by a SCR controller with a Pt/Pt-Rh thermocouple. The temperature of the sample was measured by another Pt/Pt-Rh thermocouple attached to the magnesia crucible. Preliminary experiments have clarified that the equilibrium could be made in a restricted time of less than 24 hours by adjusting the Cu2S-FeS content of the starting alloy phase so that it is near in composition to that of the pre-estimated equilibrium value reported by Roghani et al _._ [1]. Sample was cooled rapidly by flushing a large amount of argon gas onto a surface of the slag layer to pre- _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1288 _Distribution of Precious Metals between Matte, Slag and Solubility in Slag_ vent the segregation of the slag components during the solidification. #### 3 Results and Discussion 

##### 3.1 Distribution of Precious Metals between Matte and FeOx-SiO2 Slag 

The experiment of iron silicate slag and Cu2S-FeS equilibrium was carried out at the oxygensmelting conditions with _p_ SO2=0.1 atm and controlled partial pressures of O2 and S2 at 1573 K. The slag separated completely from the Cu2S-FeS matte with copper content from 50 mass % to 75 mass %. The MgO content in the present slag at 1573 K was less than 8 mass %. Thus the influence of MgO in the distribution of minor elements can be considered small. 

Experimental data obtained on the copper content in the slag as a function of copper content in the matte are shown in Figure 2. As part of the fundamental study related smelting of copper sulfide and the recycle of electronic materials, the phase relation between the Cu2S-FeS melt and the iron-silicate based slag and the distribution of gold, palladium, platinum, rhodium and ruthenium between these phases in a magnesia crucible was investigated at 1573 K under controlled dimensionless _p_ SO2 at 0.1 atm and _p_ O2 and _p_ S2 in ranges between 6.3Ч10<sup>-9</sup> ~ 2.5Ч10<sup>-8</sup> and 5Ч10<sup>-4</sup> ~ 0.01 atm, respectively. 

It is suggested from the distribution ratios that precious m

etals are preferentially dissolved in the matte phase. The distribution ratio is around 10<sup>-2</sup> for Ru, 10<sup>-3</sup> for Au, Pt and Pd and 10<sup>-4</sup> for Rh. There is a clear tendency that for a grade of matte up to 60 mass % Cu, the distribution ratios increasing with increasing copper content in the matte. 

The platinum solubility in the iron silicate slag was measured under controlled _p_ O2 using a mixture of CO-CO2 gases. The platinum solubility in the slag increases with increasing oxygen partial pressure. Platinum solubility in the slag depends on the copper content in the slag platinum. Therefore, lower copper content in the slag tend to lower slag loss of the precious metals.

### Effects of SiO2, Al2O3, MgO and Na2O on Spinel Liquidus in Calcium Ferrite Slags with Cu and Fixed Po 2 

B. Zhao, P. Hayes, E. Jak C. Nexhip, D. P. George-Kennedy The University of Queensland Rio Tinto Pyrometallurgy Research Centre (PYROSEARCH) Kennecott Utah Copper LLC Brisbane, Australia Magna, Utah, USA 

**Keywords:** Liquidus temperature, calcium ferrite slag, copper converting, EPMA 

#### Abstract 

Calcium ferrite slags, with the major components Cu2O, "Fe2O3" and CaO, have been successfully applied to a number of existing continous copper-converting processes. Knowledge of phase equilibria in this slag system is important for optimal control of the furnace performance. In addition to the major components Cu2O, "Fe2O3" and CaO, variable concentrations of  SiO2, Al2O3, MgO and Na2O are also present in the copper converter slag. Accurate information on the effects of these components on liquidus temperatures in this slag system is important for optimal control of the furnace performance. Extensive investigations have been undertaken to characterise the liquidus temperatures and phase equilibria in the "Cu2O"-Fe2O3-FeO-CaO-SiO2 system. Present paper is focused on the investigation of phase equilibria in the spinel primary phase field in the range of conditions relevant to the copper converter slag at Rio Tinto Kennecott Utah Copper LLC (KUC). 

Experimental methodology has been developed based on the application of the equilibration/quenching/Electron Probe X-Ray Microanalysis (EPMA) techniques using substrates. Effects of SiO2, Al2O3, MgO and Na2O on liquidus temperatures and phase equilibria of calcium ferrite slags in spinel primary phase field have been investigated in the temperature range of 1200 to 130

0 °C and the oxygen partial pressures of 10<sup>-6.5</sup> to 10<sup>-4.5</sup> atm in equilibrium with metallic copper. 

It was found that SiO2 and MgO can significantly increase the liquidus temperature in the spinel primary phase field. Addition of up to 2 wt. % Al2O3 does not have significant effect, and addition of Na2O significantly decreases the liquidus temperature in the spinel primary phase field. Applications of the present results in industrial practice are discussed.

#### 1 Introduction 

Calcium ferrite slags have been used in continuous copper converting processes, such as the Mitsubishi and the Kennecott flash converter [1-3]. The advantages of using calcium ferrite slags in these continuous converting processes include faster reactions, greater stability of the liquid phase over solid magnetite at blister copper saturation, a lower slag volume, lower copper losses, greater fluidity, and more efficient impurity removal from the molten copper when compared to iron silicate slags [4]. 

The major components of these slags are Cu2O, CaO and iron oxides. Phase equilibrium studies in this system were initially undertaken in air and argon by Hino et al. [5]. The experiments were carried out at 1200 and 1300<sup>o</sup> C using MgO crucibles. Up to 2 wt. % MgO was found to be present in the equilibrated slag samples. In a later study Takeda investigated phase equilibria in the system “ “ “ “ CaO- FeO - Cu2O at copper saturation using magnesia crucibles [6]. The compositions of the equilibrated slags were analysed using a wet chemical assaying technique. Liquidus isotherms were constructed from 1100 to 1400<sup>o</sup> C at 50<sup>o</sup> C intervals. Magnesia was again found to be present within the liquid slag and solid phases. The magnesia concentration was dependent on the temperature and the copper oxide concentration of the slag (average MgO concentration at 1250<sup>o</sup> C was reported to be approximately 1.3 wt. % in slag and 10 wt. % in spinel). The oxygen partial pressure of the system in that study was measured using an oxygen probe. 

One of the principal difficulties in obtaining accurate chemical equilibrium data in a controlled laboratory environment is that this system is extremely aggressive chemically. The combination of liquid copper metal and calcium ferrite slags results in the chemical attack and dissolution of all known metal and refractory containment materials. In addition, low-silica calcium ferrite slags have very high fluidity, very high crystallisation rates, and therefore liquid phase in this system is very difficult to be quenched. To overcome these apparent impasses new experimental procedures have been developed by PYROSEARCH, the Pyrometallurgy Research Centre at the University of Queensland. 

The new technique, the primary phase substrate suspension technique used in the present study, involves the preparation of

substrate materials that are known, from preliminary experiments, to crystallise first during solidification of the melt. The calcium ferrite slag mixture, with excess of metallic copper powder to be equilibrated, is placed on the outside of the substrate and raised to temperature in a controlled gas atmosphere with PO2 controlled by CO2/CO or CO2/H2 gas mixtures. As the slag melts the mixture is held on the surface of the substrate by surface tension forces, forming a thin film approximately 100 µm thickness. Following equilibration the substrate and sample are released and quenched directly into water. The direct contact of the slag with the quenching medium and the thin slag film leads to rapid quenching rates, much greater than can be achieved with the use of larger samples contained in metal foil or in crucibles.

Following quenching the liquid and solid compositions that coexist in the samples under the equilibration conditions are measured using the Electron Probe X-Ray Microanalysis (EPMA). 

The equilibration of liquid metal/slag samples at high temperature using the primary phase substrate suspension technique therefore overcomes the problems of contamination and fast quenching, and enables the complex chemistries present in these systems to be characterised accurately. Using the “ “ “ “ new technique Ilyushechkin et al. investigated phase equilibria in the system CaO- Fe2O3 - Cu2O at copper saturation [7]. The experiments were carried out in the temperature range 1150-1250 °C in argon gas so that oxygen partial pressures were not controlled. Recently phase equilibria in the sys“ “ “ “ tem CaO- Fe2O3 - Cu2O at copper saturation have been investigated at under controlled oxygen partial pressures by Nikolic et al. [8]. The 1200 and 1250 °C isotherms have been experimentally determined in spinel primary phase between the oxygen partial pressures of 10<sup>-4.5</sup> to 10<sup>-6.5</sup> atm. 

SiO2, MgO, Al2O3 and Na2O are also present in significant concentrations in copper converting slags in addition to the major components Cu2O, CaO and iron oxide. The effects of these additions are important for optimal control of the process. Accretion formation and dissolution directly influence the overall furnace performance. There are no information available in literature on the effects of SiO2, MgO, Al2O3 and Na2O on the spinel liquidus in calcium ferrite slag at controlled oxygen partial pressures. The aim of this study is to provide information on the magnetite stability that can be used to directly assist and guide the selection of process conditions in plant operations. The experimental data should therefore be in the range of conditions relevant to industrial practice, and should be presented in a form that is readily used in industrial practice. 

#### 2 Experimental 

In brief, the primary phase substrate suspensio

n technique used in the present study involves the preparation of substrate materials, equilibration at high temperature and followed by quenching the sample directly into water. The compositions of the phases present in the sample are measured by the Electron Probe X-Ray Microanalysis (EPMA). 

##### 2.1 Substrate and slag preparation 

The magnetite substrate used in this project was prepared from iron foil (99.5 % Fe, 0.1 mm thickness) supplied by Goodfellow Ltd. It was first made to the shape required in the final experiment and then treated at 1100 °C in a CO-CO2 gas mixture (Po2 = 10<sup>-5</sup> atm). CaCO3 was calcined at 1100 °C in air to obtain CaO. Fe3O4 powder was obtained by grinding the magnetite prepared from Fe foil in a CO-CO2 gas mixture (Po2=10<sup>-5</sup> ) at 1100 °C. The CaO, Fe3O4, SiO2, CuO, and Cu powders were mixed to obtain the required compositions. Excess pure Cu metal powder was always added to ensure it is present in the final equilibrated samples. SiO2, Al2O3 or MgO were added when necessary for the SiO2-, Al2O3- or MgO-containing slag systems. For the Na2O-containing systems,

a master slag was prepared first to reduce the rate of vaporisation of Na2O during the equilibration experiments. The CaO, Na2CO3 and SiO2 powders were mixed in desired proportions to prepare the master slag. The pellets were placed in a platinum crucible and heated in air at 800 °C for one hour, then 850 °C for one hour and finally 1120 °C for one hour. Monitoring of the weight before and after treatment confirmed that there was no significant vaporization of Na2O during preparation of the master slag. The master slag was then ground to powder for preparation of final mixtures. The final mixtures were pelletized and attached to a Fe3O4 substrate. 

During equilibration in the presence of metallic copper a number of reactions occur including: CuO (s) + Cu (l) = Cu2O (slag) (1) 

2Cu (l) + 0.5O2 (g) = Cu2O (slag) (2) 

Fe2O3 (s)+ 2Cu (l) = Cu2O (slag) + 2FeO (slag) (3) 

Where “is“ solid, “l“ is liquid and “g“ is gas. The Cu2O concentration in the liquid slag phase changes during experiment approaching the final Cu2O determined by the Po2 in the gas phase as represented by reaction 2. The initial Cu2O bulk concentration in the sample is determined by amount of CuO, reaction 1 and amount of ferric iron to be converted to ferrous iron by reaction 3. Appropriate selection of initial slag composition is very important to obtain a successful sample for EPMA measurement. If the proportion of liquid is too low at the temperature, there will be interaction between solid and liquid during quenching so that no well quenched slag areas can be found in the final sample. If, however, too much liquid phase is formed at temperature the substrate will be dissolved into the slag and the sample will be prematurely dropped from the reaction tube during the experiment. The pro

portion of liquid in the final sample is mainly controlled by the initial mixture composition and ratio of mixture to the substrate. 

##### 2.2 Control of oxygen partial pressure 

Accurate control of the oxygen partial pressure is one of the special requirements for this study. CO-CO2-Ar gas mixtures were used to obtain the required oxygen partial pressures. In the range of Po2=10<sup>-4.5</sup> to 10<sup>-6.5</sup> atm the ratio of CO to CO2 is very small and hard to control. Diluted gas mixtures CO-Ar (20.0±0.2 mol % CO and 5.00±0.1 mol % CO) were therefore used. The actual Po2 obtained by the gas mixture was verified by oxygen probe measurements (provided by Australian Oxytrol Systems). The differences between measured and target log(Po2) are generally less than 0.06. 

##### 2.3 Equilibration 

Equilibration experiments were carried out in a vertical tube furnace with 30 mm ID recrystallised alumina reaction tube. The furnace temperature was controlled within ± 1<sup>o</sup> C. To accurately measure the sample temperature a Pt-Pt/13 % Rh thermocouple placed in an alumina sheath was located

adjacent to the sample. The thermocouple was calibrated using a reference thermocouple supplied by National Measurement Laboratory (CSIRO, Melbourne, Australia), and periodically checked against the melting point of pure gold. The overall temperature accuracy was estimated to be within ± 5 K. Approximately 0.1-0.2 grams of pelletized metal/oxides mixture were placed on the substrate, which was suspended in furnace by Pt wire. The CO-CO2-Ar gas mixture was passed through the furnace for 30 minutes in order to remove oxygen from the furnace. After flushing the sample was raised into the high temperature zone of the furnace. Most experiments have been carried out in two steps. The first step was to premelt the slag at the temperature above the liquidus. The second step was the equilibration at predetermined temperature for times long enough to achieve equilibrium. After equilibration the sample was quenched into cold water by releasing the Pt wire. 

##### 2.4 Sample examination 

The quenched samples were mounted and polished for examination. Polished samples were initially examined using an optical microscope to identify the phases present. Then the sample was coated with carbon film using a JEOL (Japan Electron Optics Ltd) Carbon Coater for electron microscopic examination. A JXA 8200 Electron Probe Microanalyser was used for further analysis. Quantitative analysis was performed at an accelerating voltage of 15 kV and a probe current of 15 nA. The Duncumb-Philibert ZAF correction procedure was applied. The standards used for analysis were from Charles M. Taylor Co. (Stanford, California): Al2O3 for Al, CuFeS2 for Cu, CaSiO3 for Ca and Si, Fe2O3 for Fe, MgO for Mg, and albite (11.46 wt. % Na2O) for Na. The average accuracy of the EP

MA measurements was estimated to be within ± 1 weight percent of the element concentration. Iron is present in the slag in both Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> forms. Copper is present in the slag in both Cu<sup>+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> forms. EPMA cannot measure Fe<sup>2+</sup> and Fe<sup>3+</sup> , or Cu<sup>+</sup> and Cu<sup>2+</sup> separately. All iron is calculated as “Fe2O3” and all copper is calculated as “Cu2O” in this article for presentation purposes. 

#### 3 Results and discussions 

The calcium ferrite slag system is a difficult chemical system to study experimentally. The new primary phase suspension experimental technique enables multi-phase equilibria to be determined at controlled temperature and oxygen potential conditions, however all experimental data points must be carefully and critically examined. 

##### 3.1 Conditions for acceptance of experimental results 

A large number of experiments have been carried out in this study. However, not all of them have been successful for a number of reasons. First, magnetite substrate was used to hold the slag sample at high temperature. The substrate also takes part in the high temperature reaction with slag. The extent of the reaction between substrate and slag depends on the slag composition and ratio of slag

to substrate. If too much liquid is formed at temperature the substrate is dissolved and the sample drops before it is equilibrated. If only a small fraction of liquid is formed there is an interaction between the liquid and substrate during quenching so that liquid is not properly quenched. Second, calcium ferrite slag is very fluid and difficult to quench. Only the liquid first in contact with water can be quenched to glass or fine microcrystalline structures. This quenched area is usually located on the surface of the sample and is small in size. Although all efforts have been made to ensure the well quenched areas of the sample are mounted on the surface of the polished section, however, in some samples it was still not possible to find a well quenched area for EPMA measurement. Lastly, metallic copper should be present within the well quenched liquid phase to be measured. Since the density of the metallic copper is much greater than that of liquid slag, at equilibration temperature the copper tends to separate from the liquid and settles on the substrate. Therefore, metallic copper may be present in the sample but not necessarily in the quenched liquid. Samples without metallic copper observed within the glass were rejected.

It had previously been reported in Kennecott converting practice that entrainment of smelting slag during matte tapping may result in high SiO2 concentration in the converting slag [3]. New practices have recently been developed at Kennecott to avoid silica contamination of matte. Increases of the SiO2 concentration in the converting slag in the past resulted in an excessive sidewall magnetite build up within the furnace so that settler volume in the furnace was significantly reduced. With the present results it is clear now that increased SiO2 concentration in slag significantly increased liquidus temperature of the converting slag. As a result, at a given operating temperature, the fraction of solid spinel was increased and built up within the furnace. Figure 12 shows correlation between CaO/Fe weight ratio and SiO2 concentration in liquid at 1250<sup>o</sup> C. It can be seen that there is linear relationship between CaO/Fe weight ratio and SiO2 concentration in liquid. If SiO2 concentration in liquid is increased, to maintain the same liquidus temperature the CaO/Fe weight ratio in the slag should be increased. This can be achieved by adding CaO flux. However, high-CaO phases such as Ca2Fe2O5 or Ca2SiO4 could be formed at high CaO/Fe weight ratios [9]. In the primary phase fields of these high-CaO phases the liquidus temperatures increase with increasing CaO/Fe weight ratios. It is very important to understand the phase equilibria in the complex caicium ferrite slag because the CaO/Fe weight ratios can have opposite effect when the slag is located in spinel primary phase field or primary phase fields of the high-CaO phases.

#### 4 Summary 

Experiments have been carried out to characterize the liquidus temperatures and phase equilibria relevant to the copper converter slag at Rio Tinto - Kennecott Utah Copper LLC (KUC) in the system CaO-

“Fe2O3”-Cu2O-SiO2-Al2O3-MgO−Na2O at controlled oxygen partial pressures and at metallic copper saturation. It was found that SiO2 and MgO can significantly increase the liquidus temperature in spinel primary phase field. Addition of up to 2 wt. % Al2O3 does not have significant effect on the liquidus temperature in spinel primary phase field. Addition of Na2O can significantly decrease the liquidus temperature in spinel primary phase field.

### Simulation Study of Intensified Flash Smelting Process 

Chen Zhuo, Wang Yunxiao, Meichi Liu Anming Central South University Jinlong Copper

Co., Ltd. School of Energy Science and Engineering Changsha, P.R. China, 410083 Tongling, P.R. China, 244021 Zhou Jun Tongling Non-ferrous Metals Group Cooperation Ltd. Tongling, P.R. China, 244000 

**Keywords:** Flash smelting, CFD simulation, reaction shaft, intensified smelting process 

#### Abstract 

The flash smelting process has been widely acknowledged as an advanced pyrometallurgical technology for its good production performance. In past decades, great successes have been achieved in equipment improvement and process intensification. However, along with expansion of furnace size and production capacity, technical problems, for instance, that unsmelted materials are found in the settler and the dust generation become increasing, are encountered more frequently. 

A coupling simulation is carried out to study the mass and heat transfer, combustion and reaction processes in a flash furnace. A steady-state numerical model of the reaction shaft and upper part of the settler is developed to simulate the velocity, temperature and species concentration of the gas phase; and a discrete phase model is included to investigate the temperature and composition changes of the concentrate particles when they move along the reaction shaft. The numerical model has been proved to be of a good accuracy, of which an error of less than 6 % is found between the simulation result and test data for the gas phase temperature in the reaction shaft. 

Comparisons are made between the intensified production process concerned in this paper and two lower-productivity processes reported in the literature. The main reason for operation difficulties confronted under intensified flash smelting process is considered to be the ignition delay of concentrate particles. As particles begin to burn and intensely react after they move along half height of the reaction shaft, they may not be fully reacted before falling down into the settler. This also explains well why the temperature of settler’s wall is found higher than before. Measures are then suggested to help accelerate the ignition of concentrate particles and improve interactions between gas and particle phases.

#### 1 Introduction 

Since its birth in 1949, flash smelting process has been gradually acknowledged as an advanced copper smelting technology for its merits of high productivity, high sulphur capture, high automation and low operational cost [1]. In past decades, great efforts have been made to tap the latent capacity of the production line. As a result, capacity of the furnace expanded continuously and productivities were doubled or even tripled. In particular, the “Four highs” operation, i.e. high feed rate, high matte grade, high oxygen enrichment, and high heat-load in the reaction shaft brought about process intensification and productivity enhancement. However, along with the upgrades in operation, technical troubles are also e

ncountered in production management and equipment maintenance, such as high dust generation, unsmelted materials piling up in the settler, furnace over-heat and more frequent equipment maintenance. 

Studies have been persistently carried out to investigate the flash smelting process for more than half a century. However, due to the limits in detection and monitor technologies, experimental research is comparatively less reported than theoretical modelling, and mainly concentrated on performance studies of part of the furnace, such as concentrate burner, particle sampling in the reaction shaft etc [2-4]. On the other hand, numerical simulation becomes an important method for research of flash smelting process because it reflects detailed information of fluid flow and metallurgical process inside the furnace, which is of great help to equipment design and improvement. In this paper, a numerical model is developed and CFD computations are carried out to investigate changes of temperature distributions and reaction process occurring in an intensified flash smelting process [5-8]. 

#### 2 Numerical model of Intensified Flash Smelting Process 

As its name indicated, an intensified flash smelting process is a process which has much higher productivity and heat intensity than its original design. The flash furnace simulated in the paper was expanded from its originally designed capacity of 100,000 tpa primary copper and currently produces 300,000 tpa primary copper. The expansion was performed by enlarging the diameter of the reaction shaft by 0.5 m whilst the settler was kept unchanged. 

To carry out a numerical simulation, a computational geometry of the flash furnace is constructed by including the concentrate burner, the reaction shaft and part of the gas passage in the settler. Considering the axi-symmetric structure of the furnace, only half part is taken as the computation domain (as shown in Figure 1). A compromise is then made between the computational accuracy and the computational time. As a result, finer grids are adopted near the concentrate burner area, and coarser grids are used in lower part of the reaction shaft and the settler; grid sizes then gradually increase along the reaction shaft. With such a grid structure, an error of less than 5 % would be ex-

In order to verify accuracy of the numerical model of flash smelting process, an industrial experiment was carried out with the same operation parameters as that in the simulation. Temperature measured in the test indicates that the numerical model has a good accuracy and provides comprehensive detailed information about the interaction and reaction between flows of gas and particle phases. ##### 3.1 Computational results ###### 3.1.1 Velocity distribution of gas flow As shown in Figure 2a, after being injected into the furnace, the process air moves down rapidly and the volume expands along the reaction shaft, thus a gas column in shape of bell jar can be found in the cross section of the reaction shaft. The central oxygen, however, emerges into the column quickly after it leaves the burner, as the momentum of the central flow is far smaller than that of the process air. The big gas column then disperses in all directions after it hits the melt surface in the settler, and changes to move upwards along the shaft wall. As a result, circumfluence is formed inside the furnace. As illustrated in Figure 2b, two circumfluences can be found in the cross section of the reaction shaft, of which one near the gas exit and one along the end wall. As the exit circumflu- _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1317 _Chen, Zhou, Wang, Liu, Meichi_ ence is stronger than that along the end wall, the gas column is pushed towards the end wall side, or even hit the shaft wall, as found in hereinafter discussed. - (a) Diagram of Velocity Contour (b) Diagram of Velocity Vector Figure 2: Diagram of velocity distribution in the cross section of computational geometry (a) velocity contour in the cross section of computational geometry, (b) velocity vector in the cross section of reaction shaft ###### 3.1.2 Temperature of gas flow In the computational results of the gas temperature (shown in Figure 3), a low temperature region of about 1m in length can be clearly found below the central concentrate burner. From 1.5 m or so from the shaft roof, the gas temperature begins to increase, and a stable high temperature region is formed in the centre of 2/3 shaft height. The highest temperature of gas phase along the shaft centre is 1667 °C, located at 5.2 m from the shaft roof, and the highest temperature along R=0.9 m (shaft radius) in the axial cross-section of the reaction shaft is 1622 °C, at a height of 4.8 m away from the shaft roof. These numbers in

dicate that the concentrate particles could not be ignited and burn as rapidly as they are supposed to be. This is, on one hand, because of the low temperature region existing below the concentrate burner. Since the combustion process is evidently delayed, particles can only be heated and react slowly; and intense smelting reactions don’t take place until particles reach the high temperature region at the lower part of the reaction shaft. On the other hand, as particles react slowly below the concentrate burner, little heat is released and it is obviously not enough to heat and ignite the bulk particles instantly. So the existence of the low temperature region and the delay in particle ignition and reaction below the concentrate burner are just two sides of coins. If any improvement can be achieved in minimizing the low temperature region, the particle ignition and reaction processes will undoubtedly be accelerated, and vice versa. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1318 _Simulation Study of Intensified Flash Smelting Process_ Figure 3: Temperature distribution in the cross section of reaction shaft Comparison has been made between computational results and studies in literatures. Figure 4 shows change of gas temperature along with the reaction shaft, or which (a) is our computation result, (b) is simulation carried out by Xie [10] for the same flash furnace simulated in the paper, but at a production capacity of 180,000 t/a, and (c) is result of work of Themlis [11] for a flash furnace with Ventury concentrate burner. Difference between figures in Figure 4 is apparent. Results of Xie and Themlis indicate that, for early flash smelting process with low and mid intensity, highest gas temperature appears at location about 1 meter away from top of the reaction shaft, with the maximum value varying with smelting intensity from a little bit higher than 1500 K in 1980s to around 1700 K in 2005. However, situation changes significantly in the high-intensity flash smelting process, especially the highest temperature point. As shown in Figure 4, the highest temperature point moves 4 meters down to 5 meters away from the shaft roof, when the production capacity is nearly doubled, and the value increases to above 1900 K. The moving-down of the highest temperature point indicates that particles begin to react intensively much later under intensified smelting conditions. This will then result in insufficient time for particles staying and reacting in the reaction shaft. As a result, some unsmelted materials may drop into the settler, continue to react and release heat, which then explains why the temperature of settler’s wall is found higher under intensified conditions. However, some particles may keep unreacted and accumulate in the settler, which is extremely undesirable in practice. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1319 _Chen, Zhou, Wang, Liu, Meichi_ 2500

As displayed in Figure 5, O2 is found highly concentrated below the concentrate burner whilst SO2 concentration increases slowly in the same area. Due to the smelting reactions are greatly influenced and restricted by the low temperature, consumption of O2 and generation of SO2 can take place only at a limited rate before particles are thoroughly heated and begin to intensively react with gases. Judged with the distributions of both O2 and SO2 concentrations, intensive smelting reactions occur after gas and particles drop along more than haft shaft height, which coincides with the results of temperature distribution. _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1320 _Simulation Study of Intensified Flash Smelting Process_ Moreover, the result of concentration distributions implies that the gas column tilts and hits the western side of the reaction shaft. The tilted gas column brings gases of not only high concentrations but also high temperature to the west. In such a case, the west wall of lower part of the reaction shaft is more likely to be damaged at high temperature and special attentions must be paid to protect the furnace linings at high temperature conditions. shaft top)|R = 2.015 m|1658|1626.28|-1.91| #### 4 Conclusions A numerical simulation has been carried out for a flash smelting process. Comparing to its original design, the production capacity of the flash furnace has been tripled, whilst the furnace structure keeps almost unchanged except that the reaction shaft is enlarged by 0.5 m in diameter. Thus the intensity of the smelting process and the heat-load are greatly increased. Simulation work then reveals that some unexpected technical difficulties may be confronted under intensified flash smelting conditions, such as high furnace temperatures, unsmelted materials found in settler, high dust generation ratio etc. All these difficulties, however, are associated with the delay of particle ignition and reaction inside the furnace. As concentrate is fed at a far higher rate into the furnace, it is more difficult to heat particles instantaneously to their ignition and reaction temperature point. The delay in ignition and reactions then seems to be unavoidable and thereupon influence the effective time of particles staying and reacting along the reaction shaft. Computational results of gas temperature and concentration fields indicate that the low temperature region below the concentrate burner and the slow reaction rate of gases and particles coincide with each other. Therefore, any improvement in minimize or eliminate the low temperature area will undoubtedly accelerate the burning and reaction process. Proposals are then given aiming at increasing gas temperature right below the concentrate burner. These include inserting an oil lance in the centre of the burner, having a blunt body to cause backflow of high temperature gas to the centre of the reaction shaft etc. Preliminary research indicates _Proceedings of Copper 2010_ 1322 _Simulation Study of Intensified Flash Smelting Process_ that the rule of “three focusings” must be followed in operation, namely focusing high temperature, focusing oxygen of high concentration and focusing particles in the same area for rapid ignition and reaction process. Moreover, careful computations are needed to optimize the structure and operation of a flash furnace, for each proposed scheme will more or less cause negative effects on the structure and operation of the flash furnace. #### References - [1] Kojo I.V., Jokilaakso A. and Hanniala P.
